chapters.title: Validation Error
chapters.html:
A note to file is what you write when you want it on record that you told someone. It carries a date and a subject line and no particular reader, and it goes into a folder where it sits unread until the day it matters, when everybody reads it at once. I have written a few hundred of them, about late fees and a dishwasher in 2D and a tenant’s ferret, and until this one I never needed anyone to believe me.

This one begins on Monday, 6 October, because that is where it began. At ten to nine that morning I was at my desk in the management office at Harwick Terrace, 114 East 31st Street, and the software that had kept the rent roll for twenty-two years was about to be switched off. RentWise 2.4 ran green letters on a black screen from a computer in the basement that I had never seen and had come to think of as plumbing. Corvane Property Group, which manages seventeen buildings, was being bought by a bigger company called Larchmont Residential Partners. Larchmont wanted a clean data room, Corvane wanted Larchmont’s check, and Tenantry 9 was the broom.

Noreen had hung the banner on Friday. It was a strip of blue vinyl with grommets, stretched across the front window in the white capitals of a gym that is about to raise its prices, and it said EMBRACE THE CHANGE.

“Today we do not mourn RentWise,” she told the room, coming out of her office at 8:45 with her lanyard chiming. Noreen Whitmore has managed Harwick Terrace since 2006. She carries fourteen keys on that lanyard and you hear her arrive the way you hear an ice-cream truck, and she keeps her hair cropped and dyed a burgundy she says is called Merlot and I believe is called something else. She was working a piece of nicotine gum. “We thank it for its service and we put it in a drawer. Dev, hon, you’re my canary.”

“Technically, the canary is the one that doesn’t make it,” I said.

“Then be a hardy one,” said Noreen, and went to refill her tea.

“Noted,” said Joyce Lim, from the cubicle by the night-drop safe, without looking up. Joyce is accounts receivable. She has a plain black bob and a calculator whose enter key has worn down to bare metal, and in all the time I had known her she had said that one word in answer to a birthday, a fire drill and the death of a tenant’s mother, meaning something a little different each time.

At the leasing desk by the window, Espie Salcedo was filming a coffee. That month her nails were pumpkin orange with a tiny black bat on each ring finger, and she held the phone at arm’s length behind a ring light clamped to her desk, an umbrella drying open on the radiator beside her. “Ok so we’re giving go-live,” she told it. “We’re giving new era, we’re giving, like, caffeine? No because, look at the foam.”

I said good morning to the room in general and sat down, and my knee met the drawer, and I said sorry. Technically it was the drawer that hit me. The desk is gray steel and came with the job, along with a chair that fits my spine better than any chair I have chosen myself and a drawer that sticks. In the drawer there was a tin of lemon drops older than my employment and a loose horn button, and I had never found a reason to throw out either. On the front counter the butterscotch dish had been topped up over the weekend, its gold cellophane going soft in the damp, a bowl of small yellow coins that nobody eats and nobody lets run out.

Tenantry does not have a button that says Check Everything. It has a button that says Run Validation Sweep, in a green meant to make you feel supported. At 8:52 I pressed it. The rent roll came up as a table of forty-one rows, each with a unit and a tenant and a balance, and a progress bar crossed the top of the screen in about four seconds while the rows turned over down the list. Each got a small green tick and a small click from the laptop speaker. I will admit that I enjoyed it. I like a column that agrees with itself.

Forty of them agreed. The forty-first sat in the middle of the fourth floor, where in thirteen months and seventeen days I had never had a reason to open it, because it was the only line on the roll that had never given me any trouble. It went red. A banner dropped from the top of the screen like a window blind.

HT-4B | Unit 4B | Tenant: OCCUPANT | Rent: $1,840.00 | Balance: 0.00 | Lease start: 01/00/1900 | FLOORPLAN_ID: (blank) | PERMIT_NO: (blank) | DOOR_COUNT: (blank)

VALIDATION ERROR. HT-4B: 3 required fields are empty. Row not valid.

I read it left to right, the way I read everything, pushing my glasses up by the taped hinge. The lease start was 01/00/1900, which is the date a database invents when it has been told nothing. The tenant was OCCUPANT, which is what a person writes when the database has beaten them to it. Three fields that every unit in the building has, a floor plan number, a permit number and a door count, were empty. I do not know what a unit without a door count is. I know what it is on a form: incomplete.

Then I did what I always do with a bad row and opened the payment history, because that is where a bad row gives itself away. The rent was $1,840.00 and the balance was nothing. Every month on the ledger, back to the first import in 2003, there was one payment of $1,840.00, received on the twentieth. No month late, no month short, no month skipped. I had forty tenants who paid on time when reminded, and one who had never needed reminding, and it was the one the new software could not find a floor for.

Behind my left shoulder a lanyard chimed, and stopped. I did not turn around. For about as long as it takes to read a banner the keys were quiet, and then they started up again and moved off. “Look at all that green,” Noreen said, to the room, and shut her door. I took it for encouragement.

Lunch & Learn is Corvane’s monthly training lunch, and that month’s topic was Tenantry. At 11:30 Noreen wheeled the conference TV out of the filing room on its cart, Espie set out two trays of wraps from Halloran’s across the street, and Brent from Tenantry appeared on the screen in a headset, his face lit from below by something on his desk, his virtual background swallowing his left ear.

“Hi team, super excited,” said Brent. “So I’m just going to do a quick refresher on data hygiene, because in Tenantry, clean data is happy data.”

He covered trailing spaces. He covered double spaces, and phone numbers with the word cell typed into them, and the sin of putting N/A in a date field. “Tenantry will accept it,” he said, “because it’s a super forgiving platform. And then it will remember.”

Espie raised a hand with a bat on it. “Can it auto-fix vibes?”

“Super question,” said Brent. “Not at this time. There’s a Notes field. Two hundred fifty-five characters.”

“So no,” said Espie, to her wrap.

“One more super important thing.” The ear went again, and came back. “Any entry over a thousand dollars needs a Source of Funds attestation. Basically Tenantry asks where the money’s coming from. It defaults to the preparer, so super easy. You won’t even see it.”

“Noted,” said Joyce.

I wrote SOURCE OF FUNDS in the margin of my handout and drew a box around it, because I write everything in the margin of the handout. It seemed an odd question to put to a rent payment, and I assumed it was somebody else’s compliance. Brent added that the sweep results posted automatically to the regional dashboard, so Randall could see where we stood at a glance. Randall Pugh is the regional director. I had met him twice, both times on a screen, both times in front of the sea.

When the questions came I put up my hand. “Technically I have one red row after the sweep. HT-4B. Three required fields blank, and a lease start of the zeroth of January nineteen hundred.”

Brent’s face did something under the lighting. “Does it have a tenant?”

“It has an Occupant.”

“Yep, OCCUPANT, that’s the placeholder. That’s a migration ghost. Super common. Just delete it.”

“It has a payment history.”

“Super common,” said Brent. “There’s a delete button top right. It’ll ask you to confirm.”

“Let’s circle back on that,” said Noreen, who had not looked up from her wrap in some time. “Brent, hon, we have so much to cover.”

“Super,” said Brent.

By half past twelve the wraps were down to the ones with cilantro, the TV was back in the filing room, and I had walked to Joyce’s cubicle with a pen in my hand for no reason. She was counting money orders into stacks of ten and squaring each stack to the edge of her blotter.

“Joyce, do you know anything about 4B?” I said, quietly, as if the safe might hear.

“Noted,” said Joyce.

I waited. She squared the stack. Then, as if she had been rude, she put it down. “Four-B pays on the twentieth. In cash. It’s in an envelope in the night drop and I put it in the bag with the rest. I’ve never asked.”

“Who’s it from?”

“I’ve never asked,” Joyce said again, a degree more gently, which for Joyce amounts to a hand on the arm. “It balances.”

She went back to her money orders. I stood there a little longer than a man with a question should, and then I printed the unit list, forty-one lines on two pages, because I trust paper to be where I left it, and took it and a ham on rye I would not eat to the elevators.

The lobby clock is six minutes slow, like every other clock in the building, and nobody has ever fixed one. It said 1:19. Harwick has two elevators, called Left and Right, and Left is the older, and on Mondays it sticks. I pressed its button anyway, being a creature of routine, and the button was warm. Not hot: warm, like a coin that has been in a pocket. The lobby was empty. The mailbox wall sits over a radiator, which I decided was the reason. Left came down with its Monday groan, opened halfway, thought about it, opened the rest, and carried me to four without incident. I mention the lack of incident because I had been braced for one.

The fourth-floor corridor runs east and west from the elevators, with maroon carpet in a diamond pattern that repeats every three feet, and doors. I turned west. The list in my hand said that along this wall, from the end of the hall, I would find 4A, then 4B, then 4C. In front of 4A a rubber mat held a pair of green hospital clogs, toes to the door, which belonged to Chioma Eze, a respiratory therapist who works nights and whose name I knew from a lease and nothing else. A blue bicycle with a bell on the handlebar leaned against the wall by 4C. Between them, where the list said B should be, there was a red cabinet with a glass front and FIRE HOSE in white capitals, the hose folded inside it like a concertina, the brass nozzle on top.

The corridor smelled of toast. Not burnt: clean and brown, the smell of bread at the moment you decide it is done. Every door in the hall was shut. I stood and listened for a toaster, a radio, a person, and heard the lights.

I would like it on record that I checked the corridor for witnesses before I started, which is how I know I felt foolish. I am a person who counts. I know my pace is thirty inches because I once walked a hallway beside a tape measure on a quiet evening, for reasons I would not defend. I put my heel against the sill of 4A and walked to 4C.

Nine. At thirty inches, that is twenty-two and a half feet, which is two eleven-foot intervals and a man’s shoe, which is how far an A should be from a C with a B between them. I mention it so the record shows the arithmetic came out. I turned around and walked back.

I reached the green clogs on the twelfth pace.

I stood there with the list in one hand. Twelve paces is thirty feet. Corridors do not grow eight feet in the time it takes a man to turn around, and I am aware of that. I did what you do. I walked to 4C again: nine. I turned. I walked back: twelve.

Then I ran a control, which is the thing I am proudest of that day. The carpet gives you a ruler for free, one diamond every three feet, and I counted diamonds both ways: seven and a bit going, seven and a bit coming. The pattern had not changed. Going out, a diamond took me a pace and a bit. Coming back it took nearly a pace and a half, and it felt, I can only say, like walking the same diamonds with a longer wait in each.

I ended in front of the cabinet, because it was in the middle and I had been walking toward and away from it for ten minutes. Up close the glass was clean, and the brass nozzle had a small paper inspection tag tied to it with string, the date punched out in a hole the size of a grain of rice. I was reading the tag when the knocks came.

They came from inside the wall, to the left of the cabinet, about the height of my chest. Two. Knuckles on plaster, unhurried, spaced the way a person knocks who knows you are in and only wants to confirm the delivery. I would like to say I stood and weighed it. I know what I did instead, which was that my right hand came up and knocked on the plaster beside the cabinet, twice, at the same interval, and then I was standing in a corridor with my fist in the air, looking at it.

Nothing came back. I listened for what I think was ten seconds. The smell of toast went out of the corridor between one breath and the next, the way a radio goes quiet in the next apartment, and the lights hummed.

“Sorry,” I said, to a fire-hose cabinet, and went down by the stairs.

In the lobby the clock said 1:54, which was two o’clock. Nobody asked where I had been. In the office Espie was filming Joyce’s shortbread tin and Joyce was not enjoying it, Noreen’s door was shut, and on my monitor the banner was exactly as red as I had left it. I sat down. I pressed my cowlick flat with my palm, and it came back up. Then I put both hands on the desk where I could see them and told no one anything.

chapters.title: Delete This Row
chapters.html:
Eleven umbrellas stood furled in the aisle of the 14 bus on Tuesday morning, held upright between knees, and by the third stop every one of them was steaming. The bus smelled of wet cardboard and somebody’s egg sandwich. When it braked on the slick road the umbrellas swung together like a committee, then swung back, dripping on the loafers of a man who watched them do it and did not move his feet.

I had the sideways seat behind the driver, my bag on my knees. The 14 takes twenty-two minutes from Kessler Avenue to the stop at 31st and Merrow. From the gate of Tolliver Court to the shelter on Kessler is twenty-two steps, which I counted in my first week there and have not stopped counting since. I have never found a use for the coincidence. I have also never found a way to stop noticing it.

That month my whole life would have fit between two stops. A studio at Tolliver Court, 3F, rent $1,125, with a window onto the dumpster enclosure. Two mugs, because the set came as two. A steel tiffin that was my mother’s, three tiers and a dent in the bottom clip, which holds rubber bands and AA batteries now. A job. It had edges you could see from the street, and I liked that, and I made a note that I liked it, and did not look at the note.

Between the third stop and the fourth the bus goes past the Gaslight, which puts a chalkboard on the sidewalk on Thursdays and, for reasons of its own, leaves it out on Tuesdays. For that block I read the advertisement over the opposite window, for a personal-injury lawyer with enormous hands. I know it well.

At the next stop someone at the back pulled the cord twice, as people do, and two chimes sounded over my head, and I found I was looking at my own hands. It was not my stop. Mine was the one after. I got off there, stepped across a gutter running the full width of the curb, and walked the last block with my umbrella held out in front of me like a man delivering it.

Noreen’s door was open when I came in at 8:31, which on a Tuesday means a conversation, and her keys were not chiming. She was standing behind her desk with the lanyard gathered in both hands, all fourteen keys in her fists so that none of them could speak.

“Close it, hon,” she said.

I closed the door and apologized to it. She let that go.

Her office is at the back of the suite, past the filing room, and holds one desk, one visitor’s chair and a plant that has outlasted two regional directors. Above the filing cabinet hangs a wooden sign in white script, LIVE LAUGH LEASE, which came from a conference along with the lanyard. Beside it is the vision board: a cork square carrying a lake with a dock, a camper trailer, a woman in a sun hat who looks as if she has never been asked a question, the word EXHALE in stick-on letters, and a yellow Post-it that said 31 MO in Noreen’s round hand.

“Sit.” She sat, and the keys came down into her lap in a heap. “Gum? No, you don’t. I’m on my ninth and it isn’t nine o’clock.”

She slid a sheet of paper across the blotter. It had been printed, which told me more than the words did. Noreen reads everything on a screen and prints only what she means to hold on to. A second Post-it was already stuck to the corner, with 4B on it, underlined once.

From: Randall Pugh | To: Noreen Whitmore | Date: Tue 7 Oct, 7:12 AM | Subject: PHANTOM UNITS: ACTION REQUIRED BY 10/31

Noreen, following Monday’s validation sweep the regional dashboard shows one non-validating line at Harwick Terrace (HT-4B). Going forward we cannot carry phantom units into the Larchmont data room. Please have the line removed ahead of the 10/31 freeze and confirm back to me. I know everyone is at capacity, so I appreciate your bandwidth. Let’s not boil the ocean on this one. Best, Randall

I read it the way I read a lease, for what it leaves out. It left out whether anyone had asked what the line was.

“He gets the sweep on a dashboard,” Noreen said. “Nobody can turn it off. I asked.”

“Technically it’s a data quality issue.”

“It’s a migration ghost, hon. They happen. You heard Brent.”

“Brent said it’s super common.”

“Brent is right about one thing a quarter and I take it where I find it.” She tapped the Post-it with a fingernail. “So you go to your desk, you click delete, you stick this on your monitor so you remember you did it, and Randall gets his green. Done by lunch.”

“It has a payment history. One payment a month, back to the import in 2003. It has never been late.”

“It doesn’t exist, hon.” She said it kindly, the way you tell a child what the vet said about the goldfish. “That’s the whole point.”

“Whose point?”

“Everybody’s. Randall’s, Larchmont’s, mine. We close clean, nobody’s phone rings, I retire in thirty-one months, and you get a very nice letter. Let’s put it in a drawer.”

“Is the delete button a drawer?”

“A drawer with a good lock.” The gum went round once. “You took a long lunch yesterday.”

“I took it upstairs.”

The gum stopped. “Upstairs.”

“With a ham on rye. I didn’t eat it.”

“Okay,” said Noreen. “Okay. Okay.” The three okays were so polite that I looked at her hands, and found they had gone back to the lanyard without my seeing it, the way you find your own hand on a railing.

For no reason I could have given, I thought of my interview. It was August of the year before, in the same visitor’s chair, with fewer cutouts on the board. She had taken me through the form: strengths, a time I had found an error, whether I minded working alone. I told her about a county that had scanned a hundred and four leases upside down. I did not mind working alone. Then she turned the form face down and asked the one question that was not on it. “Last thing, hon. If something happened and we needed to call someone about you, who would we call?”

“My sister,” I had said. “I guess.”

She wrote something in the margin of her copy and told me I would start on the nineteenth. I took it for a phone number, though she never asked me for the number.

“No worries,” I said now, which is what I say. “I’ll take a look at it.”

“Take a look,” said Noreen, “and then take it out.”

The delete button is where Brent said it would be, top right of the unit screen, small and gray, smaller than the one for Print. I sat down. The chair took my spine the way it always does. I clicked.

Delete unit HT-4B and its payment history? This action cannot be undone. Type the unit number to confirm. | (field) | CANCEL | DELETE (disabled)

I typed 4. I typed B. The DELETE button, which had been gray, turned red with a small click of its own, like a person who has been waiting by the door with a coat on. Then I did the thing I am best at, which is nothing. The cursor blinked in the field. I took my hands off the keys and put them on my knees.

“Coffee,” said Joyce. She set a mug to the left of my keyboard on a square of paper towel folded in four, which is where she puts them, and went back to her cubicle with her cardigan sleeves pushed to the elbow.

“Thank you. No worries.”

“Noted,” said Joyce, and it came out warm. I had no idea why I’d said no worries. She had only brought coffee.

I should say that I archive. I have worked with records for seven years and have never once used the delete key on one. A tenant who moves out is marked inactive. A lease that has been replaced goes to a folder called Superseded, with the date in front of its name. Espie says this is giving hoarder, and my answer, that you can always throw a thing out tomorrow and you can never throw it back, has not persuaded her. That was the reason I would have offered Noreen.

There was another, of the kind that belongs on the record once and should then be left alone. In the year before my mother was diagnosed there was a sound in her chest, a wet catch at the end of each breath at night, and my father heard it from the pillow beside hers. A doctor in Edison and then a second doctor told us it was nothing. They said so for months, and kindly. Nobody in the family stopped hearing it. We stopped saying we heard it, which is not the same thing, and the sound was exactly what it was the whole time.

I pressed CANCEL. I printed the row to a PDF, HT-4B_Oct07, and dropped it in the Archive folder, which holds a little over two hundred files and no deletions. Then I sat looking at the monitor, where the row was still red and still there, and said nothing to Joyce, who had not asked.

At half past two I told myself I was reconciling keys.

The stairs to the basement are behind the mailroom door, concrete, painted gray so many times that the edges have gone soft. The boiler lives at one end and the tenant storage cages at the other, and in between, past the laundry room and a corridor of cloth-wrapped pipes, is Rafa’s shop. It is the size of a walk-in closet. A workbench, a vise, coffee cans of screws sorted by length, a radio turned low to a station playing a song about a horse. On the pegboard above the bench hangs the key board. I had seen it once, on my first day, when Rafa gave me the tour and I was busy memorizing the exits.

Rafa Ibarra was at the bench with a toothpick in the corner of his mouth and his reading glasses, mended at the hinge with white tape, down at the end of his nose. He is broad in the forearm and slow in everything, and his left ring finger stops at the first knuckle. He held a small brass key in that hand and a rag in the other, and he was drawing the rag along the key from bow to tip, once, slowly, the way a man does a shoe on a Sunday.

“Mira,” he said, not turning around, “somebody came down from four fast yesterday.”

“I walked.”

“The door on the one landing has a closer that complains. Everybody who comes down from four fast, I hear it.”

“I wasn’t fast. I was at a normal pace.”

“From four, normal is also fast.” He laid the key on the rag. “You want something?”

“I’m doing a key reconciliation.”

“A what.”

“Every row on the roll should have a key on the board. Technically I’m counting.”

He lifted one shoulder, which in Rafa is a whole speech, and I turned to the board. It is white pegboard with the hooks in rows and a unit number stenciled under each. I counted twice, as I do. Forty-one hooks. Forty of them held a nickel key on a white fiber tag with the unit typed on it. The forty-first, stenciled 4B, was empty, and on the pegboard beneath it was a small dark ring of oil, like the mark a glass leaves on a table.

“What’s that one for?” I said, nodding at the key on his rag. The tag was green cardboard, and it had no number on it.

“It’s for the hook.”

“A key isn’t for a hook. A hook is for a key.”

“So. Then you know.”

“Rafa.”

“Depends who’s asking.”

“I’m asking. I’m the clerk.”

“Then it depends on the clerk.” He looked at me over the tape on his glasses with great sweetness. “You ate?”

“Technically I had a coffee.”

“Coffee is not eating. Coffee is a rumor.” He dug in the pocket of his tool belt, past the flashlight he never uses, and came up with a clementine. He put his thumbnail into it, and the smell filled the shop at once, bright and cold, and he handed me half. “Eat. You’re thin for a man who counts keys.”

I ate a segment. I said, “Is it a spare for something?”

“Depends—”

“Who’s asking. I know. I’m asking.”

“Have we established that?” said Rafa, gently, and he hung the brass key on the forty-first hook, in the middle of its ring of oil, where it swung once and was still. The radio finished with the horse. I stood there with a segment of clementine in my hand and a number in my head. Forty-one hooks, forty-one keys, forty doors. The count was right for the roll and wrong for the building, and the man who could have told me why was peeling the other half of a clementine for himself.

I got home at ten to seven with wet cuffs. Dinner was a pouch of rice, ninety seconds in the microwave, eaten standing at the counter beside my mother’s tiffin so as not to make a plate. Both my mugs stood on the drainer. One of them had been used that morning.

The Harwick tenant chat has thirty-eight residents in it, and the office, which is in it the way a smoke detector is in a household. Mrs Han in 5C administers it. I had muted it in my first week and I read it in the evenings, the way you read the date on a carton. This is what the morning had held.

Sook-ja Han (5C), 6:00 AM: GOOD MORNING TO ALL, INCLUDING THE QUIET ONES.

Owen Fenske (2F), 7:48 AM: genuine question. who are the quiet ones. I have lived here two years and it is not the people above me, they are NOT quiet. also the 2F dryer ate a sock

Chioma Eze (4A), 7:49 AM: Owen, leave it.

Sook-ja Han (5C), 7:52 AM: GOOD MORNING OWEN.

Owen Fenske (2F), 7:52 AM: ok good morning

I had read Mrs Han’s sentence every morning for fourteen months and filed it under courtesy, a thing said to the hard of hearing and the shy. I read Chioma’s line three times. She works nights at Merrow General, so 7:49 would have been her coming in from the walk, and I knew her from a lease and a pair of green clogs on a mat. Nobody puts a full stop on a chat message unless they mean to have the last word. I wanted to know what Owen was supposed to leave. I put the phone face down beside the tiffin and finished the rice.

At 10:40 I did what I had been not doing all day, which was open the laptop. I am a man who writes his reasons down. If I was going to leave a red row on a regional director’s dashboard after my manager had asked me, with a Post-it, to remove it, I wanted a reason on file with a date next to it, and a date needs a source. In Tenantry the source is the audit trail, a tab on every row that keeps each change, who made it and when. Tenantry does not care where you log in from; that is all the brochure meant by work anywhere. If someone had touched HT-4B during the migration over the weekend, I could say so in a sentence and be done. The row would have had a parent.

HT-4B came up red. I clicked the tab.

HT-4B | Audit trail | Record created: migrated | Last modified: 10/06 23:58 | Modified by: DMAHAJAN

Under it, in blue, was a link: Show full history. I looked at the link for some time. I had not edited HT-4B on Monday. I had opened it, and looked at it, and closed it, and looking does not leave a line. And at 23:58 on Monday I had not been at any login at all.

I did not click. I closed the laptop the way you close a drawer on something that is not yet yours to explain, washed the mug I had used, and went to bed.

At 23:58 on the sixth I had been asleep. I am always asleep by eleven.

chapters.title: Posted by Mahajan
chapters.html:
Joyce Lim was holding a five-dollar bill up to the window when I came in on Wednesday, turning it by one corner as if it might yet show her something it had been saving. It was 7:40. Rain had run down the front glass overnight and dried in tracks, and the light she held the note to came through the backward letters of EMBRACE THE CHANGE. The bill had a red seal and a red serial number, and across the top it said UNITED STATES NOTE, which I had not known they ever printed on a five. SERIES 1963, said the small type beside the portrait.

“Good morning, Joyce.”

“Noted,” said Joyce, to the bill.

I had not slept in the way that counts. At four I had decided that a man with a problem goes in early, and at 7:15 I had gone in early, and now I sat down at my desk with my coat on and my bag still on my shoulder and clicked the blue link I had not clicked the night before. Show full history.

Tenantry lays out an audit trail the way a bank statement lays out a life: newest on top, no adjectives. I counted fifteen lines.

HT-4B | Audit | 10/06 23:58 | ACKNOWLEDGED | Amount: none | Source of Funds: PREPARER | By: DMAHAJAN

HT-4B | Audit | 08/19 23:58 | RENT POSTED | Method: CASH | Amount: $1,840.00 | Source of Funds: PREPARER | By: DMAHAJAN

Between those two stood thirteen more, and they were the same line in different months. RENT POSTED, CASH, $1,840.00, on the nineteenth of every month at 23:58, from August of last year to the nineteenth of September: one for each month I had held the job, to the day. The odd one out was the fifteenth, at the top. It was Monday’s, and it had no amount. I am a man who reads verbs. RENT POSTED is something that happens to money. ACKNOWLEDGED is what you say to someone who has knocked twice.

The nineteenth of August was my first day. I know where I was at 23:58 on my first day, because it is the kind of day you remember: on top of the covers in my work shirt, worn out in a way I had mistaken for contentment. I did not need to check the other thirteen. I am asleep by eleven, and have been since college.

The Source of Funds column said PREPARER on every line, and that was the part I could not leave alone. Brent had been clear that the field was new. RentWise’s posting screen had four boxes, date and amount and method and memo, and I had used it for thirteen months; nowhere on it could a person in August have typed a word about a source. So the migration had stamped each old line with the default, which is the sort of thing a migration does, and I wrote that in the margin of a printout. Under it I wrote the other explanation, which was that the lines had said PREPARER all along. I put a question mark beside it and drew a box around the question mark.

Before the nineteenth of August the trail fell away to a single gray line reading MIGRATED, with no name next to it. Tenantry, I learned from its help page, carries across the history only of users who still hold an account, which is a rule a vendor makes by accident and a clerk lives under on purpose. Whoever had posted 4B’s rent ahead of me no longer had an account. I wrote that down too.

I opened the banking app on my phone, since that was the other place a source of funds might be hiding. Fourteen months, and not one withdrawal of eighteen hundred dollars or any piece of it. My money is a modest, well-behaved thing. It goes to Tolliver Court, the phone company and Halloran’s.

That left the possibility that someone had my password. I changed it (nineteen characters, no words, a code that goes to my phone) and sat looking at the confirmation. Next came the Corvane help desk, which has a form for Unauthorized Access, with a drop-down for Severity and a field for Affected Record. I could see the Affected Record arriving on Randall Pugh’s dashboard before lunch, in red, with a note. Randall’s remedy for HT-4B was already built into the software. It was a small gray button, top right.

At ten past eight I carried the printout to Joyce’s cubicle. The five was in a clear sleeve in her cash tray now, and she was working through money orders with her cardigan sleeves pushed to the elbow.

“The cash from 4B,” I said. “What’s in the envelope?”

“Noted.” She squared a stack against the blotter. “Twenties, mostly. Ninety of them. Then it changes. Tens, ones, a five. Some months there’s something old.”

“Old.”

“Like that.” She tipped her head at the sleeve. “September’s. The bank’s machine spat it out. The teller looked it up and said a collector would give twelve dollars for it, and asked if I’d robbed a museum.” One corner of her mouth moved. “I said I reconcile what I’m shown. I won’t bank a five that’s worth twelve, it isn’t mine to undervalue. So it sits in the tray, and the tray counts it as five.”

“Have there been others?”

“March. A silver certificate, nineteen fifty-seven, blue seal. One dollar. I banked that. A dollar is a dollar.”

“Who leaves it?”

“It’s in the drop when I open the safe on the twentieth. Plain envelope, 4B on the front in pencil.” She looked up at me. “I don’t see it come. I see it when it’s there.”

“Who did the deposits before me?”

“I do the books. Margie did the run to the bank.”

“Margie who?”

“Dunleavy.” She said it the way you read a name off a card. “Before you. She sent a Christmas card every year with a robin on it. I have it somewhere.”

She opened her second drawer, which sticks, and went through a folder of cards, then the folder behind it, then the space under the shortbread tin. Joyce has a steady pair of hands, and I watched them go faster. She took everything out and laid it on the blotter in the order it had come out, and then put it all back in the same order, and shut the drawer.

“It was here,” she said. “Noted.” The second one was addressed to nobody. “I could tell you her handwriting. Round. I couldn’t tell you what she looked like.” She looked at me. “That’s a thing to say about someone you stood next to at a safe.”

“It’s probably in a box at home.”

“Noted,” said Joyce, in the voice that means it is not.

“Is there a receipt when the cash comes in?”

“One carbon. It’s in the tray when I get in on the twenty-first. I file it with the slip.”

“Who signs it?”

“You do.”

“I don’t.”

Joyce considered me for as long as it takes a calculator to print a total. “I assumed you did it late,” she said. “Some people like to do the cash at night.” And she turned back to her money orders and counted the same stack twice, which in fourteen months I had never seen her do.

The filing room is a windowless closet with a lock Noreen never uses, three gray cabinets and a stool that tips. The receipts were in the brown accordion folder marked CASH RECEIPTS, behind BANK REC, and Joyce had filed them the way she files everything, in order, with the staples all at one angle. There were fourteen, numbered HT-4B-0819 through HT-4B-0919, thin pink carbons from a book with a red serial number in the corner.

Received of: OCCUPANT, Unit 4B | The sum of: One thousand eight hundred forty and 00/100 | For: Rent | Received by: D. Mahajan

I held the top sheet to the bulb. The D had the long back stroke I give it. The M had two peaks of unequal height. The pen had pressed harder at the end of Mahajan than at the start, because I am always hurrying to be finished with my own name, and the j had a loop in it that I would have said was not mine, except that I have made it exactly that way on birthday cards: a little more confident than the rest of me. On the July receipt the date was 7/19, and the seven wore a bar through its stem. My mother wrote hers like that, the way she had been taught in Pune, and she taught me at eight, and a teacher in Edison marked mine wrong for a year before she gave up. I cross them still. Whoever had crossed this one had learned from the same woman.

It was my handwriting and I had not been there, which is a sentence that does not belong in a filing room.

“You’re in early, hon.”

Noreen stood in the doorway with her tea in one hand and her lanyard bunched in the other, and I understood that the keys had been silent on purpose, carried the way you carry a sleeping child.

“I’m doing a reconciliation.”

Her eyes went to the folder in my hands, to the tab, 4B in Joyce’s block capitals. The gum stopped. “Good records,” she said. “That’s why I hired you.” Then, brightly, the way you draw a curtain: “Did you talk to Randall?”

“I’m reviewing the remediation path.”

“Is that a yes?”

“It’s a path.”

“Don’t let it turn into a project, hon,” said Noreen, and went off with her keys held still.

I took the contact-verification printout up to four at a quarter past nine. It was a real task: one page per unit, a box to tick beside Phone and another beside Emergency Contact, because Corvane wanted every number in Tenantry confirmed by the thirty-first and it had not occurred to anyone that a clerk might treat that as a reason to knock on a door. I started with 4A. That meant walking past the cabinet, and I did it at the speed of a man carrying a form.

Chioma Eze opened the door as far as the chain allowed, shut it, took the chain off and opened it again, which is the correct order for a woman who has been awake since yesterday afternoon. She was six feet tall in her socks. She wore a gray hospital hoodie with MERROW GENERAL RESPIRATORY across the chest and red-framed glasses, and her twists were tied up in a scarf, the ends dyed the gold of honey that has been left in the sun. The hand on the door had an old shiny burn on the inside of the wrist, about the size of a thumbprint.

“Mahajan,” she said. It was less a greeting than a spot check.

“Good morning. Sorry. It’s contact verification, for the new system. Phone and emergency contact. One minute.”

“For the record, it’s nine seventeen. I’ve been up since four p.m. yesterday. A minute from you is a long time from me.” She held out a hand. “Give.”

I gave her the page. She read down it with her lips pressed together, like a person reading a bill from a company she intends to leave. “Phone’s right. Mother’s right. That number hasn’t changed since I was nine, she’ll outlive the cell towers.” She handed it back. “Tick it.”

I ticked it. There was a pause the width of the doorway, and I used it. “Is there anything else on the unit? Maintenance, noise. There’s a Notes field. Two hundred fifty-five characters.”

“For the record, I have no complaints. The neighbors are quiet.” She pushed her glasses up with a knuckle. “Quieter than 3B’s television.”

“Which neighbors?”

She looked at me for some time. Behind her, down a short hall, a bedroom door stood open, and on the wall beside the bed there was something written in pencil, small and in rows, like a page. Then she shifted her weight and it was only a wall.

“Mahajan, don’t.”

“I only meant, technically, that on your east side there’s a fire-hose cabinet.”

“I know what’s on my east side.” She said it at the volume you would use in a library. “The radiator asks questions.”

She said it so evenly that for a moment I took it for a clause in the lease.

“What does it—”

“I work nights. Forget I said that.” The door was already moving. “Thank you for verifying me.”

The chain went on. The green clogs on the mat stayed where they were, toes to the door.

In the corridor I put my heel against the sill of 4A and walked to 4C. Fourteen. I turned and walked back and got fourteen again, and that was worse. On Monday the two directions had disagreed, and a disagreement is at least a kind of measurement. Now they had settled on a longer corridor between them, without consulting me.

The smell of toast came and went at the cabinet, like an oven door opened and closed in someone else’s kitchen. I did not knock. I did not say anything to it either, though I wanted to apologize for something, and could not have told you what.

Randall had written at 9:48.

From: Randall Pugh | To: Devendra Mahajan | Cc: Noreen Whitmore | Date: Wed 8 Oct, 9:48 AM | Subject: RE: PHANTOM UNITS: ACTION REQUIRED BY 10/31

Dev, HT-4B is still live on my dashboard. Going forward I need a date I can put against it. Can you confirm by EOD what the remediation path is and who owns it? Appreciate the bandwidth. Randall

I do my best work in the genre of the reply that says nothing. I once held off a regional vice president for eleven days over a tenant’s ferret. I wrote:

From: Devendra Mahajan | To: Randall Pugh | Cc: Noreen Whitmore | Date: Wed 8 Oct, 10:31 AM | Subject: RE: RE: PHANTOM UNITS: ACTION REQUIRED BY 10/31

Hi Randall, thank you for flagging. I am reviewing the remediation path for HT-4B and will revert with a timeline once I have confirmed the data lineage. Best, Dev

Data lineage means nothing, which is its charm. Randall answered in four minutes: Great. Let’s circle back Friday. I had bought two days. I have a method for buying days and, that morning, no idea what to spend them on.

At some point in the afternoon the office went quiet the way it does around three, when Espie is out showing 2B and Joyce’s calculator is the only thing awake, and I sat back and my knee went into the drawer, where it always goes. I said sorry to it. Then, for the first time in fourteen months, I opened it on purpose.

It stuck, and gave, with a sound like a cough. The lemon-drop tin was flat and old, with a lemon on the lid worn to a yellow smudge by other people’s thumbs. Inside were two lemon drops, fused at one edge by their own sugar. Beside the tin lay the horn button, the color of oatmeal, with four holes and a quarter inch of oatmeal thread still through one of them. It had been pulled off something, not cut.

I had assumed, the way you assume things about a chair, that whoever sat here before me had left these behind by accident. I now thought they had been left the way you leave a pot on a low flame for someone arriving late. Joyce had a name for her. Margie, who sent a robin every Christmas and did the run to the bank, had held this job, and the job had come with a chair, a drawer, a tin and, I now suspected, a standing appointment at two minutes to midnight on the nineteenth. I had believed I was hired to keep forty-one rows. I had been hired to keep one of them, and I had kept it for fourteen months without once being awake. I had been working for 4B since the morning I first sat down.

On the screen the payment history for HT-4B had a column I had never read, between Method and Balance, headed Posted by. I scrolled it from the top. D. Mahajan. D. Mahajan. D. Mahajan. Below the fourteenth the column said MIGRATED, all the way down to 2003. I have signed things I did not read: a lease, a gym contract, a consent form in a hospital corridor. Everyone has. I had never signed for something I was not there for. I put the tip of one finger against the glass at the first of the lines, where the monitor had warmed it, and it read, in Tenantry’s calm gray type, Posted by D. Mahajan, which is the sort of sentence you cannot un-sign.

chapters.title: The Quiet Ones
chapters.html:
A measuring tape came around my shoulders before the door of 3B had closed behind me, cool through my shirt, and a voice somewhere near my collarbone said, “Don’t breathe.”

I didn’t. It is the kind of instruction you take from a person with a pincushion strapped to her wrist.

Zofia Baran is four feet eleven. She wore a man’s gray cardigan with the sleeves turned back twice and a second tape around her neck as a spare, and when she spoke I could hear that two of her back teeth were missing, because her s’s came out with a small whistle in them. She read the tape where it crossed my back, took it away, ran it from my neck to my cuff, and let the end snap into its case.

“You lost two centimeter,” she said.

“Lost from what?”

“From you. Shoulder.” She wrote in a small black notebook with a rubber band around it. “August last year you come in lobby with bag. I look. Now I look again. Forty-two, forty. In fourteen month.”

“You measured me in the lobby?”

“I measure everybody in lobby. Is not rude. Is like weather.”

Her front room was her shop. A dress form stood in the window wearing half a gray suit, a black machine with gold lettering sat on a table beside a lamp, and along one wall hung a rail of garments in dry-cleaner plastic, each with a tag pinned to the collar bearing a name in pencil. A radio on low was reading the news to itself in Polish. I had come about the contact verification. I held the page out and she took it and slid it, unread, under a bolt of cloth.

“Yes, yes. Later. Come.”

Her kitchen was yellow and very small. She took a broom from behind the door and pointed its handle at the ceiling, where a brown stain the shape of a boot had been painted over twice and come back.

“Is lady,” she said. “Four step, turn, four step. Many years. Evening, mostly. When I cook, when I sew.”

“What lady?”

“Don’t know. Heel is soft. Man heel is flat.” She lowered the broom. “I ask Mrs Han. I ask super. All say, ‘Is building.’” She lifted a shoulder, and the cardigan lifted with it. “Is not normal. Is building.”

“What’s above you?”

“Four-B.” She said it the way another person would say it was raining. “You are clerk. You tell me.”

“Technically there isn’t a 4B.”

“Technically.” She pointed the broom handle at the stain again. “Then is technically very loud.”

I laughed, and then I stopped, because she hadn’t. She opened a drawer under the toaster and took out a spike with a stack of carbons on it, and drew off the third from the top. “I don’t make nothing without write. Look.”

Z. BARAN, ALTERATIONS & MADE-TO-MEASURE | Invoice 0412 | 3B, 114 East 31st Street | 14 Sept 2020 | 1 pair curtains, lined, oatmeal wool-linen, 38 x 62, for Four-B | $140.00 | PAID CASH: N. Whitmore

I read the line for Four-B three times and the name once. Whitmore is not a rare name. I had known two people who carried it, and one of them wore fourteen keys on a lanyard.

“Curtains,” I said.

“Lined. Is good cloth. Window I never see. She give me paper with numbers, thirty-eight by sixty-two, I make to number.” Zofia took the invoice back and squared it on the spike. “Is not my window.”

“My manager paid for curtains for a unit that doesn’t exist.”

“Curtains exist. I made them.” She looked at me with satisfaction, as at a hem that had come out even. “Come back six o’clock. I make soup, she walks. You hear.”

Oatmeal is the color of everything that is bought in a hurry. I thought of a button in a drawer and decided it was a color and not a clue, and I went up to five with the contact page still on its way to nobody.

Mrs Han opened the door of 5C before I could knock, which I would learn is her practice, and looked me over from my shoes upward. She is a very small woman who stands as though somebody told her to be taller and she took it as an order. She wore a quilted vest the green of a pine needle, a steel thermos in the crook of her left arm, and white hair in a bun pinned with a jade stick.

“Mr Mahajan. You are the office.”

“Technically I’m the clerk. Dev.”

“I know who you are. You muted my chat in your first week.”

“How could you—”

“I am the administrator. I see who reads and I see who does not. You read in the evenings. Seven-forty, I think. Standing.” She stepped back from the door. “Shoes.”

Her apartment was spare and warm and smelled of roasted barley. A low table, a shelf of books with cloth spines, a framed photograph of a man in a short-sleeved shirt squinting beside a rowboat, and in front of it a tea light no bigger than a thimble. She poured from the thermos into its own lid and handed it to me with both hands, and set down a plate of rice cakes dusted in roasted bean powder, and sat across from me with her back not touching the chair.

“Eat.”

I ate one. It was soft and a little sweet, and it stuck to my teeth.

“Owen asked on Tuesday who the quiet ones are,” I said. “I’ve been wondering since.”

“Everyone wonders. Only Owen asks.” She folded her hands. “Since 2013 I say good morning to this building. Six o’clock, every morning. I write the quiet ones because it covers.”

“Covers what?”

“Whoever is there.” She said it as if reading out a reference number. “Some are shy. Some are in bed. Some I do not know. Nobody in my building is not-said-good-morning to.”

I decided not to ask what had happened in 2013. It had the look of a date with a door behind it.

From the pocket of the vest she drew a tablet in a cover the color of a tangerine and held it where I could see. It was the group chat, the whole thread, a long column of her capitals. She touched a corner and a list came up.

Harwick Terrace Residents | Admin: Sook-ja Han | Members: 40 | 4B | Added by: no record | Messages sent: 0 | Seen: every message

I had muted that chat for fourteen months and never opened the member list, and had told myself the building held thirty-eight residents and an office. I counted again. Thirty-eight, the office, and one more at the very top, where the numerals sort ahead of the letters: 4B, with a gray circle where a face should be.

“I did not add that one,” said Mrs Han.

“Then who—”

“Someone who wished to be added. I did not remove it.” She turned the tablet back toward herself and drew her thumb across the row, as you would smooth a sleeve. “It has never written. It reads everything. It is the first to read, every morning. Six o’clock and three seconds. I have not yet put down the telephone.”

“Mrs Han, there is a 4B. Technically. On the roll. But there’s no—”

“Good,” she said. “Then it should be greeted.”

At five to four I was standing on the half landing of the west stairs between three and four, one hand on the rail, in the ordinary posture of a man waiting for nothing. I had told myself I was checking the fire door. The landing at the west end of four, past 4A, is a small square of marble tile with a window onto the alley and a sill as deep as a bookshelf. In fourteen months I had walked past it perhaps a hundred times and had never noticed that the sill was bare, until it was not.

He came down from six, one flight at a time, with a rest between each. I saw the shoes first, black oxfords, resoled, and the hems of brown tweed trousers, and then the cane, with a brass duck’s head for a handle, held across his body like a rifle at ease. I knew him from the roll and the mailboxes. Ptolemy Grieve, 6A, tenant since 1974, whom I had seen every weekday at ten past nine collecting his mail in a three-piece suit, and to whom I had never been introduced. He had a long gray face like a well-kept letter, a pencil moustache, and large ears with a hearing aid in each that whistled when he turned his head.

He carried a white saucer in his left hand at the height of a waiter. On it were a cup, full and steaming, and one Rich Tea biscuit squared to the saucer’s edge. He set it on the sill with a small click. He turned the cup until its handle pointed left.

“Four o’clock, Mr Ambler,” he said, at the volume of a man announcing a train.

Then he coughed. It was a long cough with a drawer in it, a drawer being drawn out as far as it would go, and he took a folded handkerchief from his waistcoat and held it to his mouth until it was done, and looked at the handkerchief, and put it away.

“Stenographers have ears, Mr Mahajan,” he said, without turning around.

I came up two steps with my hands where he could see them. “I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to be on your—”

“Tol-uh-mee,” said Mr Grieve, to the window. “You have been reading it with the P. Everyone does. Saturday at four, I think. Six-A. Bring the question.”

“Which question?”

“If you have to ask, you have several. Bring the better one.” He took up his cane and went off along the corridor toward the elevators, tapping on the carpet, past 4A, past the cabinet, past 4C. At the cabinet he inclined his head to it, a small bow, the one you give a neighbor on the stairs, and went on.

The tea steamed on the sill. The cup’s handle pointed left, as he had set it. It was 4:03. I had a 4:15 about tenant notices, and I am a man who keeps his appointments with computers, and I went down.

At a quarter past five I made a spreadsheet, and I am aware of how that sounds.

It had four columns: Unit, Ritual, Since, Who knows. In the first row I put 3B, a broom handle against a ceiling, a pair of curtains made to number. Then 4A, pencil on a wall (I typed the question mark), a radiator that asks. Then 5C, good morning at six, since 2013. Then 6A, a plate at four. The first three columns went in without argument. The fourth I could not fill. The answer was everyone, and also no one, since not one of the four had said any of it to another; Mrs Han knew nothing about the curtains, Zofia knew nothing about the plate, and the tenant in 4A had told a man holding a form to forget it. Four people in one building had each decided, separately and without comment, to be polite to a wall. I typed Everyone in the cell and deleted it and typed No one and deleted that.

Tenantry’s dashboard has a line for occupancy, which had been climbing since I started, and Randall was fond of the arrow. It has columns for turnover and days vacant and average time to repair. It has the Notes field, two hundred fifty-five characters, and I tried it, to see, and managed Mr Grieve’s plate before the characters ran out. Nothing in the software could say that people stay in a building when somebody says good morning to it, or that some of them had been saying it to a room.

At six I went down. A pot of beet soup was going on Zofia’s burner, the red of something freshly cut, and she had a finger to her lips before I was through the door. She pointed at the ceiling with the ladle, and we stood in her small yellow kitchen like two people waiting for an elevator.

“Always four,” she said, so low I read it off her mouth. “Since first time I hear. Four step, turn, four step. Today—”

“Shh.”

I shushed. I heard the radio in the front room, and a bus, and the soup. Then the steps came. They were soft and a little uneven, with a short drag at the end of each, like slippers on a worn carpet: one, two, three, four, five.

Zofia’s eyes came around to me. “Five,” she said. “Is first time five.”

I did not tell her about the corridor. I had a corridor that had gone from nine paces to fourteen to fifteen in four days, and a ceiling that had gone from four to five, and I know that a person who writes numbers down will see a shape in them whether there is one or not. As far as I could tell, the one thing that had changed in that building between Monday and Thursday was that someone had started to look. I wrote the numbers in the margin of the Lunch & Learn handout, where I write everything: 9, 14, 15, and beside them 4, 5.

“What you did?” said Zofia.

“Nothing.”

“Mm.” She measured me with her eyes, shoulder to shoulder, and wrote nothing down. “Is something.”

Above us the steps went on. Five of them, a pause the length of a held note, the scuff of a turn, and five back.

chapters.title: No Saved Messages
chapters.html:
The phone buzzed face down on the kitchen counter at 5:58 on Sunday, and I had it in my hand before the buzz could finish. I have done that with every call from my family since last January. It is a habit with a date on it. I will get to the date.

Saturday first, because Saturday was the day I counted everything.

Counting is not new with me, but that week it had begun to spread. From my door at Tolliver Court, 3F, to the head of the stairs is fourteen steps along the breezeway, and I walked them with the laundry bag over my shoulder and my lips, a neighbor with a stroller told me later, moving. Thirty-four stairs down. Eleven items in the basket at the market on Kessler, and when I laid them on the belt I counted them again, and the cashier, who had been counting along with me, said “Eleven,” as if we had agreed a price. Since Monday every number had become something I wanted to check, the way you pat your pockets after you have been told about a theft on the bus.

My apartment is a studio on the third floor of a complex built in the seventies for people who were meant to move out of it. I had lived there four years and the walls showed it: nothing on them. The bed was made with the corners tucked. The table had one chair at it and a second folded behind the door, for company. On the counter by the stove stood my mother’s tiffin, three tiers of steel with a dent in the bottom clip, full of rubber bands and AA batteries, and leaning against it was a photograph I had never framed. She is in the yard in Edison, the August before the sound in her chest began, holding a trowel and a tomato and squinting. I took it, so she is looking at me, and that is why it has never gone on a shelf where I would see it from the bed.

Under a stapler, on the end of the counter, sat the mail. I open what has a window and stack what doesn’t. On top was a postcard from the Gaslight. WE MISS YOU, QUIZZY RASCALS, it said, over a drawing of a pint glass with a face. THURSDAYS AT 8. FIRST APPETIZER ON US. Somebody there keeps a list, and I was on it, and I had not turned the card over in twenty-one months.

I did the laundry, which took an hour and forty minutes and two rolls of quarters. I folded it into thirds. I ate a bowl of rice and an egg, standing, and washed the one bowl and the one pan and set them on the drainer beside the two mugs.

That evening I sat at the table with the one chair and did not turn on the television. Under the kitchen window the radiator ticked as it warmed, the first week the complex had let it, and I listened to it with the particular attention of a man who has lately been knocked at by a wall. It ticked. It did what radiators do. I wrote down the time it started, 7:12, and then felt foolish and tore the page out of the pad and put it in the bin.

On Sunday I propped the phone against the tiffin at 5:58, and Anjali’s face filled it.

“You answered,” she said. “You always answer. Do you sleep on it?”

“It’s a good phone.”

“It’s two minutes early, I know, Tia goes in the bath at six-fifteen and she has something to show you.” My sister is five foot two and built like a person who lifts small children for a living, which she does. She had her hair in the claw clip, so she had come straight from a day of getting four-year-olds to hold pencils, and the gap in her front teeth showed when she smiled, and the pale scar through her left eyebrow, from a scooter when she was eight, rose with the rest of her face. “Okay. Okay. Tia, come here, bring it, no, the whole page.”

Tia’s face replaced hers, a small round close-up in dinosaur pajamas, and then a sheet of paper unrolled itself in front of the camera. It was a grid in orange crayon, four rows of four, and in the bottom right square there was a very small person with glasses.

“It’s you,” said Tia. “It’s a spreadsheet. Mama said you live in one.”

“Technically I only visit.”

“Why are you in the corner?”

“That’s where the total goes.”

“What’s a total?”

“The number at the bottom that tells you whether everything added up.”

Tia considered this with her whole face. “Did it?”

“I’ll check,” I said.

Behind them a large figure crossed the kitchen holding a pumpkin like a sleeping dog. Ben Kowalczyk is six foot four and does most things with great gentleness, including the knife in his other hand. The pumpkin had half a face already.

“Hey, Dev.”

“Hey, Ben. It’s the twelfth.”

“You have to let it settle,” said Ben, with dignity, and left.

Anjali took the phone back and walked it to the table. “I’ve been scanning Mummy’s recipe cards. I’ve done forty-one. You have to see them, they’re all in her hand, and the stains, Dev, the stains are exactly where you’d think.” She held a card up to the lens.

DAL TADKA | Serves 4 | 1 cup toor dal, 3 cups water, ½ tsp haldi, salt. Pressure cooker, 7 whistles. Tadka: ghee, jeera, hing, 2 dry red chilli, curry leaves. | (in pen, beside Serves 4: always makes 8)

“Always makes eight,” said Anjali. “She wrote it herself. She knew.”

I looked at the card for longer than the call required. In the line about the cooker, the seven in 7 whistles had its bar through the stem. Hers, then mine, and four days earlier a pink carbon in a filing room that said I had written it. I said it was a good card. I said she had always cooked for whoever might come in.

“Which brings me to the twentieth,” said Anjali. “Diwali. It’s a Monday, I know you know. We’re driving up to Edison on the Saturday. Dad asked.”

“Dad asked what?”

“If you were coming.” She did something with her mouth. “He asked the toaster. He stood in the kitchen and said to the toaster, ‘Dev is coming for Diwali?’ So I’m counting it as a question.”

“It’s a Monday. Technically it’s the week of the freeze, there’s a data room, it’s a work thing.”

“It’s Diwali, you idiot.”

“I’ll be on a call. In the evening. I’ll wear a shirt.”

“Fine. Dad will say hello to the ceiling.” She let that sit. “He’s talking to her tomatoes now. Thursday I watched him from the window, out in the yard in his slippers, telling them something in Marathi for ten minutes. Then he turned every pot a quarter turn, the way she did. He didn’t water them. He just turned them toward the light.” She looked down at the table. “Somebody should tell him it’s October.”

“Tell him the quarter turn was right.”

“Tell him yourself. On Monday.”

“On the call,” I said.

“On the call,” she agreed, as though it were a concession from us both. Then her eyes went past my shoulder, the way they do. An occupational therapist reads a room the way other people read a menu. “You have two mugs out.”

“The set came as two.”

“One’s dry and upside down. One’s been used. You’ve had that set four years and you still put the second one out.”

“That’s where the drainer is.”

Anjali waited. She is very good at it. It is her job, and she was doing it on me through a phone from six hundred miles away, with a four-year-old’s elbow in the corner of the frame. “Is something wrong?”

“It’s a data migration.”

She laughed, and it did not go all the way down. “Okay,” she said. “Okay. Okay.” Then, in her ordinary voice: “Sunday at six.”

“Sunday at six,” I said, which is how we end every call, like a signature.

When the screen went dark I did what I do on Sundays. I opened the phone app, then Voicemail, then the tab marked Saved, where one message sits, and held my thumb above it.

Voicemail | Saved (1) | MUMMY | Thu, Jan 11, 9:41 PM | 0:23

I hold my thumb there for twenty-three seconds, the length of the message, and then I close the app. It seemed the fair amount.

On Thursday the eleventh of January last year my mother was in a hospice bed in Edison with my father and my sister beside her, and I was at the Gaslight with the Quizzy Rascals, who needed a ninth. I had told Anjali I would take the Friday train. At 9:41 my phone lit on the table with MUMMY across it, and the host had just asked for the capital of Burkina Faso, and I had my hand up and was spelling it, and I was on the second G. I turned the phone face down. We got the answer right. She left a message twenty-three seconds long. She died at 3:12 in the morning, and at 3:30 my sister called me, and I have never told Anjali that I saw the call. I have never listened to the message. I left the Rascals the next week, and I had not been back to the Gaslight since.

That Sunday, after forty-one recipe cards held up one at a time to a camera, I decided to press it. I cannot tell you why that night. Somebody was at last doing something with what our mother had left, and I had the one piece nobody had asked about.

I touched the line. The screen thought about it.

Voicemail | Saved (0) | No Saved Messages

I assumed I had touched the wrong tab. I went back to Inbox, and forward to Saved, and the line was the same. I shut the app and opened it. I restarted the phone and watched the logo come up and go. On the laptop I logged in to the carrier’s site and clicked through Inbox, Saved and Deleted, and got three zeroes. The cloud backup keeps three copies, and none went back as far as January. In the kitchen drawer, under takeout menus and a handful of soy sauce packets, lay the phone I had owned before this one, a cracked gray thing that I now understood I had kept for exactly this. I charged it for ten minutes, which were long, and it came on with a picture of a lake I used to like, and I opened Voicemail, and it said what the other one said.

What came first was relief. I know the second it arrived, because I was holding the old phone, and my shoulders came down, the left one first, and I let them. A man who has carried one object for twenty-one months and is told it is gone has been told that he may put his arms down. Then I noticed what my shoulders were doing, and I set the old phone on the counter very carefully, as though it could still say something, and stood there with my hand over my mouth.

That week I had cleaned up some sixty rows for go-live: trailing spaces, three phone numbers, an emergency contact for 1C. I did not connect that to the phone for more than a week, and I put the two facts side by side here only so that they are on the record together. I know now what that voicemail was worth to the building, which was almost nothing. I had carried it for twenty-one months, and for none of them had I been holding it.

At eleven I got up to brush my teeth. My bed is six steps from the bathroom door. I have walked it every night for four years, and I know it the way you know your own phone number. I took six, and the door was not there. I took a seventh.

I went back to the bed and walked it again, with my arms at my sides, counting out loud, and it was seven. I turned and walked it back, and it was seven. Nothing in the hall had moved. The carpet was the carpet, with a stain by the baseboard the shape of Ohio, and the light switch was where the light switch is, and the hall had grown by a step and given no reasons.

I ended up on the kitchen floor, which is not a place I go, with my back against the cabinet under the sink and the old phone on the tile beside me.

“Okay,” I said to the empty room, in Anjali’s voice, because it was the only voice I had to hand. “Okay. Okay.”

Under the window the radiator knocked twice. It was not a pipe banging. It was two knocks, unhurried, spaced the way a person knocks who knows you are in, and I knew the spacing. I looked at the radiator for some time. I did not knock back.

chapters.title: Unit Tour
chapters.html:
Espie switched on the ring light at 9:05 on Tuesday, and the lobby of Harwick Terrace, which has not been flattered since 1986, took it like a patient told to say ah. The brown-and-cream terrazzo came up the color of caramel. The brass H in the floor lit like a coin at the bottom of a fountain. The dead doorman’s desk gleamed in a manner I would have said it did not deserve.

“Ok so we’re giving original features,” said Espie, to a phone on a gimbal. Her hair was up and her gold hoops were in and her nails were still pumpkin, with the bats. “No because look at this floor? It’s giving 1927. It’s giving someone important got married in here.”

“Nobody got married in here,” I said.

“Dev. You’re in my shot.”

“I’m at the mailboxes.”

“You’re in my shot with your face.” She lowered the phone. “Ok so the thing is, I need a rent guy. For the background. The building has a person, the person is handling something. Mood: responsible. Do you have a lanyard?”

“I have a lanyard.”

“Put it on. Walk from the office to the mailboxes with a folder and look like you’re about to evict someone, but warmly.”

“I’ve never evicted anyone.”

“Then do the warm part.”

We did it five times. On the third take I held the folder wrong, on the fourth she said I was giving hostage, and on the fifth she said that was literally it, and I understood I had been cast. In the last take I stopped at the mailboxes, because it was where the script told me to stop, and for the first time in fourteen months I looked at the box for 4B. It was so full of circulars that its small brass door had given up closing. The name card in the slot said OCCUPANT, in blue ink, in a round hand. I thought of Joyce, saying round, and went back to the office with my folder.

The rest of the tour was Noreen’s idea, in the sense that Noreen had said yes to “a tasteful walk-through, no tenant faces” without reading the word walk-through as a plan. We did 5D first, vacant since spring, with new vinyl plank and a ficus that was not a ficus. “And this is our biophilic moment,” Espie told the phone, touching a leaf. “It’s fake but it’s trying. That’s so real.” I stood in the doorway being responsible.

“Ok, and now, for a sneak peek of the vibes,” she said, in the elevator, “we’re doing four.”

“Why four?”

“The carpet. It’s old hotel. Old hotel is literally an aesthetic now.”

“It was a hotel.”

“Exactly. It’s giving provenance.”

She walked the corridor slowly, holding the gimbal low with both hands like a woman carrying a full bowl, narrating over her shoulder. I followed with my folder, where the shot would not catch me, and counted. Past the clogs at 4A, past the cabinet, to the bicycle at 4C, and what I got in my head was seventeen. The smell of toast came up around the cabinet and went again. “Is someone making toast?” said Espie, without stopping. “Ok that’s giving home.” My lips must have been moving, because she said, “Stop moving your mouth, you’re giving ventriloquist,” and I stopped, and seventeen stayed where it was.

At the cabinet she slowed even further. “And this is a fire safety feature, which, important. We love safety.” She held the lens on the red glass for a full second, and I felt the carpet under my shoes go on being carpet, and she said, “Ok that’s the tour, besties, link in bio,” and lowered the phone.

At 10:20 she propped her laptop on the leasing desk and played it back, and I stood behind her chair with my folder against my chest. Joyce came to the edge of her cubicle without being asked, which she does for fire drills and cake.

It was a good video. The lobby looked like money. The ficus looked almost real. At 0:12 the picture went into the fourth-floor corridor, low and slow, the maroon diamonds sliding underfoot, and at 0:14, between the clogs on their mat and the bicycle by the far door, there was something beige.

I would like to put this carefully. It was there for one frame, or two, and then it was a red cabinet with a hose in it, and the video went on to the stairs. The first time I told myself it was the gimbal. The second time it was a shape, a tall pale rectangle with an edge. The third time it had brass on it, two small numerals at the height of a face, a 4 and a B, the B slightly out of true. On the fourth time I saw that it stood open a finger’s width, and on the fifth there was a lamp in the gap, a thin vertical line of amber the color of strong tea.

“Is it a jump cut?” said Espie. “I didn’t cut. I don’t even have an edit. I’ve literally never cut anything in my life.”

“Noted,” said Joyce, from behind us, very quietly. Then, which she never does: “Play it again.”

Espie played it again. When she stopped it on 0:14 and zoomed, the frame went soft and gray and showed us a cabinet and a hose. Only when the video moved did the door arrive, like a word you know on a page you have been staring at.

“Dev.” She had turned the chair around to look at me. Without the ring light she looked younger and more tired, and her eyes were doing something I had not seen them do in fourteen months, which was not performing. “You saw it right away. Not like, what is that. Like, there you are.”

“I was squinting.”

“Mm-hm.” She picked up her phone and held it against her chest, and I saw the thumb move on the glass. “I have a note about this building.”

“What kind of note?”

“Later,” said Espie. Then, being Espie, she brightened. “Ok, but this is content. This is, like, so much content. Dev, people make whole careers out of one door.”

“Please don’t post it.”

“It’s a corridor.”

“It’s a corridor with a door in it, which you just said.”

She posted it at 10:31 as The Mystery Unit.

@harwickterrace | The Mystery Unit | Live at Harwick: a sneak peek of the fourth floor. Rewatch 0:14. No, don’t. Yes, do. 1BRs from $1,395, tours daily | #oldbuilding #apartmenttour #mysteryunit

pauline.reads: what is the door at 0:14??

bigmike_1987: lol it’s a fire cabinet, you people need sleep

tessaroo: ok i watched it 3 times and the gap gets WIDER

It had eight hundred views by 10:50, when the keys in Noreen’s office stopped, and her door opened and nothing chimed. I knew before I looked at her. The color went out of her face in sections, forehead first. She came and stood behind Espie’s chair and watched 0:14 four times with the sound off, and her hands found the lanyard and closed on it, all fourteen keys, until they were silent.

“Take it down,” said Noreen.

“It’s doing numbers, Noreen. It’s my best day since the pumpkin.”

“Esperanza.” She almost never uses the whole name. “Take it down. Now. Okay. Okay. Okay.”

Espie took it down at 10:52. By noon a stranger who had recorded it off her screen had put it up under the title MYSTERY APARTMENT IN OLD HOTEL, and that one had eight thousand views, and Noreen had shut her door.

At 1:41 an email came, in capitals.

From: Randall Pugh | To: Noreen Whitmore; Devendra Mahajan | Date: Tue 14 Oct, 1:41 PM | Subject: UNIT 4B DOES NOT EXIST (ACTION REQUIRED)

Team, following this morning’s social post Larchmont has asked for written confirmation that no unit 4B exists at Harwick Terrace. It does not. Going forward the post stays down, the line comes out ahead of the 10/31 data-room freeze, and nobody posts about 4B again. Zoom at 2:00 PM, please come with a date. Randall

We took the call in the filing room, on Noreen’s laptop, propped on the stool that tips. Randall appeared in front of Positano. In my experience the backgrounds change by the call and the man does not: the quarter-zip, the tan, the white square of a ring light in each eye. Behind him a hundred pastel houses were stacked up a cliff toward a sky that nobody would ever need to account for. He looked like someone in excellent health who had never once been rained on.

“Team, thanks for jumping on. I’ll be brief, I’ve got Larchmont at 2:30.” He steepled his hands. “I want to be transparent that I have watched this video eleven times.”

“Eleven,” said Noreen. Her hands were out of the frame, below the shelf of the stool, and I could see her elbows working.

“And every time, what I see is a fire-hose cabinet. Dev, you’re closest to the data. Do you see a door?”

There are questions you can answer truthfully and questions you can answer in good standing. “Technically,” I said, “what I see is a compression artifact.”

“Love that. Compression artifact. I’m going to use that.” He leaned in. “Here’s what’s keeping me up, and it isn’t a door, because there is no door. It’s eight thousand people in a comment section asking about a unit that Larchmont’s data room says we don’t own. Their integration lead sent me the link with one question mark. One. I have equity that vests at closing and I’m being asked about a question mark.”

“We understand,” said Noreen.

“Going forward I need the line out, I need it before the freeze, and I need us to not boil the ocean here. It’s one row.” Randall put his palms on the desk in Positano. “Four-B does not exist, Dev. That is the whole point of the exercise.”

I thought of asking whose exercise. I said “Noted,” in Joyce’s voice, which is the only time I have borrowed it.

“Super,” said Randall, who had been in the Tenantry training too. “Let’s circle back Friday.”

When the screen went blank Noreen did not move. The stool tipped a little under the laptop and she put out one finger and steadied it.

“It’s a row, hon,” she said, to the wall. “It’s a row.”

I left at twenty past five, in rain that had settled in for the evening, and I crossed 31st Street not to the bus stop but to Halloran’s, because at about 2:40 I had decided I needed a notebook and I had not had the courage to say so to myself until I was holding my coat. Halloran’s sells ham on rye, lottery tickets, umbrellas on a cardboard spinner, and, next to the batteries, a small yellow notebook with a rubber cover and pages made for surveyors and anyone else who must write in the wet. It cost $4.29. I bought a pencil, because pencil takes the rain, and stood under the awning among the soaked cardboard boxes and wrote.

Mon 6 Oct: 9 going, 12 back. Wed 8: 14 / 14. Thu 9: 15 (Z. 3B: steps 4 to 5). Tue 14: 17.

I looked at that for some time. A column of figures is the nearest thing I own to a prayer, and it was going up.

I had now been told twice in nine days that 4B did not exist: once in an office by a woman holding her keys in both hands, once on a screen by a man in front of the sea. Each had said it kindly, as a favor. And I knew what I had not said to either of them, because I have not said it to anyone, which is that I was already familiar with this sentence. In the year before my mother was diagnosed there was a sound that my father heard from the pillow beside hers, and two doctors told us it was nothing. They were wrong. The sound was exactly what it was. I know what it is to be told that something you can hear does not exist, and I know how it feels to agree, to be a good sport about it, to take the Post-it.

Under the numbers I wrote Not deleting. I underlined it once, as Noreen does, and put the notebook in my inside pocket, where the rain could not get at it.

By the time I came back across 31st Street the rain had gone from the kind you walk in to the kind you carry. I had left my umbrella hooked over the lobby radiator at half past eight that morning and had not thought of it for nine hours, which is the sort of thing that happens to a man who has had a day. I pushed the glass door open with my shoulder, wet to the cuffs.

Left was open.

It stood on the ground floor with its doors drawn back and its ceiling light on, and nobody in it. Nobody stood by the call button. The lobby was empty, the bench, the doorman’s desk, the forty-one mailboxes, the brass H under my shoes. It was Tuesday, and Left only sticks on Mondays. It was not sticking. It was waiting, with the patience of a thing that knows you are coming.

I crossed to the radiator and took my umbrella, and when I turned, the display above the doors, which reads L when the car is at the lobby, said 4B.

It said 4B for about as long as it takes to read it. Then it said L. The doors slid shut on the empty car, and the lobby clock, six minutes slow, said 5:44, which was ten to six. I stood on the brass H with my umbrella in my hand. I did not get in.

chapters.title: The Extra Washer
chapters.html:
The light in the Harwick laundry room is the orange of a parking structure at night. It comes from a single fixture in a wire cage, and under it everything looks like a photograph of itself taken in 1974. Six washers stand along the east wall with their lids up. Six dryers face them across a strip of linoleum the color of weak tea. At the far end, past the last washer, where the wall turns toward the boiler, there is a seventh, and it is avocado green.

I got there at 6:55 on Thursday evening with a notebook, a pencil, my phone and a printout folded in thirds. “Thursdays,” Rafa had told me on Wednesday, at the foot of the basement stairs, with the toothpick traveling from one corner of his mouth to the other. “Bring nothing.” I had taken this for a figure of speech.
