To be fair to myself, I had considered a thermos, a folding chair and a second pencil, and had held myself to the one pencil.

Each machine wore a card reader. The coin changer on the wall had said OUT OF ORDER on a strip of masking tape since before my time. A folding table stood in the middle of the floor with a laminated sign taped to it, and on the lid of dryer 4 lay a white bra, underwired, which has lain there since before Labor Day. Every resident of Harwick has agreed not to see it. It is the nearest thing the building has to a constitution.

LAUNDRY ROOM 7 AM TO 10 PM. Please remove lint. Please do not dye. Please do not sit on the machines. Items left over 48 hours will be donated. Thank you, The Management.

Rafa sat on a folding chair beside the green machine with a steel thermos between his boots and a canvas bag across his knees. The bag was the size and shape of a sleeping dog. Stenciled on it, in blue gone to gray, were the words HARWICK HOTEL LINEN SVC.

“You brought a notebook,” he said.

“You said nothing.”

“A notebook is nothing. Sit.”

I did not sit. I went to look at the green washer and read the plate on it. It was brass, the size of a playing card, screwed to the panel above the dial and engraved in the plain capitals of an old trophy shop. It said 4B. The enamel had chipped at one corner and showed white underneath, and the screws had been painted over with the rest of the panel more than once, which told me the plate was older than the paint.

I took out the printout. I had pulled it at four that afternoon from Corvane’s shared drive, and I had been rather proud of the idea, the way you are of a spare umbrella.

CORVANE PROPERTY GROUP | Fixed Asset Register | HT / Basement / Laundry | LW-1 to LW-6, washers (6) | LD-1 to LD-6, dryers (6) | Card readers (12) | Folding table (1) | Last physical verification: 30 June | Asset count: 25

I counted the washers, then the lines on the register, then the washers again. Six and six. “Technically,” I said, “it isn’t on here.”

“It’s a washer.”

“It isn’t an asset.”

“An asset is a thing somebody wrote down,” said Rafa, and shifted the toothpick. “This is a thing that washes.”

“Who pays for the electricity?”

“Who pays for anything?” He looked at me over the white tape on his glasses with great gentleness. “You tell me. You have the roll.”

At 6:58 he got up, as slowly as he does everything, and lifted the lid of the green machine. The tub was dry and empty. The enamel had gone cream at the rim, and a white plastic cone stood in the center for an agitator. “Look,” he said. I looked. I put my hand in, because a man who is shown a thing is entitled to touch it, and the metal was cold. “Behind.”

Behind the machine two hoses lay in coils, bound with zip ties, their ends capped with brass fittings that someone had painted the color of the wall. Neither went near a tap. The drain hose hung four inches above the floor drain, over nothing, like a man holding a door for no one.

“Nothing,” I said.

“Nothing,” Rafa agreed, and shut the lid with the heel of his hand.

At seven exactly by my phone, which keeps carrier time and is therefore six minutes ahead of every clock in the building, the machine started. No coin went in. No card touched the reader. The dial moved itself a quarter turn with a small ratcheting click, and from inside the tub came the sound of a washer filling. It is a loud sound and a familiar one, water meeting a drum. There was no water. I stood with my palm flat on the lid and felt the vibration come up through it, steady and honest, a machine doing the job it was built for.

I opened a spreadsheet on my phone. I am aware of how that sounds, but a man with a stopwatch and a free evening is only a few keystrokes from a spreadsheet. Column A for the phase, column B for the clock. By 7:35 I had four phases down and a growing suspicion that the cycle was an honest one.

“Mira,” said Rafa, from his chair. “You are doing math at a miracle.”

“I’m timing it.”

“You time the bus also?”

“The 14 is twenty-two minutes.”

“And does the bus care?”

I put the phone away. A few minutes later I took it out again, in the dark of my pocket, with the screen turned down, like a man checking the score in church.

At twenty past seven Zofia backed through the door, towing a two-wheeled wire cart with her hip. She had on the gray cardigan, the tape around her neck and the pincushion at her wrist, and the cart held a heap of men’s slacks, charcoal and navy and one pair of mustard corduroy, each with a pencil tag pinned to the waistband. She did not look at me first. She looked at the green washer, and she gave it a nod, short and level, the kind you give a colleague across a shop when you both have a long evening ahead.

“Tonight is slacks,” she said.

The washer went on filling with nothing.

“Rafa. Mister clerk.” She had the tape out and round my chest before I had finished saying good evening. “Don’t breathe.” I didn’t. “Same. Is same as Thursday last, no worse.” She turned on Rafa. “You.”

“Me, no.”

“One centimeter more at waist.”

“It’s the bread.”

“Is always the bread,” said Zofia, with enormous sympathy, and wrote it in the notebook with the rubber band.

She loaded a third of her cart into washer 2, tapped the reader with a plastic card from her cardigan pocket, where it lived among the pins, and sat on the folding table under the orange light with a needle and a pair of trousers across her lap. She hemmed by hand. She did not look at the green machine again. It was the way you do not look at a pot. Every few minutes her eyes went up to its lid and came down again.

“Do you come every Thursday?” I asked.

“Thursday I wash. She washes. We don’t talk.” She bit a thread. “Is professional.”

From a quarter to eight until about ten past, nothing happened, and I want that on the record, because in my experience it is what most of it is: a basement, a thermos, a woman sewing, a man working a toothpick, and an avocado-green machine going through a perfectly ordinary cycle on nothing. Rafa poured coffee into the cap of the thermos and gave it to me. It tasted of cinnamon and the cap. He told me, apropos of nothing, that the way to wait is not to watch the clock but to watch somebody’s hands, and I watched Zofia’s, which went in and out of the wool at a speed I will never have at anything, and I felt a little better.

At 8:07 the spin began, a low, stuttering roar that rose and then settled, and the other washers in the row hummed along with it, faintly, as glassware does when a truck goes by. Zofia stopped sewing. Rafa took out the toothpick. I held my phone against my chest. At 8:12 the motor wound down, and a latch inside the lid went over with a flat clunk.

19:00 fill | 19:06 wash | 19:28 drain | 19:32 rinse | 19:50 drain | 19:54 spin | 20:12 stop | Total 72:00

I looked at the column for some time. It footed. I do not know what I had expected, but I had not expected arithmetic to be on its side.

Rafa lifted the lid. Warm air came out of the tub, and with it the smell of toast. It was not the smell of laundry. The drum was full.

“Hold the bag,” he said, and I held it open.

He took things out one at a time and folded each on the table with his eyes on his hands. They were dry. They were warm, with the particular warmth of cloth taken out of a dryer by someone standing right there, a temperature I had not expected to meet in a basement where no dryer had run. I will list what I saw. Three sleeveless undershirts, white gone ivory, each with a woven red tape at the neck reading T. AMBLER. A chambermaid’s apron in gray-blue cotton, with a bib and a pocket, and in the hem, in white thread, V.P. A pair of heavy wool socks, navy, with a ribbed turnover, which I took for a sailor’s without knowing why, until I found in the cuff a laundry mark in black thread, N.H., and a number, 72, that could have been a room or a year. A silk scarf, green and gold, printed with small fans, which Rafa folded into a square the size of a coaster.

“You’re not reading them,” I said.

“Somebody told me a long time ago. Fold it, don’t read it.” He squared an undershirt. “A man who reads starts to ask.”

“I’m reading them.”

“Yes,” said Rafa. “You’re the clerk.”

I had seen the name Ambler once before, on a sill, in the mouth of an old man in tweed. I did not say so. I took the first undershirt from the pile and held it by the shoulders, and it hung from my hands like something that had been recently worn by a person of exactly my height.

Zofia had come to stand at my elbow. She held her tape over the red letters without touching the cloth and looked at the stitching on the name. “Hand,” she said. “Small stitch. Every stitch same. Somebody who like to do it.” She considered. “Wife. Or very good mother.”

“Which?”

“I measure. I don’t guess.” She went back to her slacks.

The last thing in the drum was a balled pair of gray work socks, thick, with a reinforced heel. Rafa put them in my left hand. “Fold,” he said. “I do the string.”

I folded them the way my mother folded socks, one inside the other, the cuff turned over the toe, and I did not look at them. I was looking at him. He drew the string of the bag tight, knotted it with a single movement of the thumb and swung it over his shoulder. Zofia, behind us, said something to the green machine in Polish, low and brisk, as one says good night to a coworker, and then we were in the corridor, and then in the elevator, and I still had the socks in my hand.

We took Right. The car smelled faintly of toast by the time it reached four. On the fourth floor I counted without wanting to, the way a tongue goes to a tooth: eighteen, which went into the notebook later, between the seventeen of Tuesday and a nineteen I would have the next morning.

Rafa set the bag down at the foot of the hose cabinet, squared to the wall, as you would leave a delivery. He did not look at the wall. He looked down the corridor toward 4C and the blue bicycle, with the courtesy of a man in an elevator pretending not to hear another man’s phone call.

Two knocks came from the plaster just left of the cabinet, at chest height. They were unhurried, like someone confirming a delivery. My hand came up. Rafa watched it come.

“Margie used to say,” he said, to the bicycle, “if you ever hear the radiator ask a question, answer it.”

“Margie Dunleavy.” It was the first time I had said the name in front of anyone but Joyce. “What does it ask?”

“Depends who’s asking.”

I knocked twice on the plaster with my right fist. This time I thought about it first, and it made no difference. Nothing answered. The smell of toast thickened by one degree, the way a kitchen does when the person at the stove turns around. Rafa breathed out through his nose and said, “Good. Now it’s polite.”

He went to the stairwell door and held it open with a boot, his eyes on the floor. I stood at the cabinet with my left hand shut. When I opened it I had not yet looked at the socks, and now, under the corridor light, I did. They were a man’s, heavy, gray, with a darn at one heel in thread that did not quite match. On the cuff of the left one, in black marker, in the upright capitals of a woman who has been told all her life that her handwriting is nice and has made it her business to deserve it, were the words G. WHITMORE.

Whitmore is not a rare name. I had told myself so in 3B, over a carbon of curtains. I told myself so again, and it did less each time. I laid the socks on top of the bag and squared them to its edge, as Rafa had squared the rest.

In my first week, at the coffee machine, with the gum going round, Noreen had told me that her husband had gone out for cigarettes in 2016. “And he’s still looking for the right brand, hon,” she had said, and laughed, a big laugh that took a moment to get started and then ran a beat too long. I had laughed too, because that is what one does. She had said it the way you pin a joke over a hole.

chapters.title: The Bricked Window
chapters.html:
The ticket said 241. The sign above the counter at the Municipal Annex said NOW SERVING 238. Between those two numbers I sat down on a bench bolted to the floor and understood that I had made a plan on the strength of a website.

The website, last updated in the spring of 2022, said that Permit Records was at Window 3, that it opened at nine, and that a records search with up to three printed pages cost $4.25, cash only. I had $4.25. I had assembled it the night before out of the jar of quarters and a drawer of singles and carried it in a sandwich bag, like a man bribing a very small official.

I had put in for the afternoon on Tenantry that morning, reason Personal, no description. Noreen approved it from her phone inside a minute with a thumbs-up and no remark, which in Noreen is an essay. Before I left I went up to four and counted the corridor at twenty past eight. Nineteen. The Annex is nineteen minutes downtown by bus. I wrote both numbers in the notebook, side by side, and crossed out the second, because a man has to draw the line somewhere.

The Annex is a flat building of buff brick, put up in the years when governments liked to look as if accountants had built them. On the second floor a hall of windows, numbered one to six, ran away from a red take-a-number machine that had given me my 241 with a sound like a hiccup. About thirty of us sat on benches. Nobody read. Everyone held a ticket the way you hold a boarding pass for a flight you do not believe is going to leave.

The man beside me wore a maroon satin bowling jacket with LEON stitched over the heart in cursive. He had a roll of drawings between his knees. “Deck,” he said, before I asked. “Twelve by sixteen. Six months. Now they want the joist hangers in a different galvanization.” He shook his head at the sign. “What’s yours?”

“A certificate of occupancy.”

“Oh, you’re one of the easy ones.” He said it wistfully. His ticket said 242.

The sign went to 239 at 12:20 and to 240 at 12:41. At 1:09 it said 241, and a bell rang, and I stood up with the sandwich bag in my fist.

Window 3 belonged to a woman of about sixty-five in a lavender cardigan buttoned to the throat. Her white hair had been set in a style that had agreed with itself years ago and had not been consulted since. Reading glasses hung on a chain. At her elbow stood a mug that said WORLD’S OKAYEST GRANDMA, and the nameplate on the counter said B. TUCK, RECORDS SPECIALIST. She did not look up when I reached the glass. She finished the line she was on first, the way a surgeon finishes a stitch.

“Parcel address.”

“114 East 31st Street.”

“Nature of request.”

“A certificate of occupancy. And the floor plan for the fourth floor.”

“I don’t have floor plans. I have plan sheets, as filed with the permit.” Her fingers moved on the keys, two at a time, and every stroke landed. “A floor plan is what an owner has. A sheet is what the county has. They are different documents and the county does not mix them up.”

“Then the sheet, please.”

“Level four is A-4. Anything else?”

“Any permits that touched the fourth floor. Since the conversion, in eighty-six.”

“Mm.” The printer behind her woke up and began to work through a stack, and she took each page from the tray and squared it against the counter before passing it through the slot, naming it as she dealt it, like a croupier. “Certificate of occupancy.”

MUNICIPAL ANNEX, PERMIT RECORDS | CERTIFICATE OF OCCUPANCY | 114 East 31st Street | Issued 3 Nov 1986 | Use: Multiple dwelling, seven stories and basement | Dwelling units: 40

The roll at Harwick says forty-one. I read the figure twice, as one does, and then I saw that in the margin beside it someone had written in pencil, in a neat hand, 41 per owner, verbal, and drawn one ruled line through it.

“There’s a note,” I said.

“There is a struck note,” said Mrs Tuck. “A struck note is a corrected note. The document says forty.”

“Who struck it?”

“Whoever had the pencil.” She took a sip from the mug. “In 1986 we had pencils.”

“Plan sheet A-4.” She slid it across. It was a photocopy of a photocopy, in gray, of the fourth floor of a building I had walked through every working day for fourteen months. The elevators and stair in the middle, the corridor in a double line, the doors as small arcs. Five apartments were drawn and lettered. Four A. Four C. Four D, E and F. Between 4A and 4C sat a hatched rectangle with the legend R-4 RISER, and nothing else. I looked at the lettering for some time. On a plan the letters come in order, like hours. Someone had skipped B.

“There’s no B.”

“Architects skip letters.” She did not look up. “I had a man in who wanted to know why his building had no thirteenth floor.”

“Why hadn’t it?”

“I don’t know, and it’s not on the sheet. The sheet shows what was built. It doesn’t give reasons.” She passed me the last page. “Permit abstract. That’s the only one that touched four.”

BP-1986-04417 | Issued 14 Aug 1986 | Work: Infill existing window opening | Location: North elevation, level 4, bay 2 | Inspection: FINAL, signed 29 Sept 1986

“Final means closed,” said Mrs Tuck. “It can’t be reopened except by a new permit. In my experience that is the most dependable word in a building.”

“Is there a unit 4B in your records? At that address?”

She typed. The screen thought about it. I have seen a good many screens think, and this one thought with the face of a woman who has been telling the public for thirty-one years that there is no such thing. “There is no unit 4B at that address,” she said. “Forty dwelling units, no 4B. Is that what you needed?”

“Can anyone look up a permit number? Not just me?”

“Anyone. It’s a public number. It’s on the website, and it’s all a system needs. You type it in, the county tells your system whether it’s real, and your system takes the county’s word. It never reads the file.” She set the mug down. “Landlords ask if they can use one for something it wasn’t issued for. The system will let them, I’ll say that. I tell them a number is only as true as the work it’s attached to.” She squared the pages. “That isn’t county policy. That’s me. Four-fifty.”

“The website says four twenty-five.”

“The website went up before July.” She tipped her head at a laminated sign by the glass, and it said what she said. “Exact change. We don’t make change at the window, I’m afraid. We never have.”

I had four singles and a quarter. I went out into the corridor with my bag of coins and stood in front of a vending machine that sold pretzels, gum and a sleeve of crackers. A laminated notice under the coin return read THIS MACHINE GIVES CHANGE IN DOLLAR COINS ONLY. THE CITY REGRETS THE INCONVENIENCE. I put in a single and pressed the return, and received a dollar coin, heavy and gold, the same amount of money in a form no window could use. I did this twice. I now had two dollar coins, two singles and a quarter, and was no nearer to fifty cents.

“Machine does that,” said Leon, from the doorway. He held out a quarter between two fingers, as one offers a tip to a child. “Pay me back by putting in a good word at Window 1. My deck is structural.”

“I don’t know anyone at Window 1.”

“Nobody does. Say it anyway.”

Mrs Tuck took the coins without comment. She counted them against the ledge, turned the wheel on a date stamp, and brought it down on a slip with a flat bang. “Certificate of occupancy, one-fifty,” she read. “Plan sheet, two. Permit abstract, one. Four-fifty. Cash. Paid.” She tore the slip across the perforation and gave me the top half, and she looked at me for the first time, over the glasses, for about as long as it takes to read a license plate. “You’ll want the bay numbers,” she said. “People always do. It’s a five-bay front.”

Halloran’s, across 31st Street from Harwick, sells ham on rye, lottery tickets, umbrellas on a cardboard spinner and, next to the batteries, a waterproof notebook. I took the table in the window, from which, if you lean, you can see the whole front of the building. I ate a ham on rye I had been owing myself since Monday. Then I unfolded the receipt to check the sum, because I check the sum.

MUNICIPAL ANNEX | PERMIT RECORDS WINDOW 3 | 10/17 1:52 PM | CERT OF OCC 1.50 | PLAN SHT A-4 2.00 | PERMIT ABSTRACT 1.00 | UNIT FILE 4B 0.00 | TOTAL 4.50 | CASH 4.50

I had stood at that window and had the slip read back to me with a full stop after each price. I had counted three lines. I counted four now. The fourth was in the same dot-matrix gray as the rest, and the price against it was nothing, which is the price of a thing that does not exist, and I will admit it was exactly right.

I laid the papers out on the table the way I lay out a reconciliation. A certificate that said forty. A plan that drew five doors and a riser. A permit that said that in the summer of 1986 someone had been paid to close a window on the fourth floor, and that an inspector had come and agreed. A pencil line, crossed through, that said forty-one, and the pencil had been someone’s. Against these I had a roll of forty-one rows and a cash envelope on the twentieth. It is a very small list, and I stayed with it until the girl at the register turned the sign over and said they were closing at seven.

At 5:41 I saw Noreen come out of the lobby with her umbrella up and her bag on her shoulder. She stopped on the step. She did not look at the street. She looked up, at the fourth floor, as you look up at a clock, and then she turned right and walked away from me toward the bus stop, with her keys held still against her coat. She did not see me. I am not a person people see across a street.

At seven I stood under the shelter across from the building, the one at 31st and Merrow, and counted windows.

From there you can see Harwick as no one who works in it ever does, in one piece. Seven stories of red-brown brick, the cream band at the second and the seventh, the lamps going on in the lobby. Rain came off the shelter’s roof in a flat sheet. A bus braked in the gutter and threw a wave at the curb, and I stepped back on to the last dry inch of the bench. I let two 14s go by. The second driver opened his door and looked at me, and shut it.

Five bays across. I went up to the fourth floor and counted again. Bay 1, at the west end, had a lamp lit behind its curtain, which I took to be Chioma’s, on the strength of a pair of green clogs. Bays 3, 4 and 5 were dark. Bay 2 was filled with brick. It was newer than its neighbors, a shade lighter, laid with mortar a quarter inch wider than the rest, so that the opening still showed in the wall the way a patched pocket shows on a coat. I had a permit number for it, and the number could not have been plainer if it had been painted there.

At 7:40 the patch began to glow.

I want to put this carefully, as I tried to put Espie’s video. It began in the mortar, which went the color of strong tea, line by line, and then the brick between the lines, from the edges inward, the amber spreading toward the middle of the opening the way a print comes up in a tray. I have seen that once, on a school trip, and I had forgotten how slow it is, and how it seems to be nobody’s doing. Within a minute the whole oblong was lit from behind, a window in a wall that had no window. There were curtains. They were oatmeal, lined, hanging inside the brick and not in front of it, if that makes sense, and I can only say what I saw.

Someone was standing at the curtain. It was a tall figure in a cardigan, standing a little stooped, as people do who have spent a life ducking doorframes. A hand took the hem of the curtain at the corner nearest the alley and lifted it, an inch, as you lift a blind to check the street. It was a large hand, with the knuckles of someone who has done a good deal of writing by hand and some gardening. It lifted two fingers. It lowered them.

I raised my own hand. I did not decide to. Then, because a man should answer the question put to him, I put up two fingers, and I brought them down.

The curtain fell back. I had my phone out by then, and I do not remember getting it out. I took one photograph at 7:41, and my thumb shook, and I took another. The amber was going out of the window at the edges. At 7:43 it was a lighter patch of brick with wide mortar, and rain on it, and a streetlamp’s reflection in a puddle on the sill of bay 3. I lowered the phone and looked up with my own eyes. Brick. A bus went by, the 14 again, ticking, with its doors shut and four people in it who did not look at me, and I counted the bays against its lit windows. Five.

On the ride home I turned the phone toward the ceiling light. The first photograph showed what I had seen: the lit oblong, the curtains, the cardigan, the lifted hem, the hand with two fingers raised. The second showed brick. They sat next to each other in the roll, 7:41 and 7:43, as two photographs of the same wall taken two minutes apart by a man who had lost his mind between them.

I looked at the hand a long time, and then I had a thought, which I am putting down because a note to file leaves nothing out. A bricked window is the kind of place in which people get put. I thought it with a man’s gray socks in my head and a joke about cigarettes and a struck line in a margin, and it took about the length of one stop. I put it away the way you turn a card face down in your wallet. I did not say it to anyone.

chapters.title: Mr Grieve Takes Tea
chapters.html:
The cane came down the sixth-floor hallway at ten to four, one tap to every two steps, and I stood at the elevator with my hands behind my back like a boy outside a principal’s office. I had come up by the stairs, as I do when I am afraid of being early, and being early had done what it does, which is leave me ten minutes and a pulse.

He rounded the corner from 6A in a brown tweed three-piece with a watch chain across the waistcoat, carrying a white saucer in front of him at the height of a waiter’s wrist. On it were a cup of tea, full, and one Rich Tea biscuit squared to the rim. The cane hung from his forearm by its brass duck. When he turned his head to take me in, the hearing aids let out two thin notes, like a kettle a long way off.

“Mr Mahajan. You are early.”

“I wanted not to be late, Mr Pto—” The P came out of me like a cork. “Tolemy. Tol-uh-mee. Sorry.”

“Quite so.” He pressed the call button with the duck’s head. “The P is silent, like most of my family’s expectations. I say it to everyone, and everyone laughs, and I am no longer able to determine whether the laughter is for the remark or for my family.”

We rode Right to four in a silence that he conducted. At the west end of the corridor he set the saucer on the deep sill of the landing window with a small click and turned the cup until the handle pointed left. From his waistcoat he drew a gold watch, flicked the lid open with a thumbnail and bowed over it, like a man at a graveside. There is no clock on that landing. I have since learned that it is the one place in the building where he trusts the time.

“Four o’clock, Mr Ambler.” He used the voice of a man announcing a train. “I have brought the young man from the office. Mr Mahajan keeps the books. One introduces. It is the least one can do.”

“How do you do,” I said, to a windowsill.

The steam went straight up. I watched it harder than it deserved. Mr Grieve closed the watch and took my elbow with a hand that weighed nothing and held like a clamp. “We leave him to it,” he said. “Observation is a form of pressure.”

Apartment 6A is the corner unit, with a window on 31st Street and another on the alley, and it contains forty-one years of other people’s worst days. They stand floor to ceiling on three walls, steno pads in bundles of twenty tied with string, each bundle labeled on a strip of masking tape in a hand as small as a stitch: a month, a year, a courtroom number. On the desk a stenotype machine sat under a dust cloth, the shape of a small covered birdcage, and beside it lay a microcassette recorder the size of a bar of soap with its cord wound round it in even turns. On the mantel and the bookcase and the sill stood six clocks, and all six said a few minutes earlier than they should.

“They’re six minutes slow,” I said, before I could stop myself.

“I set them correct on Sundays.” Mr Grieve lowered himself into a chair with arms. “By Wednesday each has made up its own mind. I have ceased to argue. A man who has spent four decades insisting on the exact time learns, eventually, which witnesses will not be moved.”

The carpet at the window had been worn to canvas in an oval, where someone had stood for fifty years looking at 31st Street. He made tea in a brown pot under a cozy knitted in a green I would have called regrettable, and he poured with a steadiness I took for strength and later understood to be habit. “Sugar?”

“No, thank you.”

“Nor I. And I send his plain, which is not economy, Mr Mahajan. It is cowardice. One cannot write to a man to ask how many lumps he takes. I have wondered for thirty-six years.” The cup came to me on a saucer with a rose on it. “Biscuit. Now. You have brought the question.”

“I brought several.”

“I said the better one.”

I took out the index card. A man who writes his questions on an index card for a tea invitation has told you most of what you need to know about him. “What is in 4B? Who is paying for it? What happens if I delete the row?”

“The first is a question for a locksmith.” Mr Grieve drank. “The third is a question for Mr Pugh, or a priest. The second has merit. But all three, you will observe, concern the room.” He set the cup down. “The better question is always about the questioner. I will give you a week. Strictly speaking, I may not have a great deal more to give, but a week is a decent allowance.”

I put the card in my pocket. It felt, there, like a small flat lie.

“Tell me what you know.”

I told him: the row, the receipts, the washer. When I said the name on the undershirts, he stopped, with his hand on the handle of the pot.

“You have seen his laundry.”

“On Thursday. There’s a washer in the basement. It doesn’t have water in it.” I heard how that sounded. “The undershirts had his name on a tape, T. Ambler, sewn by hand. Somebody who liked doing it.”

“Quite so.” He did not move for about as long as it takes to read a short line. “I have wondered about the washing. A man who has been in a room since the spring of 1961 must have clean shirts. It is not the sort of thing a man in my position may ask.” He poured, though neither cup needed it. “I had the name from the clerk of the day, Mr Kwan, in the spring of 1990, in that chair, with a book open on his knee. Thaddeus Ambler, of Dayton, Ohio. A salesman. He checked in, and he has not checked out.”

“Did you ever see him?”

“Never. I deduce.” He said it as one gives a plea. “I came to the Harwick in 1974, Mr Mahajan, when it was a hotel with a barroom and a house detective and a switchboard run by a woman called Dolores who could tell from the way you said your room number whether you had been drinking. The night court sat at Merrow and Twenty-eighth. I was its reporter, and a man who takes down other people’s worst hours wishes to sleep where the hours are not so bad. In 1986 they turned the place into apartments, and I became a tenant instead of a guest. The difference lies chiefly in the lease.”

“And the plate?”

“In 1989 I left a cup of tea on that sill, as one leaves milk for a cat, on a day I was too tired to take it back downstairs. At ten past four it was warm and empty.” He put a finger to the bridge of his nose. “I was no longer tired. I was very much afraid, for about a week, and then I recognized the sensation as manners. One does not leave a man’s tea untended. One asks after his health. He answers.”

He nodded at the wall over the desk, where a typed card hung in a small frame. I got up to read it.

THE SAUCER | Handle left: yes. Handle right: no. Cup warm and empty: received. Cup full and cold: not today. Biscuit gone, tea untouched: ask again. | P.G., 14 Sept 1989. Amended 1996 (biscuit clause).

“I set it left each day,” he said behind me. “Left is the offer, and left is the acceptance, and I ask a question aloud, and if the answer is no, the handle is turned to the right. Thirty-six years of one-word answers, Mr Mahajan. I do not say it is conversation. I say it is correspondence.” The hearing aids whistled as he turned. “I have had three rights. The second was the day I asked whether he would care to try a different biscuit. He is a man of fixed views on biscuits.”

I laughed. It was the last time I did that afternoon, and I did it too loudly, and he permitted it with a small movement of one ear.

“You will want to know about the clerks,” he said. “Everyone who sits in that chair does, at about month fourteen.”

I did not ask how he knew my month.

“Mr Kwan was a courteous young man who counted everything. The stairs, the tiles, the minutes the Left elevator stuck, which he reported to me on a card. He sat where you are sitting, with his knees together. In 1998 he was no longer at his desk, and I was told he had taken a position elsewhere, and I did not believe it. Mrs Dunleavy was engaged the following January. Lemon drops. She wrote everything down, and then one day she had been written.”

“Written.”

“I decline to improve upon it.” He lifted the cup, put it down. “Both wrote it down. It was the one habit they shared. I should not like to hear, in a few years, that it had been a third.”

“I’m not going anywhere.”

“Nor were they.” He said this without cruelty, as a witness gives the date. “You will wish to know whether I have seen anyone go in. I have not. I deduce, which is not the same as seeing, and a court reporter is trained to know the difference. Let the record show that I am deducing.” He folded his hands over the watch chain. “I will add one item that is not evidence. Mrs Whitmore’s husband went out for cigarettes in 2016. I knew the man slightly. A pipefitter, in flannel. He fixed my radiator in 2011, unasked, and declined tea. He did not smoke, in my observation. I do not think it was cigarettes.”

I said nothing about the socks. I am a person who writes things down and does not say them. But I added, which is what I do, and by the time the sum reached my face he was looking at me with an expression of regret, as if he had passed me a bill.

He coughed. It was the cough with the drawer in it, and it did not stop at the usual place. He took out the handkerchief and held it to his mouth, and I got to my feet and stood in the middle of his carpet doing nothing, as I do. When he lowered the cloth he folded it, and put it in his waistcoat, and did not look at it.

“Pleural,” he said. “Four months, six if I am agreeable. I mention it so that the record is current.” He said it the way you give a license number, and then he reached across and moved my saucer an inch toward me, since I had not touched the biscuit.

I sat down. “Is there someone I should—”

“There is Mrs Han, who has already brought soup. There is the woman from the hospice, whose name I have not retained. There is the gentleman in four, who has been informed.” He regarded me down the length of his face. “I do not require rescue, Mr Mahajan. I should like to be attended. It is a different thing, and the building understands it better than the profession.”

At twenty to six he opened a drawer in the desk and took out a steno pad, new, still holding its cellophane, with paper tinted faint green and a red rule down the middle. He tore off the cellophane with the care of a man unwrapping a medal. “I have ninety-one of these,” he said. “I bought a gross in 1996 against a retirement I did not suppose would be so long. I have no further use for them, strictly speaking, except this one.”

I took it. It was lighter than it looked.

“A record is only kind if it is left for someone,” said Mr Grieve. “Nobody has ever left the next one anything but a key.”

He gave me a pencil from a jar of them, sharpened to a needle, and I opened the pad on my knee. The page was very white. It had that faint tooth to the paper that makes a pencil sound like something. I wrote the date, and under the date, because I could not think what else a person writes, I wrote it all on one line. Sat 18 Oct. Mahajan, D. Record begins.

He read it upside down. A court reporter can read anything upside down. He nodded once, and I thought for a moment I was dismissed.

“Strictly speaking,” he said, “that is the second line. The first is the question.”

chapters.title: A Controlled Experiment
chapters.html:
By nine on Sunday evening I had a spreadsheet of 212 possessions with a column headed Condition, and nobody had asked me for it.

It is a stranger thing than it sounds, to find out what you own. I had gone through Tolliver Court 3F room by room with my phone in one hand and a label maker in the other, and by the end the studio looked like a place I had never lived. Every item had a photograph, a number from A-001 to A-212, and a line. The bed. The chair, and the folding chair behind the door. My mother’s steel tiffin, A-044, Fair, contents thirty-one rubber bands and fourteen AA batteries. Eleven shirts. Fourteen pairs of socks, which I put on a separate tab and called the control group, and I would like it noted that I did this with a straight face.

The method was not complicated, and I had been using its relatives at work for years. If the building billed me for what I entered, then I could enter something small, count before and after, and the difference would be the bill. It is a reconciliation. The only unusual feature was that the account was me. I had thought of asking an independent party to witness the count, and found I was the only candidate on the list.

At the last minute I added a column headed Last Used, because when you photograph a drawer you ought to say when you last opened it. I did not know yet that it was the only column that mattered.

I chose three edits and chose them to be the size of the ones I had made on the Monday before my mother’s voicemail went. Each was true. I want that understood. I was not going to put a lie into the roll to find out what a lie cost. I wanted to fix three things that were wrong and see what the fixing took.

TEST A | HT-2F | Fenske, O. | Surname: trailing space removed | Queued 21:14 | TEST B | HT-5E | Obi, P. | Phone: transposed digits corrected | Queued 21:20 | TEST C | HT-1C | Ruiz, D. | Emergency contact: daughter’s new number | Queued 21:26

Owen Fenske’s name did not end in a space, and now it didn’t. Priscilla Obi in 5E, a nurse I had met once in the mailroom at six in the morning, had two digits of her phone number the wrong way round, and now she did not. Mrs Ruiz’s daughter had moved to a new number in August, and the note to say so had sat in the file since September. I saved each one. The green tick came up each time, and nothing whatever happened, and I stood in the middle of the room and listened to the refrigerator.

At 11:40 I closed the laptop, as I do every night, and sat at the table with my hands flat on the lid, like a man keeping a book from opening. At 11:57 the fan came on.

I lifted the lid. The Tenantry session was open. I had logged out at ten. The cursor was moving, and my hand was on the table beside the laptop, and it crossed the page at a steady walk, the way you cross a room you know in the dark. It opened HT-4B and clicked Payments. It typed in the Amount field with a rhythm I knew because it was mine: the small pause after the point, the two zeros a beat late. It chose CASH. It did not touch the next field, and the next field filled itself. PREPARER. At 23:58 it pressed Save, and the screen went green.

HT-4B | Audit | 10/19 23:58 | RENT POSTED | Method: CASH | Amount: $1,840.00 | Source of Funds: PREPARER | By: DMAHAJAN

I had taken my hands off the keys at the first click. The odd part, the part I have not got used to, is that I did not feel robbed. It was like watching someone else do my job, quietly and well, with no wasted motion. It was the best I had ever seen it done. I ended the session with the mouse, and the cursor went to the Log out link at the same unhurried walk, and the fan stopped, the way a refrigerator stops.

From the drawer under the stove, where I had put the label maker after the inventory, came a whir and a small chunk. I opened the drawer. It had printed a label and pushed it out, like a tongue. HT-4B / 10-25 / RCVD D.M. I peeled the backing and pressed it inside the cover of the notebook, because I could think of nowhere else it belonged.

At 2:08 I was sitting on the kitchen floor in front of the radiator under the window, with my back against the cabinet and the notebook on my knee, in the posture of a man waiting for a phone to ring. At 2:10 the clock on the stove, which says 2:10 to me more often than I like, stopped saying anything else. The pipes sang. It came up through the building from somewhere under the parking lot, a long, low, rising note, like a finger going round the rim of a glass, and the fin of the radiator under my hand went warm. It knocked twice.

I knocked back. Twice, with the knuckle of my right forefinger, on the fin. A silence followed, in which I could hear my own pulse in the frames of my glasses. Then something let out a sigh in the pipes, long, like a person settling into a chair at the end of the day, and the stove clock said 2:11.

I started the count at six, with the tiffin, and worked outward with a pencil. I will give the result in the order I found it, because the order mattered later.

Spare keys, A-017. They had hung on the hook by the door, and the hook was there. Two keys on a ring with a leather fob: my spare to 3F, and the key to my father’s side door in Edison, which my mother had pressed into my hand the day I moved out, saying you never know. Last Used: last spring. The hook hung with nothing on it like a coat rack in a room with no coats.

The gift card, A-091. Twenty-five dollars at a bookstore, from the Corvane holiday party, in the drawer with the takeout menus, unspent. Last Used: December. The menus lay flat against one another where it had been.

The gym tag, A-130. A plastic fob for a gym on Kessler Avenue that I joined in March of the year before last and had visited four times. Last Used: unknown.

One mug, A-052. The second of the set, the clean one that I never used. There was a mug on the drainer, the used one. Beside it the rack held a space the size of a mug, and the rack had not closed up around it.

Four lines I could not tick. Two hundred and twelve, now two hundred and eight. Beside each missing line stood a Last Used in my own typing, and the shortest gap was six months. Everything that was gone was a thing I had not touched in half a year. Everything I touched was still there: the mug I drank from, the keys in my pocket, the phone. If it was the building that had done this, it had taken what in the apartment had nobody’s attention.

I wrote the problem down, because it was one. Three edits, four items, and one rent. It did not match, and I did not have a theory of why. A control group of socks, and the socks were all there, and I noted with some pride that I had been right about the socks.

The fifth thing I found at seven, when I opened the messaging app to text Anjali good morning, which I do not do. The list of conversations was one shorter than it had been on Saturday. I searched for Quizzy Rascals and got nothing. I searched for Rascals, and Quizzy, and Table 4, which returned a calendar entry from the second January before. The thread was not in the trash. Two years of capitals of Burkina Faso and who-had-the-tiebreaker had not been deleted, because deleting leaves a hole, and this had left none.

I took an envelope off the pile of mail and wrote the roster the way I used to write it on the beer mat for the league sheet. The Rascals filled Table 4 at the Gaslight, which seats nine, and we filled it: eight of them and me. Priya. Big Ted. Lorraine, from the billing office at Merrow General. Amir. Femi. Hae-won, who did the music rounds. That was six. I could see the table. Nine chairs, and seven with somebody in them, six and me. Two chairs were occupied. I knew they were, the way a tongue knows a gap in the teeth, and I could not tell you who had sat in them. I could not tell you whether I had liked them. I sat with the pencil above the envelope for twenty-three seconds, which is the length of the voicemail, and then I put the envelope in the notebook, beside the label.

At the office Joyce had the night-drop envelope on her blotter, with 4B on the front in pencil. She had counted it twice. “Eighteen-forty,” she said. “To the dollar. Noted.” There were two red-seal two-dollar notes in it, 1953, with consecutive serial numbers, which she did not like. “I won’t bank what’s worth more than it says,” said Joyce. She had a row of them now in the clear sleeves in her tray, a silver certificate, a five, the two twos, laid out edge to edge like a lineup, and she looked at them the way you look at a lineup when you know it is not the right one but cannot say which man is wrong.

I wore a shirt for the Diwali call, the blue one with the collar. I propped the phone against the tiffin at five to seven and sat down at the table with the one chair, and Edison arrived.

I knew the dining room at once, by the light, which is always a little yellower than any other light in the world, and the long table with the leaf in it. On the table was everything. Puris puffed like small gold hats under a cloth. Aloo sabzi, shrikhand in a glass bowl, a plate of chakli, besan ladoo from a neighbor in a sheet of foil. The dal sat in the big steel pot that comes out for funerals and weddings, and there was a lot of it. I knew the card. Always makes eight. There were four people at the table.

“Happy Diwali,” said Anjali. She had her hair down, which is rare, and a pair of gold hoops, and she was bright in the way she is bright for Tia, at a volume she can hold for about an hour. Under it she was very tired. I saw it at the corners of her eyes and she saw me see it. “You wore a shirt.”

“I said I would.”

“You said you’d wear a shirt. Nobody said it’d be that shirt. It’s fine. It’s a good shirt.” Tia pushed into the frame. She wore a pink kurta with sequins at the collar and held a saucer with a tiny clay lamp in it. “I lit it by myself,” she said. “Papa helped. Papa held the match.”

“Happy Diwali, Tia.”

“Happy Diwali, Uncle Spreadsheet. Did your total add up?”

“I’m still checking.”

“Check faster,” said Tia, with reproach, and was removed by Ben.

At the far end of the table my father sat in the cardigan with the elbows gone, with a steel tumbler of water in front of him. Suresh Mahajan is sixty-eight and has been getting smaller, in Edison, since January of last year, the way a coat gets smaller on a hook. He did not come to the screen. He lifted one hand off the table, flat, palm out, at about the height of his shoulder, and held it there. I knew the gesture. It was what he did at the stop on Oak Street when a bus he did not need pulled in: no, thank you, go on.

“He’s being Dad,” said Anjali, quietly, turning the phone a few degrees toward her. “He’s glad you’re here. It’s this, or he’d have gone to the garage.”

“Tell him the quarter turn was right,” I said. “On the pots.”

She did. “Papa. Dev says the quarter turn was right.” My father’s hand stayed where it was, a little higher, I thought, and then it came down, and he picked up the tumbler and looked into it.

We talked for an hour. I will not put all of it down. Ben had carved the second pumpkin and was proud of it, and Anjali had put one of Mummy’s recipe cards in a frame in the hall, and I said it was a good idea, and she said it was a good card, the one for the chai, with a thumbprint of turmeric in the corner. At the end she held the phone close and said “Sunday at six” and I said “Sunday at six,” and the screen went to the picture of my own face, in the blue shirt, looking like a man who had just been handed a form.

I sat with the phone for some time. I tried to hear my father. I could see him: the cardigan, the tumbler, the hand. I could see the hand perfectly. I went for the sound of him saying my name, the way he says it, which is Dev-a, with the weight on the second part, and then Devendra, which is how he says it when I have done something, and I got a voice that was not his, a flat voice on a train platform announcing the next stop. I could not recall one sentence. I had not had a conversation with my father longer than a prescription since the funeral. If you had asked me that afternoon what I was holding least, I would have named a mug, or a postcard. I knew now that it was a man at the end of a table, and I knew it the way you know the balance in your account, without looking and to the cent.

Fourteen months. Eighteen-forty a month. I tried to think what that was, in a currency like this one. The second chair. The Gaslight. The postcard I had not turned over, and the second mug, and the Rascals, and a father’s voice that had gone out of range. I had thought I had a small life because I was a small person. It had not crossed my mind that someone was drawing it down. Zofia had measured me by eye in the lobby on my first day and with a tape in October, and had said, with the sympathy of a woman telling a man his hem was coming down, that I had lost two centimeters. She had been right to the centimeter. I had thought she was being kind.

I took the notebook out and wrote the rule, plainly, because a rule should be plain.

Everything I enter is paid for out of something I wasn’t looking after.

I looked at it for as long as it takes a kettle to boil, and then I wrote the next line.

What have I been paying the rent with?

And under it, smaller, in the handwriting I keep for things I would rather not have read:

It took two of the Rascals and I did not notice which.

chapters.title: Bernice Stays On
chapters.html:
A beige tower hummed in a closet that smelled of warm dust and lemon drops, and Rafa stood in the doorway like a man at the edge of a pool he used to swim in.

The server closet is at the end of the basement corridor, past Rafa’s shop, behind a steel door marked SERVER in strips of label-maker tape older than my employment. It holds a card table, a metal chair, a monitor with a bulging face, a green steel cabinet, a shelf with one banker’s box on it and, on the floor, in a clean square of linoleum of its own, the tower. It was the beige that every computer was before I was born, a beige that was never a color anyone chose. On the front, on three strips of embossed vinyl tape, someone had pressed out BERNICE and DO NOT UNPLUG and M.D.

I had asked Rafa on Monday where Margie kept her old records. He had looked at the ceiling. On Tuesday morning he stopped at my desk, which he never does, and said to the stapler, “One o’clock. Bring your glasses.” I do not need to bring my glasses. I wear them. We were two men with mended spectacles, mine in green electrical tape and his in white, the kind of equipment a building produces.

“Corvane took RentWise off every desktop at go-live,” I said. “I assumed they’d taken the server.”

“Nobody told it to stop.” Rafa leaned on the frame. “Margie asked.”

“Margie asked what?”

“That it stays on. She said, when I’m gone somebody is going to want to look at it. She said put a label.” He moved the toothpick across. “She wrote the letters on a piece of paper. I pressed them out.”

The old monitor took a full minute to warm, and then it lit, green on black, with a white cursor that blinked like a patient man. RENTWISE 2.4. COPYRIGHT 2003. USER: I typed DMAHAJAN, which had worked for thirteen months at my own desk, and it worked here. A banner crossed the top. READ ONLY. SUPERSEDED BY TENANTRY 9. Below it were the old function keys, F1 UNITS, F2 TENANTS, F3 LEDGER, F4 REPORTS, as plain as the buttons in an elevator. I felt a warmth for it that I had not felt for the new software, the warmth you feel for a man who never pretended to be anything but a clerk.

I typed HT-4B and pressed F6, which is History.

RENTWISE 2.4 | HT-4B | TENANT HISTORY (10) | 04/11/61 ******** | 06/04/68 ******** | 11/18/72 ******** | 03/02/75 ******** | 10/27/79 ******** | 12/09/83 ******** | 11/20/98 ******** | 05/22/03 ******** | 01/16/16 ******** | 08/30/19 DUNLEAVY, M. PD THRU 10/25 | END DATES: NONE | NAMES OLDER THAN 7 YRS MASKED PER RETENTION POLICY RP-7

I counted the rows twice. Ten. Each had a start date and not one had an end. In sixty-four years nobody had left. Nine of the names had been replaced by asterisks under a retention policy I could picture the committee for, and the tenth, the only one the rule had not reached, was a name I knew from a Christmas card Joyce could not find. Dunleavy, M., paid through October. My payment on Sunday night had gone to her. She was current.

I looked for some time at 01/16/16. It was a Saturday, as I checked later. There was no name to go with it, and I did not need one.

“There are ten of them,” I said.

“I don’t read the screen,” said Rafa.

“No. I know.”

The banker’s box on the shelf said HOTEL REGISTERS in black marker. It held a dozen cloth-bound volumes with their spines flaking, and I took out Vol. 14 and opened it on the card table. The paper had gone the color of tea. The columns had been ruled in blue by a machine in a printing house that no longer existed, and the entries ran down them in the upright script of a man who had been taught penmanship as a form of discipline.

HARWICK HOTEL REGISTER | Vol. 14 | AMBLER, T. (Mr.) | Dayton, O. | Rm 412 | Arrived 11 Apr 1961 | Departure: indef.

The line above him had left on the fourteenth of April. The line below him had left on the twelfth. Ambler, T. (Mr.) had written his city in the careful circle of a man who signs forms for a living, and under Departure someone at the desk had put indef. and a small flourish, the way a clerk puts a full stop on a sentence he does not expect to have questioned.

The green cabinet had two drawers, and the upper one carried a strip of white tape that said NOTES TO FILE. I had expected an archive. I had half expected nothing. It held three hanging folders, and the first two had tabs.

KWAN, E. had one sheet in it, yellowed, folded in thirds, with one line.

DUNLEAVY, M. had a page torn from a legal pad, covered in round upright pencil that had been pressed hard, and under it a greeting card with a cartoon pigeon in a necktie on the front, carrying a briefcase.

Nov. 1998. Whatever you enter comes out of somewhere. E. Kwan

30 Aug. Keep the row. Be kind to Noreen. She is trying. M.D.

I had needed a spreadsheet and a voicemail and four missing items and two missing people to write on Sunday night what Ellis Kwan had written in one line, in the same November that stood against the seventh row of the history I had just read. I sat on the metal chair. I felt, for a moment, as one feels on being handed the answer key by a teacher who has thoughtfully put the date on it.

Inside the pigeon the printed words said WE’LL MISS YOU. Under them a dozen people had signed in a dozen inks. J. Lim, in a hand like type, Best wishes, and a space after it where she had begun a second sentence and stopped. R. Ibarra, pressed hard enough to emboss the card. A big purple gel-pen scrawl across the bottom half of the page, round, in a hand I had seen on a Post-it that said 31 MO.

Margie, you’ll be missed! (Kidding. You’re not going anywhere. Ha!) N.W.

I read the Ha! twice. It did not improve. It had been written by a person in good spirits, or one performing good spirits for a card, and nobody in that office had asked what the joke was a joke about. There was the third folder behind the two, with no name on the tab but a word in pencil, NEXT, and nothing inside it, not a sheet. I shut the drawer on it the way you shut a door on a sleeping child.

“Rafa.”

“Mm.”

“You said Margie asked for the server. What else did she ask?”

He pulled out the other chair and sat, which I had never seen him do anywhere but his own stool, the way a man sits in a pew when the service is not his. The toothpick came out of his mouth. He turned it over in the fingers of the hand that stops at the knuckle.

“The thirtieth of August,” he said. “A Friday. She came down to the shop at ten after four. She had her purse, and the cardigan, and no box. Her things she left in the drawer. She said, somebody will want the tin.” He looked at the toothpick. “She said, ‘Rafa, would you bring the key.’ I said, which key. She said, ‘You know which one, dear.’ I asked had she eaten.”

“Had she?”

“She said yes. It was a lie. She never ate lunch. She sucked those lemon candies and said it was the same.” A smile came and went under the moustache. “We went up in Left. It opened on four by itself. Between the doors, where the cabinet is, there was a door. Like in an office. Beige, with the number, and a knob. I had walked by that wall for twelve years.”

“What did you do?”

“I turned the key.” He said it flatly, like a man reading a figure off a meter. “She said thank you. She walked in. The door stood there exactly as long as it took her to walk through, and then it shut, and I put my hand on the wall, and it was a wall. I went downstairs and I oiled the key.”

“And you’ve oiled it every morning since.”

“Every morning.”

“Why?”

“In case she wants to come out.” He put the toothpick back, a little roughly, as a man puts back a cigarette he has promised to give up. “You do not turn a key for a person and then let it go stiff.”

I asked it as gently as I could. “Where is she now?”

“Upstairs.”

“Upstairs where?”

Rafa looked at the ceiling.

Behind me the monitor had gone on glowing, and I turned the chair to it with the reluctance of a man turning back to a stove. I pressed F1 and typed HT-4B. The unit screen came up. UNIT, TENANT, RENT, BALANCE, LSTART. Below SQFT was a field I had passed for thirteen months without noticing, because I had never had a reason to, two letters wide. DR.

RENTWISE 2.4 | HT-4B | DR: 1 | LAST EDIT: DUNLEAVY 08/30/19 16:02

DR is doors. A one, under Margie’s name, at two minutes past four on the last afternoon anyone saw her. I paged through the other forty units. Every one said DR 1, last edit IMPORT, March 2003. Only HT-4B had a human hand on it.

The mapping sheet from the Tenantry migration had come to me in September in an email called MIGRATION PLAN v3 (FYI), which I had read the way I read every FYI. It said that DR would be carried across to DOOR_COUNT for rows with a valid FLOORPLAN_ID. Forty rows had one. HT-4B did not. As far as I could tell, the importer had looked at a door with no plan to hang it on and left it on BERNICE like a coat on a hook. That was why the row had gone red on the sixth of October and not in 2003, and the field it had dropped had a one in it.

I thought of the beige door in Espie’s video, standing a finger’s width open at 0:14 and a hose cabinet at 0:15. A door in a field nobody had cleared. An afterimage. I wrote DR=1 in the notebook and underlined it once, which is Noreen’s habit, and which I caught myself in.

At twenty to three I was at my desk. The office was doing what it does at that hour. Joyce’s calculator ran along like a man on a treadmill. Espie was out, showing 3D. Noreen’s door was shut, and her keys silent behind it.

I opened the drawer. It stuck, and gave, with the cough. The tin and the button were where they had always been, and I took out the button and held it in my palm, a four-hole horn button the color of oatmeal with a quarter inch of thread still through one hole. It had been pulled off something, not cut. I put the tin to my ear and shook it. Two lemon drops, fused. Somebody will want the tin, Rafa had said, in Margie’s voice, ten minutes ago, in a closet. I had been somebody. I had had it for fourteen months and thought it was rubbish.

The chair took my spine as it always does, and I knew now why it fit so well. It had not been broken in to me. It was a chair that had spent twenty years learning a different back, and had been kind enough to find the common ground.

I pulled up the PDF I had saved from the application portal in the summer of last year, the posting I applied to, and which I had read, I would have said, closely. I read everything closely. It was my best quality, and I had listed it as such. I scrolled to the top. The font was the font of a document that wants to be taken for granted.

CORVANE PROPERTY GROUP | Position description | Rent Roll Clerk, Harwick Terrace | Budget line 4100.07 | Reports to: Property Manager | Replaces: M. Dunleavy (vacant since 08/30/19) | Posted 04/22

I could have recited the budget line. I had read that sheet on the day I applied, and again on the day I accepted, and once more, in the lobby, on the nineteenth of August, with my bag on my shoulder and my first day in front of me. I had not once looked at the name.

chapters.title: Required Field
chapters.html:
Publish blocked | 3 required fields are empty for HT-4B | FLOORPLAN_ID | PERMIT_NO | DOOR_COUNT | Resolve all required fields to continue. | OK | Learn more

The box arrived at 8:52 on Wednesday morning, when I clicked Publish to Data Room on the rent roll, which I had done sixteen times the week before as a rehearsal, and which had worked. It had a red border. The OK button did nothing. The Learn more button opened a help page on required fields in general, which began, A required field is a field that is required.

Behind it the queue stood where it had stood since go-live. HT-4B was at the top, in red. Behind it, in amber, were the 211 data-quality flags the sweep had raised on the sixth: trailing spaces, transposed digits, a lease that ended on a Sunday, a phone number with eleven digits and a hopeful look. They had been grayed out, like tickets in a queue where the front window has closed. I could edit them one at a time and each edit would save. I knew now what a save cost. I did not click on any of them.

At 9:20 I opened the Support chat, a small blue bubble with a headset, because I wanted a record that I had asked.

Tenantry Support | Brent K., Tier 1 | Dev: HT-4B is blocking publish. The three fields are not in the legacy export. What do I enter? | Brent K.: Super question! Have you tried entering the missing data?

I asked which data. He answered that it was the data that was missing. I thanked him, and the bubble closed, and the headset went on smiling after it had gone.

At 9:58 Randall wrote, in capitals.

From: Randall Pugh | To: Noreen Whitmore; Devendra Mahajan | Date: Wed 22 Oct, 9:58 AM | Subject: DATA ROOM PUBLISH BLOCKED: HT-4B (ACTION REQUIRED, DAILY UNTIL RESOLVED)

Team, the publish gate will not release the Harwick rent roll to the Larchmont data room while any line fails validation. Going forward this is a hard stop. I have asked Tenantry to queue the 211 data-quality flags behind HT-4B so nothing gets cleared out of order, and Brent advises the missing fields are, quote, self-explanatory. Please advise status by EOD. I appreciate the bandwidth. Randall

At noon I went up and counted the corridor. Twenty-four. I had been at twenty-one on Monday, and I had not counted on Tuesday, being underground, and I stood by the bicycle at 4C with the notebook open and wrote 24 beside 21 and looked at the two numbers as a man looks at a blood pressure. I did not knock on anything. On the way down I met Chioma at the mailboxes, signing for a box, in the green clogs and the red frames, and I said, because I had been rehearsing it, “I may be in the building late tonight.”

“Define late.”

“Technically after midnight.”

She looked at me over the frames and said nothing, and it was a long nothing, with a lot of work in it. Then she picked up her box. On Monday, in the lobby, over the package locker, she had put her number into my phone with the air of a woman installing a smoke detector. I took the way she did not ask as a sign that she was an excellent neighbor.

At ten to five Noreen came out of her office with her coat over her arm and her bag on her shoulder. She stopped in the doorway of my side of the room, a thing she never does, with the keys held silent in her left hand, and she looked at the banner, at the backward letters of EMBRACE THE CHANGE, and not at me.

“Put something in, Dev.”

“Which field?”

“Put a one.” The gum had stopped. “Just put one.”

“I’m not sure I can enter data I haven’t verified. DOOR_COUNT is a count. I’d want to know—”

“It’s a one.” She said it with an odd flatness, a woman reading a number off a card. “The system takes a one. Randall gets his tick. It won’t hurt anything.” She had said that last in the tone you use with a child about a needle, with the exact amount of conviction the situation requires and not a gram over. Then, because she is Noreen, she said “Let’s circle back,” and went out into the lobby, and the glass door sighed behind her.

I sat for some time looking at the box. I tried the field. I typed a 0 into DOOR_COUNT, to see, and the cell went pink. Enter a whole number from 1 to 9. A unit may have one door or nine and may not have none. It is a reasonable rule, the sort I would have written myself. It had never before sounded like a sentence.

I considered the others. I had the permit number, on a half sheet from the Annex in my wallet, and I did not type it. It was the permit for a window. I know the difference between a field and a fact, and a woman in a lavender cardigan had told me, for nothing, that a number is only as true as the work it is attached to. The floor plan I could not have done at all: there was no sheet, and nothing in the county’s cabinets drew a B. But DOOR_COUNT I could do honestly. There was a door. I had seen it on a video, and RentWise said so in a one with Margie’s name on it. I would not be inventing a value. I would be carrying one forward, which is all a migration is. Technically, it was data entry.

I wrote that on the handout from the Lunch & Learn, and then I looked at it for a while and wrote beneath it, Technically so is anything.

At 9:12 that evening, in the office, with the lights off except mine and the rain ticking in the gutter outside the front glass, my phone lit.

Chioma Eze, 9:12 PM: For the record I’m on shift till seven. Don’t do anything stupid.

Dev Mahajan, 9:13 PM: It’s data.

Chioma Eze, 9:13 PM: That’s what stupid people say.

At 11:30 the glass door opened, and Rafa came in. He was in boots and his canvas coat, with a steel thermos in one hand and the brass key in the other, its green tag hanging from his fist. His face was a face you see at the back of a funeral.

“You came.”

“I didn’t say I would come.”

“No.”

“I didn’t say I wouldn’t.” He set the thermos on Joyce’s blotter, where nothing is ever set, and it left a ring. “Is the kind of night you bring coffee to.”

We did not talk much. He sat in Espie’s chair and turned it a quarter turn, back and forth, with his foot. I watched the clock in the corner of the screen. At 11:57 I put my cursor in the field. At 11:58 I typed a 1 with my right forefinger, the split thumbnail of my left hand pressed against the edge of the desk to steady it, and saved. The screen thought about it, and the banner stayed red, and a small line changed in the corner.

HT-4B | Validation | 2 of 3 required fields remain.

Nothing happened in the room. Behind me Rafa took the toothpick out of his mouth, looked at it, and put it back.

We did not wait in the office. Rafa said that he was not going to climb four floors like a man going to a hanging, and that if it wanted us it would come, and if it did not we would have drunk the coffee. At five to two by the lobby clock, which meant one minute past, we sat on the bench by the mailboxes under the brass H with the thermos between us. He had poured the cap full. It tasted of cinnamon and the cap.

I watched the clock. At 2:01 by it the pipes began, low, from the basement, a note climbing through the risers behind the mailboxes. At 2:04 on the lobby clock, which is 2:10, the second hand reached the fifty-four and stayed there. My phone said 2:10 and then said 2:10 again. The radiator under the mailboxes knocked twice, and the doors of Left slid back by themselves, with the ceiling light on and nobody inside it. The display above read 4B.

Rafa stood up and put a hand flat on the frame of the car, as you touch a doorframe in a house where someone is ill. Then he stepped in. I went in after him. Neither of us touched the buttons. The doors closed, and the car rose through the numbers in no hurry, and it opened on four.

The corridor was a corridor. For about four seconds that was the whole of my report: the maroon carpet, the lozenges every three feet, the green clogs on their mat at the far west end, the blue bicycle at the far east. I walked to the mat and stood on it. I turned and faced the cabinet, with the notebook open in one hand and the pencil in the other, and I counted, and I stopped counting, because it was happening.

The red glass of the cabinet clouded as a window does when it is breathed on. The paint around it lifted. It did not peel. It lifted in one long clean line, the way laminate lifts at the edge of a lunchroom counter that has been wiped with the wrong cleaner for years, and under it the plaster was not plaster. It was a pale grain, like a cabinet door seen from very close. Three brass pins rose from the wall one after another at the left-hand edge, each turning a little as it came, like staples being drawn by a very slow remover. A molding drew itself around the lifted line with a sound like a thumbnail running down a comb. Two brass numerals sweated up through the paint at the height of a face, beading first, like drops on a cold glass, and then setting. A 4. A B, a little out of true.

Rafa crossed himself, forehead and chest and both shoulders, with his thumb, quickly, as a man does who has done it for years in places where he did not think it showed. “Mira,” he said. It was all he said, and he did not say the rest.

I would like to report a sound. There was very little of one: the comb, the small ticks of the pins, a faint dry pressure in the ears, as when a door is opened somewhere else in a house. It was quieter than an elevator. It was quieter than the office printer warming up. I have thought since that a building does not hurry what it has done a hundred times, and I stood in it with my notebook open and wrote nothing, as a man stands in a church who does not know when to sit.

The glass cleared. Where the hose had been, in the frame the cabinet had been, there was a door, beige, with a knob. As far as I could tell, to anyone who had not spent two weeks knocking on it, it still looked like a cabinet.

The corridor had changed too. I did not notice when. I noticed it in the way that the east end, where the bicycle should have been five paces off, was further, as though someone had taken the corridor by both ends and drawn it out, like a tape from its case, and the carpet had been drawn with it. The diamonds went on. I walked it, with my lips moving, from the mat. Fourteen paces to the door. Seventeen more to the bicycle. Thirty-one. I turned and walked it back and got thirty-one. On the sixth of October the two directions had disagreed, and a disagreement is at least a kind of measurement. These agreed. I would have given a great deal for a disagreement.

I put my hand to my belt loop for something to hold, and found the ring lighter than it should be. I do not mean it hung wrong. The ring carries ten keys, in an order I could draw in the dark: office, filing room, mailroom, night drop, basement, roof, and four more. It carried nine now, evenly spaced, as if the tenth had never been cut. I went round them twice by touch. The one that was gone was the key to 3F.

I had turned that key twice a day for four years, going out and coming in, and I could not have told you what color its head was, and now I could not, and that was the answer. It was not use the building counted. As far as I could tell, it was looking.

Rafa had his hand over his mouth. At the height of my waist, in the door, a rectangle appeared that had not been there a minute before, cut without a saw, with a brass flap on it and the word LETTERS in capitals.

The flap lifted. A folded square of yellow paper came out of the slot, through the gap, and stopped, quivering a little, like something being held out. I took it. It was a Post-it. I unfolded it under the corridor light, in the round hand of an OCCUPANT card in a mailbox and a note in a green cabinet.

You’re late. M.

chapters.title: The Tenant of Record
chapters.html:
The doorknob was warm. I mean warm the way a hand is warm when it has been round a cup, and I took my fingers back and looked at them as if they might be the ones at fault. Then I touched it again. Brass, worn pale on the side where a thumb goes, a hotel knob from the nineteen-twenties on a door that, at nine o’clock that evening, had been a fire-hose cabinet with a paper inspection tag on its nozzle.

“Is locked,” Rafa said.

“How do you know?”

“Because it is a door.” He held the key out on his flat palm, the green tag curled against his wrist. “Six years I put oil in that lock every morning. Is a good lock. Nobody has ever asked it anything.”

The key was cold. I had expected warm, and was obscurely relieved. “You’re not coming in.”

“I only oil it.” He pushed both hands into the pockets of his canvas coat, a man making sure of where they were. I saw then that he had a folding chair under his arm; it had been there in the elevator, and I had taken it for part of the coat. He shook it open on the maroon carpet and sat with his knees apart and the thermos between his boots. “Mira. I turned this key once, for her. A man gets one. If she asks for me, tell her the lock is good.”

“I’ll tell her.”

“And come out.”

“Technically that’s the plan.”

“Is not a plan,” said Rafa. “Is a hope. Go.”

The key went in without being asked twice. The lock turned over with a sound like a drawer finding its track, and the door opened inward on no hinge I could hear, onto a brown light, the light inside a paper bag held up to a window. The smell came first. Toast, a great deal of wet wool, and under both something I knew and could not place until I was over the sill: an iron radiator that has been running since before I was born.

I counted. I counted aloud, under my breath, with my lips moving, as I had at the Annex and on the stairs at Tolliver and at my own bathroom door. One put me over the sill. By three the corridor light had thinned behind me to a yellow stripe on the boards, which were oak, narrow, worn into a shallow path down the middle by sixty years of somebody walking to a window and back. The room was long and eleven feet across, I judged, with a hotel’s high ceiling. At the far end rain ran down the glass in a steady film with no wind behind it, and the light it let through was the brown of weak tea. The window had curtains. They were oatmeal, lined, hung in the bay as if it were an ordinary bay, and I knew how wide they were without measuring. Thirty-eight by sixty-two.

Five, six. Under the window stood an iron radiator, and beside it a card table with a hot plate on it and a brown pot on the hot plate. At the hot plate, with her back to me, a tall woman in a cardigan was doing something with a kettle. There were two chairs, a wing chair with the nap rubbed off its arms and a kitchen chair with a cushion tied to the seat. On the wall above the radiator ran a shelf of teacups, white, ten of them, in a row, and above the shelf a clock. It said ten past four. The second hand was not moving, and gave the impression of not intending to.

Seven. Through the walls on both sides, or near them, if walls was the word, there were other noises. A woman hummed three notes and then the same three. A pipe was being tapped, slowly, with something that wore a ring. A man a long way off whistled the opening bars of a tune and gave it up, and under all of it, steady as a refrigerator, someone slept.

Eight. Nine. My knees met the iron of the radiator, and I said “Sorry” to it.

“It’s used to that, dear,” said the woman at the hot plate, without turning round. “You took your time.”

She turned. She was a head taller than the figure I had watched lift a curtain from across 31st Street, or else the street had made her small, and she stooped as I do, from desks. Short gray hair, cut by someone who valued speed. Reading glasses on a cord. The hands were the hands I remembered, large, with a writer’s knuckles, one holding the kettle in a dishcloth and the other held out a little, palm up, as I had seen it held out to the rain. The cardigan was oatmeal. The third button down was missing, and a bit of blouse showed through the gap like a fact about her that she wasn’t hiding.

“I came as soon as the door—”

“I meant fourteen months, dear. The door was only the last four minutes.”

I had prepared three openings in the elevator, and each began with the word technically. I used none of them. I put my hand into my shirt pocket, where it had been since eleven o’clock, when I took it out of the drawer without deciding to, and held the horn button out on my palm.

She looked at it for about as long as it takes to read a short line. “Third from the top,” she said. “It went in the spring of 2011. I kept it in the drawer to sew back on, and never did, and I think I was holding a place.” She closed my fingers over it with her large dry hand. “Keep it for me, would you? I’d only lose it again. Is the tin still in the drawer?”

“Two lemon drops. They’ve fused.”

“They do that. Sit down. You’re a color I don’t care for.”

The wing chair had a dent in it the shape of somebody else. I said “Sorry” to that too, and she said “Oh, he’s fine,” and put a cup into my hands, plain white, with a chip in the handle. The tea was strong enough to stand a spoon in. It was the best I have had, which I put down to the hour and to the fact that it was the first thing anyone had given me in a month without a form attached.

“Not Mr Grieve’s, if you’re wondering,” she said, lowering herself onto the kitchen chair and arranging the cardigan over the gap. “That’s out of my tin. But what he leaves on the ledge at four goes down the room warm, and I’ll say for this building that in thirty-six years it hasn’t once come cold. I can’t tell you how I know. One does.” She looked at me over the glasses. “How is he?”

“He’s dying,” I said, because the tea had taken my manners. “Pleural. Four months, he says, six if he’s agreeable.”

“He would say that.” She nodded slowly. “He told me once in the lobby he’d outlast the boiler. I never learned which of them he meant to spite.”

I held the cup in both hands. “The note said I was late. Late for what?”

“For reading you, dear. I’ve been reading you since August of last year.” She reached under the card table and brought up a stack of white slips held with a rubber band, and put it on her knee. The top one said HT-4B-0825 in a printed box, and under it, Received by D. Mahajan, and in the date the seven had its bar through the stem. “The tenant’s copy. Fourteen of those, and the rest is whatever else you’ve sent me, which, dear, has mostly been mugs.”

“I haven’t sent you any mugs.”

“You cross your sevens. Somebody taught you.”

“My mother.”

“Then she’d want you to know it’s a lovely seven.” She said it as one reads out a figure, and it arrived as comfort, and I looked into the tea.

“I thought I’d found it,” I said. “The room. I thought it was here all along and nobody had looked.”
