“It was here all along. It was always here. It was a row that wanted a door, dear, and you filled it in.”

“I typed a one.”

“You typed a one in the right box, and it stands as long as you hold the desk. Ellis held it open from ‘eighty-six and I from ‘ninety-nine, and for anyone who’d attended, there it was in the corridor, plain as a cupboard. When a clerk is filed, the door shuts behind them and the number goes dead. Mine shut behind me on a Friday in August. It stayed shut six years. Then someone typed a one.”

“Filed.”

“Put in the room. It’s what the building would call it, if it called it anything. I find I say the word without feeling it.”

I set the cup down on the arm of the chair, where it left a ring that I immediately wished to apologize for. “I worked something out in a notebook,” I said. “On Monday. Everything I enter is paid for out of something I wasn’t looking after.”

“Yes.”

“That’s all? Yes?”

“The books must balance, dear. It isn’t a punishment. It’s accounting.” She said it with the tenderness of a woman who has had to say a hard thing so often it has become a household phrase. “You’ve found the cheap end of it. Spare keys, a card from a bookshop, a mug. It takes what you are holding least, and not by what it weighs, and if the sum is bigger than the thing it takes, the difference is simply lost. It doesn’t give change. And nothing is destroyed. I want you to hear that part, because I took a long time to. Nothing is destroyed. It’s filed.”

She nodded past my shoulder.

I had taken the long plank along the wall for a baseboard. It ran from the radiator past the wing chair and a good way down the room at the height of my waist, on iron brackets, and along it things had been set out like a museum that could not afford labels. Each had a paper tag tied on with string. Each tag was in capitals I could have drawn blind. A ring of keys: A-017, the spare to 3F, and the side-door key to a house in Edison. A bookstore card, twenty-five dollars. A gym tag. A white mug, the second of a set of two, A-052. On a nail by itself hung a single key, and now I saw the color of its head, which was blue rubber, and which I had no memory of whatever.

Beyond my things the plank went on. Tortoiseshell glasses. A cassette player with the tape still in it. A man’s wristwatch stopped at ten past nine. Beyond those, a pair of knitting needles stuck in a ball of gray wool, a hymnal, a church cookbook, a Polaroid of a cat on a windowsill. Twenty-one years of Margaret Dunleavy fitted on four feet of board.

At the end, where my things stopped, lay a microcassette the size of a book of matches. It had a label on it, in my capitals. I did not read the label. I knew the length of it, and where the line broke, and I looked at the tape for as long as I could and then at her.

“Yes,” said Margie. “Those go first. I’m sorry.”

I nodded. I could not think of anything to say that would not have been an apology to a cassette.

“Twenty-one years, I had,” she said, after a while, to the radiator. “There came a day I looked along that board and there was nothing on it that I hadn’t been using. I’d run through what I neglected and I’d started on what I loved, and I won’t pretend I was brave. Then I had the room.”

“I could quit,” I said. It came out in the voice of a man asking where the restroom is.

“Of course you could, dear. Nobody’s chained you. Then someone else sits in that chair and types, or no one does, and the pipes freeze, as they did in my absence. I heard them go. You’d be surprised what comes through a radiator.” She turned the kettle a quarter turn on the plate. “I’m not telling you what to do. I’m telling you what it costs, which was my whole job for twenty years and I was reasonably good at it.”

“How many of you are there?”

“Ten, dear. Mr Ambler’s the oldest tenant, April of ‘sixty-one. Miss Pruitt, who does the humming, ‘sixty-eight. Mr Haraldsen, who taps. ‘Seventy-two. Miss Marrero, who sings when she’s in voice, ‘seventy-five. Mr Tipps, the whistler, ‘seventy-nine. Miss Fiske, who says her lines, ‘eighty-three. Ellis, in ‘ninety-eight, and you’ve read his note. Mr Salazar, who snores like an honest man, 2003. Mr Whitmore, 2016.” She stopped. “And myself.”

“Whitmore,” I said aloud. It came out sounding like a tool.

“Ask Noreen how long she’s been not asking.”

I opened my mouth, and she shook her head very slightly. “You’ve worn the face since the socks, dear. It isn’t a hard face to read.”

There was a little rain on the glass. I told her the rest because there was nothing in my arrangements to stop me. That Corvane was being sold. That the buyer was called Larchmont, and was going through the books with a fine comb, and that on the thirty-first the roll would freeze, and a row that would not validate was a row someone in capitals wanted deleted. That I thought it did not stop at a delete button. There was an integration, a script, that would clean the roll, and I did not have a date for it, and I had not wanted to find out.

She heard it with her hands in her lap. When I had finished she took her glasses off and let them fall on their cord, and looked at the window, and the bay, and the curtains that Zofia had sewn for her.

“Then they’ll unmake us,” she said. “Ten of us and a radiator.” It was very quiet in the room. Somebody, far down, snored, and turned over. “I’ve had six years. I’d have liked to see a spring. But I’m not asking, dear.”

“I’m not going to let them.”

“Don’t promise. You’ll only have to keep it.” She put the glasses back on, and the whole face went back to a ledger, and I saw how much work the ledger did. “Go on. You’ve been here forty minutes by that clock, and that clock is not the sort one relies on. My regards to Rafa. Tell him the lock is good.”

“He said you’d say that.”

“Did he?” And she smiled for the first time, and it changed her from a column of figures into someone’s aunt.

I thanked her. I stood, and said sorry to the chair, and walked the length of the room with the horn button in my fist. I was thinking about a spring. I was thinking about a plank of things, and a name that sounded like a wrench, and a tape I had not read. When my hand found the knob it was the corridor, and the door had shut behind me with the small sound of a drawer, and I was standing on the maroon carpet in the light of the fourth floor.

The flap in the door, the one marked LETTERS, lifted an inch. “Count in, count out, dear,” said a voice through the slot, a good voice, level and kind. It was late. I was already in the corridor.

I had not counted. I stood with my mouth open and tried to find the number, as you reach for a step that is not there, and it was not anywhere. I did not know whether I had taken nine or twelve or twenty.

Rafa was asleep on the folding chair with his chin on his chest and the thermos between his boots. A newspaper lay open across his knees. It was the thick one, the Sunday edition, with the date at the top of every page, and I read it twice. SUNDAY, OCTOBER 26.

It had been Thursday. It had been a quarter past two on a Thursday morning, and I had gone in and said sorry to a radiator.

My pocket buzzed against my hip, once, and went on buzzing. I got the phone out. For the length of a breath the lock screen was lit, and across the telephone icon was a red circle with a number in it, and beside the number a name. 41. Anju. Then the little battery in the corner went red, and the screen went black in my hand, and I stood in a corridor that smelled of toast, looking at a reflection of a man with his mouth open.

The first thing I did was count the diamonds in the carpet between us and the elevator. It was the only arithmetic I could still do. Eleven.

chapters.title: The Missed Calls
chapters.html:
The phone came back to life on Rafa’s workbench, between a coffee can of washers and a bench vise, and for the better part of two minutes it would not stop. Every notification arrived with its small flat tick and slid down the cracked corner of the screen, a crack I had been meaning to see to since August, to make room for the next. I stood with half a bread roll in my hand and watched my sister’s name go by again and again in a column, like a rent roll.

“Eat,” said Rafa. “You look like a man who has read his own obituary.”

He had walked me down to the shop with a hand under my elbow, the way you walk a person out of a church, and had put me on the stool and the charger in the wall and a plate in front of me: a bolillo from the bag he keeps for lunch, a wedge of white cheese in a paper napkin, one pickled jalapeño, a knife with a taped handle. I hadn’t known I was hungry until the cheese. Then I ate all of it, standing, in six minutes, and he watched me with his arms folded and the toothpick going and said nothing about it.

On the pegboard behind him the forty-one hooks hung in their rows, the forty labeled keys and, at the end of the fourth row, one hook with nothing on it, marked 4B in his square capitals. He had taken the brass key from me at the elevator, with two fingers, and hung it back where it lived, and stood looking at it like a man returning a library book that he fears may be overdue.

“Three days,” he said.

“I was inside an hour. A little over.”

“Thursday I sit until seven. Nothing. I go do the boilers. I come at noon, nothing. Friday I come at six, at noon, at six. Yesterday I eat my lunch on the chair.” He took the toothpick out and looked at it. “This morning I bring the paper, and I think, today he comes. Then you come.” He put it back. “I did not know whether to wake you or call a priest. So I slept.”

The ticking stopped at forty-one. The screen went still, like a street after a parade, and presented the thread.

Anju, Thursday 8:14 PM: Dev. Call when you get this. Nothing wrong. Just call.

Anju, Friday 6:02 AM: Dev. Dev. Dev.

Chioma Eze, Friday 7:31 PM: For the record you have not texted. Neither has the wall.

Anju, Saturday 3:07 AM: Call me or I’m calling the police.

Under the texts were the calls, which the phone, being fastidious, summarized as a number. Anjali does not leave voicemails. She says a voicemail is a letter to a stranger. I took the phone out to the loading dock at the back of the basement, the one place under the building that gets a signal, and sat on an upturned milk crate under the awning with the alley running with rain, and pressed her name.

She answered before it could ring. I heard the connection and then a breath, held.

“Where are you.”

“Anju, I’m sorry, I—”

“Where. Are. You.”

“Harwick. The basement. The dock, it’s raining. I’m fine.”

“You’re fine.” Her voice was shaking, and I understood that it was temper, because my sister shakes with temper the way a bridge shakes in a wind. It means the structure is sound. “Forty-one times, Dev. I counted. You’d like that.”

“My phone died.”

“For three days.”

“We had a thing with the data room. A freeze. I was in the system, I lost track, there’s a, it’s an enormous—”

“I called your office on Thursday. A woman answered and said ‘Noted.’ I said, is my brother there, and she said ‘Noted.’ I said please, and she said ‘Noted’ and put me through to a recording of a man selling software. Nine times, Dev. I thought she was a bot.”

“That’s Joyce. She’s in accounts.”

“Then on Friday I got your manager. Noreen. She said you were at your desk, very sure, like a woman reading it off a card. I said put him on, and she said you had just stepped out. I said I’d hold. She said, ‘Let’s circle back,’ and hung up on me. Politely. I have been hung up on by experts, and that was a master class.”

I looked at the rain. Somewhere above me, I thought, in a file in a system, a woman had written that I was sick on Thursday and sick on Friday. Two stories, one for the system and one for my family, and neither of them true, and both of them useful.

“Noreen’s always like that.”

“She sounded frightened. I wasn’t going to say that, I was going to be furious for ten more minutes. She sounded like someone doing a bad impression of a person who isn’t frightened.” A silence, with Tia’s voice in the far part of it, asking something about a sock. “Have you seen someone?”

I thought of a wall, a woman in a cardigan, a plank of mugs. “I see people all day. It’s an office.”

“Dev.” It was the occupational therapist, the voice that waits. “I mean someone you can tell.”

I understood her then, and it was worse than the temper, because I understood what she had been counting. A brother whose mother died in January and who cannot be reached in October is not a scheduling problem. “It’s work, Anju. It’s only work.”

“It’s never only work with you. You can quit a job, you idiot.” She breathed. “I’m calling every day now. Every day, at six, not just Sundays. If you don’t pick up I’ll call that woman and say ‘Noted’ to her until she cries.”

I laughed, and she did, a little, and it didn’t go all the way down for either of us. “Tia wants to know if you checked the total,” she said.

“Tell her not yet.”

“Okay. Okay.” Then, quietly: “Say it.”

“Sunday at six.”

“It’s Sunday. It’s twenty past eleven.” But she said, “Good,” and hung up, and I sat on the crate in the noise of the alley with the phone held against my chest.

Rafa drove me to Tolliver Court in a white pickup with a ladder rack and a rosary on the mirror. I had said I would take the bus. “You don’t have a key,” he said, and I hadn’t told him that. He had watched me pat my pockets at the elevator for the third time. He parked outside Building F, and we went up the thirty-four stairs and along the fourteen steps of the breezeway, and at 3F he got down on one knee on the wet concrete with a leather roll of wire and did it in under a minute, with his tongue between his teeth and the missing finger held out of the way.

“Is not a good lock,” he said. “You should tell someone.”

“I’m the someone. I mean it’s mine to be concerned about.”

The apartment was mine. That was the first thing, and I stood in the door and let it be true. The bed was made with the corners tucked, the one chair stood at the table, the tiffin sat by the stove with the photograph leaning on it, and the radiator under the kitchen window ticked as it warmed. The second mug was gone from the drainer, which I had known, and there was a clean space on the counter where it had been, as in a mouth.

What was different took me a minute, and it was the hall. The hall runs from the kitchen to the bathroom, seven steps, and on the left there was always a length of off-white wall with a stain the shape of Ohio at the baseboard. The stain was there. Beside it, where nothing had ever been, stood a door.

It was beige. It was a hollow-core door of the color of a hotel corridor, with a brass knob and no number on it, and it fitted its frame as if it had been put up with the building. I had not typed anything about Tolliver Court. I looked down the hall at the bathroom, and back at the door, and Rafa, in the entrance behind me, said “Mira,” very softly, which is what he says instead of a prayer.

I thought of Chioma’s wall. I thought of the key that had gone from my ring, and of the clerk’s own life, which the building’s rules seemed to follow wherever it went, and I turned the knob, which was cold, and opened the door.

Brick. It was a wall of brick, painted white, close enough to touch, and cold the way the inside of a cellar is cold, and the smell that came off it was toast. There was no room behind it and no corridor. I would call it the place a sentence runs out.

Two knocks came from the other side of the brick, at chest height, unhurried, like someone confirming a delivery.

This time I didn’t wait. I put my knuckle to the paint and knocked twice, and two came back.

I closed the door. I had a theory, and I give it with the caveats it deserves. As far as I could tell, the building’s reach stops at its own walls with one exception, which is the clerk. I am the extension cord. Wherever I go, a little of Harwick goes with me, and where the cord is plugged in at Tolliver, the brick is what the record looks like at its margin: a surface where the writing stops. I did not know who knocked. I did not want to know what a margin sounded like when it answered.

Rafa had taken off his cap. It is the only time I have seen him do it indoors. “Is not my building,” he said.

“It might be mine.”

“Then paint it,” said Rafa, and put the cap on, and went down the stairs to his truck.

I took the 14 back, and Chioma was sitting on the mat outside 4A when the elevator opened, in the hospital hoodie, her clogs off and her bare feet on the maroon carpet and her phone in both hands. The red frames came up. She looked at me for a long time, like a nurse reading a face on a gurney.

“For the record,” she said, “I have been knocking on that wall since Thursday night. Three nights. Nothing. In six years it has never not answered, Mahajan. Not on Christmas. Not the night my mother went in to hospital. I thought you’d killed her.”

“I was inside.”

“Inside what?” But she said it quickly, and turned her head a little down the corridor, and I looked too. The door stood in the wall exactly as I’d left it, beige, with its brass 4 and the B that was a little out of true. Fourteen paces from where she sat. “I saw it Thursday morning,” she said. “Seven twenty, coming off shift. A door with a B on it between my wall and the bicycle. I walked past it like a woman who has decided something isn’t there.” She held up a hand. “Before you say anything, I’ve been very good at that for six years.”

“I typed a one.”

“That’s what stupid people say.”

“I know.”

“I told you.”

“I know. Her name’s Margie. Margaret Dunleavy. She was the clerk before me. She’s in there, there are ten of them, and I was inside an hour. It’s been three days.”

Chioma went still. She holds still the way she must at a bedside, when a number on a monitor has changed and she has not decided yet what it means. “Is she all right?”

“She’s making tea.”

“Okay.” She let a breath out through her nose. “Okay. I’m going to be angry for one minute. It will be very loud inside my head and quiet out here, because I’m a professional.” She was silent for ten seconds, and I counted them. “Three days. You didn’t text.”

“The phone—”

“You didn’t text.” She turned the phone over in her hands. “New rule. Eight in the morning and eight at night, you text me. Say your name.”

“I know my name.”

“Say it, Mahajan.”

“That’s ridiculous.”

“In an ICU, when somebody is going under, you say their name. Out loud, to their face. Mr Alvarez, it’s Chioma, you’re at Merrow General. Nobody tells you why. You just do. It works, on people the monitor has already given up on.” She tapped the glass. “Something in this building has been keeping a count of you since August of last year. I would like somebody else to be keeping one.”

“A text isn’t saying it.”

“I know it isn’t.” She said it with an anger that had no object left. “I don’t trust a text to count. So I’ll say it too. At night, when I do my note. Rain tonight, Margie. Dev Mahajan. Out loud, to the plaster, like an idiot.”

I got out my phone, whose screen had a crack across one corner and four percent of its battery, and typed it. Dev Mahajan. Her phone buzzed in her hand. She read it, and nodded once, and did not say it was good. She said, “Tonight at eight.”

At six my sister called. I answered on the first ring, on the stairwell landing, and we talked for nine minutes about a loose tooth of Tia’s, and not once about me, which I understood was a gift and which I took.

At twenty to eight I rode up to four a last time, and looked at the corridor. The door was there. I had half expected it to go when Chioma left for her shift, the way a reflection goes when you look away, but it was where I’d left it, with a faint line of lamplight under it that I told myself I was imagining. Fourteen paces. Seventeen more to the bicycle. I did not knock, and I did not try the knob.

I sent it from the lobby bench by the mailboxes, under the brass H, at eight by my phone and six minutes to by the clock. Dev Mahajan. I rode the 14 home with the rain sliding down the window beside me.

The answer was waiting when I let myself into 3F, which Rafa had left on the latch with a strip of masking tape across the bolt, by the light of the stove. I will say here that I did not look at the hall.

Chioma Eze, 8:01 PM: Good. Sleep.

Under the kitchen window the radiator ticked and ticked, and then knocked twice, spaced as a person knocks who knows you are in.

I knocked back.

chapters.title: A Salesman from Dayton
chapters.html:
The first thing I heard in 1961 was a ball game, described by a man who sounded pleased about the weather, through a radio that was just short of out of range of itself. It was playing to a room with nobody in it. I will come to the room. The morning comes first, and the morning is why I went.

At nine on Monday the conference TV in the management office showed Randall Pugh against a white village on a cliff, with a dome of such a final blue that it seemed to have been put in afterward. Santorini. He wore a navy quarter-zip and the tan of a man who has been told he looks well in it. Noreen sat on my left, with her lanyard in both hands, and I on her right, and between us on the table lay a form that had been printed that morning and had my name on it.

Corvane Property Group | Documented Coaching Record | Employee: MAHAJAN, DEVENDRA | Position: Rent Roll Clerk | Concern: Unplanned absence (2 days, 10/23 and 10/24); unresponsive to management contact (1 day, 10/25) | Expectation: Reliable attendance; respond to management contact within 4 business hours | Review: 30 days

Employee acknowledgment: signature required | Manager: N. Whitmore

“I’m not here to punish,” Pugh said, in the voice of a man who has said it before. “This is a coaching conversation, Dev. We’re coaching. I’d just ask going forward that when bandwidth is limited you let Noreen know.”

“I’m sorry. I was unwell.”

“Totally. Totally get it.” He had stopped looking at me; he was looking at a corner of his own screen. “Okay. Timeline, so we’re all on the same page, and I’ve also put it in an email because I know how you love an email.” He read it out anyway.

From: R. Pugh | To: N. Whitmore; D. Mahajan | Subject: DATA ROOM FREEZE FRI 10/31: 211 DQ FLAGS (ACTION REQUIRED)

Team, going forward the timeline is as follows. Fri 10/31: data room freezes, all 211 DQ flags cleared. Wed 11/12: Larchmont physical walk-through, Harwick Terrace. Fri 11/21, 02:10: Larchmont integration run, incl. orphan-unit purge. HT-4B is on the exception schedule for that run, so Dev, nothing for you to do on 4B. The integration runs under the existing RRCLERK service credentials. Just the flags. Let’s not boil the ocean. R.

I read it twice, the second time for the number, and found I had memorized it. 02:10. I thought of the lobby clock stopping, and the pipes, and the radiator under my window, and of Margie turning a kettle a quarter turn on a plate, saying then they’ll unmake us, and I wrote nothing on the form. I signed it. I signed D. Mahajan in the blue box, and Noreen’s keys, which had been silent through the whole call, gave a single chime.

When the screen went to its blue Corvane standby, Noreen stayed in her chair. She took a butterscotch disc from the dish on the counter, which was not within her reach, and I watched her get up, and fetch it, and sit again.

“You’ll want to be careful what you enter, hon,” she said.

“Careful how?”

“Let’s put that in a drawer.” She unwrapped the disc. The cellophane sounded very loud. “Mrs Han wants to know if the lobby can have orange lights on Friday. For the party. I told her I’d ask the fire marshal.”

I tried to give the flags away. I am not proud of how hard I tried. Joyce was at her cubicle with the calculator, doing something with the old notes in their sleeves, and I put the laptop in front of her and said that there were forty rows of formatting that anyone could do.

“Noted,” said Joyce. Then, after what looked like a negotiation: “I would, Dev. I can’t. I’ve tried to change a phone number in there since go-live. It says View.” She tipped her head. “It says it kindly.”

Espie, at the leasing desk, was laying out an application fan, nails the color of cooked beets with a gold fleck. “Ok so I literally cannot edit a tenant,” she said. “I’m leasing. I lease. But I could, like, caption them?”

Pugh’s answer to my email came back in eleven minutes and was a single line, and I will set it down exactly, because it is the nearest thing in this note to a statement of policy.

RE: DELEGATION OF DQ FLAGS | SEGREGATION OF DUTIES: ONLY THE CLERK EDITS TENANT MASTER DATA. NO EXCEPTIONS (AUDIT). R.

Noreen read it over my shoulder. She had come up without her keys chiming, which I have only otherwise seen her do on the evening of the sixth. “A clerk who misses the freeze,” she said, very quietly, “is a clerk Randall replaces. And whoever he gets will have a delete button and a boss who’s allergic to a red row.” She looked at the ceiling, toward four. “Don’t give him the reason, hon.”

I considered the arithmetic. Two hundred and eleven flags in five days is forty-two a day, and I had learned on a Monday three weeks earlier what a single trailing space cost. I decided I could afford a few a day. A few a day was what I told myself on Monday, and I did not do the larger sum until Tuesday, and I would like it on the record that I knew I was doing that.

I cleared six before lunch. They were the cheapest I could find: a ZIP code with the plus-four missing, a lease date saved as text, an apartment letter in lower case. I watched each one go from amber to green. I learned in the morning what the six had cost. The building took a ring of keys from a nail by my door, four apartments’ worth, from places I had left, and I could not have told you what any of them opened. It took the second drawer in the kitchen, with the takeout menus, the soy sauce packets, and the old cracked gray phone; not the contents. The drawer. There was a clean-edged hole in the cabinet the size of a shoebox, and in it, when I knelt and looked, was the back of the cabinet, painted, as if the cabinet had never had a drawer there to be missed. The label maker lived in the other one, and was fine. I was grateful to it in a way I can’t defend.

At lunch I went and looked at the row. I do not know why I had not done it first thing. In Tenantry, where for fourteen months it had said OCCUPANT, the Tenant field read AMBLER, T. (MR).

I stood with my sandwich and looked at it for some time. I told myself it was the tea. A plate goes out onto the landing at four every afternoon, and has since 1989, and I had begun to suspect that the building’s idea of who stood nearest the door was whoever was being thought of hardest by someone outside it. Nobody in Harwick thought harder, or more regularly, or with more manners, than an old man with a saucer.

Rafa gave me the key off its hook without a word. He turned a clipboard around on the bench for me to sign, which I had not known he kept, and under Purpose I wrote Depends and he nodded.

The radio was on the nightstand, a walnut set the size of a bread box, with a cloth front and a dial lit amber, and a man on it was saying that there was a runner on second and a good deal of wet in the air. The paper on the walls was cream with narrow green stripes. There was a bed with a chenille spread, a luggage rack with a gray sample case on it, a bow tie hanging on a hook by the mirror, a black telephone on the night table with its cord laid straight. The calendar over the desk was a free one from a hardware store in Dayton. The days of April up to the tenth had been crossed off in pencil. The eleventh was circled, and nothing came after it.

A man in shirtsleeves sat on the edge of the bed with one hand resting on the telephone, the way you keep a hand on a sleeping child’s back to know when it turns.

“Come in, come in, shut the door, you’re letting the hall in.” He was forty-one by the look of him, with a round, quick, pleasant face and a side parting wet with comb, suspenders, a collar open at the neck. He stood and put out his hand. “You’ll be from the desk. I rang down about the biscuits. Ambler. Tad. Rosewell Dental Supply, Dayton.”

“Dev Mahajan. I’m in the, I do the records.”

“A records man! Good, good, somebody has to.” He shook my hand with the whole arm. “Sit, there’s the chair. Don’t mind the case.” He glanced at my sneakers and did not ask.

I did not sit. I had counted nine from the door to the window, under his patter, and written the nine in the notebook before I let myself look at anything else, with the pencil I had carried since the Annex. It was the right number, and I was glad of it, as one is glad of a handrail. Now I stood at the glass and looked at 31st Street in 1961. A green awning stood over the entrance, with HARWICK in gold script, and a doorman in a long coat under it held an umbrella for nobody. The road was wet and black. A tan Pontiac as long as a boat idled at the curb with its wipers going, and a woman with a hat tied under her chin stopped at the hydrant to shift her bag, and in the window opposite, where there is a laundromat now, I saw a barber’s pole.

“Lively house,” said Ambler at my shoulder. “A woman hums in the hall at all hours, and an old Norwegian taps the pipes, and I’ve asked down about the whistling. They say they’ll look into it.” He chuckled. “I’m in no hurry. I’m expecting a call at a quarter past four.”

“From Dayton.”

“My wife. Lorna.” He looked at the telephone, and his hand went to it again. “She hasn’t answered my cables, you see. Twelve I’ve sent. It’s the lines, I expect, they said at the desk it’s the lines. She’ll ring at four-fifteen, she knows I’m here till Friday, and she’s a stickler. She’d not leave a man hanging.” He said it lightly. It was the lightness I had heard all my life from my father on the subject of the tomatoes.

I asked what the date was. It was the eleventh of April. I asked what year, and he said, “Well! I hardly know, with the way I move about. Sixty-one.” He was not being funny. I looked at the calendar, and at the clock beside it, which said ten past four, and at his face, and said nothing at all, and I think it was the decent thing and I think I will never be sure.

“Now,” said Ambler, brightening, and went to the sample case. “I can’t let a man leave without a sale. It’s a rule. Floss. Waxed or unwaxed? The mint’s new this spring, you’ll like the mint, the dentists swear by it.”

I bought the mint. I had a dollar in my wallet, and he held it to the lamp, and turned it, the way Joyce holds a five-dollar bill.

“Funny-looking dollar. They’ve done something to the eagle.” He wrote me up in an order book with a pencil on a string, Mr D. Mahajan, 1 pkt. floss, mint, 35c, and he tore the slip off and put it in my hand and put the book away. He did not make change. I remembered afterward that the building does not, and I was in the middle of wondering whether that was the building or the man.

“A fellow leaves me tea, you know,” Ambler said, when I was at the door. “Every afternoon at four, on the sill, there’s a cup, and a biscuit, a plain one, and I don’t know who. A good man. I turn the saucer left, to say it’s good tea, and I can’t recall that anyone ever told me to. I should like to thank him. Tell him if you meet him he’s welcome to come up.”

“I’ll tell him.”

“Do,” said Ambler. “Mind the stairs, they’re wet.”

I counted out, window to door. Nine. Same corridor, same maroon lozenges, and my phone said 1:21, and I had gone in at ten to one by the same phone. I stood on the carpet with a packet of mint floss in one hand and a pencil slip in the other, and the door shut itself behind me with its small sound. I had lost nothing but the thirty-one minutes I had spent, and I could account for every one.

I went to 6A at six. Mrs Han had been, and left a thermos on the tray, and Mr Grieve sat in the wing chair by the window with a rug over his knees, in the three-piece suit, with the duck-head cane across his lap, his hearing aids whistling very faintly as he turned his head. The mantel clocks all said different times, and each of them was slow.

I told him all of it, the way Ellis Kwan might have: the room, the wallpaper, the radio, the telephone, the calendar. I said that the gentleman was well. That he was courteous, and talked a good deal, and had sold me floss. That he took his tea. That he turned the saucer left every afternoon, because he thought it was good tea, and that he did not remember being told to. That he would like to thank the man who leaves it, and that the man was welcome to come up.

Mr Grieve did not say anything for what must have been a minute. He looked at the window, where the sky was going out over the alley, and his hand on the cane was quite still. He coughed once into his handkerchief, as one opens a drawer, and put the handkerchief away and folded it first.

“Did he say,” he asked, “whether it needed sugar?” His voice had gone very formal, as it does when it is trying to hold something level. “Thirty-six years I have wondered about the sugar.”

chapters.title: Everyone Came as Something
chapters.html:
Somebody had put plastic spiders in every drawer of the dead doorman’s desk, and by half past five that Friday they had all been found. They sat in a row along the blotter, black, hairy, the size of a thumb, each one placed with the care of a person who thinks it is funny to have been the finder. Behind them, on the lobby bench, Mrs Han had laid out her trays.

There were rice cakes in three colors, pink and white and a green that tasted of mugwort, and squares of jelly cut with the office box-cutter into orange and black, and Joyce’s shortbread, which Joyce had wrapped in orange cellophane and left without a note. Orange lights had been strung along the mailbox wall with the fire marshal’s blessing, which turned out to mean that they were LED. Mrs Han stood behind the bench like a general behind a map. She had a pointed hat over the jade pin and the thermos in the crook of her arm and a phone held out in front of her at the length of her arm, so that she could see the chat without her glasses.

I had cleared the last flag at 4:51. I want that on the record, because it was the last thing I did on that machine as a person who owed it anything. The banner had come up green across the whole of the screen, and I had read it with my hand flat on the desk.

Data Room | Freeze complete 5:00 PM | 211 of 211 DQ flags cleared | 1 scheduled exception (HT-4B)

I went to the party as a spreadsheet. Espie had said that nobody came to a party as a person, and I had made a grid from a flattened box, in four rows of six, with A1 in black marker over my heart and a cardboard arrow on a headband for the cursor, and I walked through the lobby doors in it like a man delivering a very small fence.

“Mr Mahajan,” said Mrs Han. “You are late and you are a cell. Eat.”

She put a plate into my hands. Then everybody said my name. I do not know how else to give the sense of it. Owen from 2F, under a bedsheet with two eyeholes and a pair of headphones, said “Dev! Spreadsheet guy!” and Espie, a bee in black-and-yellow tights with a pair of felt wings, the nails striped to match, said “Dev, no because that is so good, hold still,” and filmed me. Zofia came up in her man’s gray cardigan with a tape measure worn across her chest like a sash. She said that she had come as a seamstress, and had been told that this was a costume, and did not understand. Rafa stood by the mailboxes in a black hoodie with white felt bones stitched to it, front and back, by a woman who has never in her life done a thing carelessly, and the ribs were exactly spaced. He raised his paper cup to me. He did not say anything, but he raised it, with the toothpick behind his ear.

“Dev,” said Chioma, from the bench. She wore a green scrub top and the clogs and the red frames, and she had pinned a sign to her chest that read OFF SHIFT. DO NOT ASK ABOUT MY LUNG. “For the record, you came as a cell. You are a cell. There’s no joke in it.”

“There’s a small joke.”

“There’s a pun.” She handed me a napkin. “Eight o’clock, Mahajan. I’ll take it in person tonight.”

Owen cornered me by the jelly. Owen Fenske is a graduate student in something to do with watersheds, and he complains the way other people breathe, and I will say that I had always liked him for the consistency. “Someone fixed my name on the portal,” he said. “There was a space after it. Fenske-space. For two years, I’ve been Fenske-space. I put in four tickets. Last week it was just gone.”

“That was me,” I said.

He looked at me with his eyes through the sheet, and put a hand on my cardboard shoulder, which crumpled. “Then you’re my favorite person in the building,” he said. “Also the lights are the wrong orange.”

I had paid for that space with a spare key, in the first week of the experiment, and I did not tell him.

Mr Grieve sat in the folding chair nearest the radiator with the cane across his knees and a rice cake on a napkin he had not touched, in the brown tweed three-piece, with a card pinned to the lapel. COURT REPORTER, it said, in a very small neat hand. “Strictly speaking, I have come as myself at a more respectable hour,” he said. “Mrs Han tells me I am to eat something with a pink center and hold no opinions. I find that I am equal to the second.” He looked at my grid for a time. “You are a most convincing cell, Mr Mahajan. I should hate to be the one to merge you.”

I should say what the week had cost, because I was a man with a plate in his hand in a lobby of people who knew his name, and I have to put it on the page somewhere. On Tuesday the building took a toolbox I had never opened. On Wednesday, a box of spare light bulbs and the liner for the shower curtain. On Thursday it took the second chair, the folding one that stood behind the door for company, and the table at Tolliver Court was set for one for the first time honestly. And on Friday morning, on my way to the bus, I noticed that the bicycle cage at the foot of Building F held a chain lock, still locked, looped through the rack and through nothing at all. I would have told you I did not own a bicycle. I had owned one. It was blue, it had ten speeds, and I had ridden it last in a university town, and the lock sat there still fastened, the way a coat is left on a chair to say that a seat is taken.

That was the bicycle. The other thing I found out at six.

Anjali called as she had called every day since the twenty-sixth, and I took it on the stairwell landing with the door to the lobby open an inch on the noise of rice cakes and a bee. She was in the kitchen in Raleigh; I could hear the extractor fan. She said Tia had been told about the costume and had demanded a photograph of a spreadsheet. She said she had a long day. She said, “Ben says hi.”

“Tell—” I said.

There was nothing after it. I stood on the landing with my mouth in the shape of the next sound, and I heard myself breathe in the gap, and then I said, “Tell him hi back.”

“Tell him yourself on Sunday,” she said. “He wants to see the arrow.”

When she had gone I scrolled the thread with my thumb, back and back, forty screens of it, past the fourteenth and the twelfth, through recipe cards and a photograph of Tia’s tooth, until a text from the twelfth of October gave me a line. Ben says you have to let it settle. I read the word the way you read a plumber’s name on a work order. Ben. I said it twice in the stairwell, and it was two sounds I had been told. I went to the building chat, which I had muted for fourteen months, and opened it, and typed Does anyone, and looked at the cursor for as long as I could stand it. Forty people, any of whom might have a sister. I deleted the words and went back into the lobby.

By half past eight Noreen was not in it. She had been there at seven, in a pair of black cat ears with a felt tail pinned to the seat of her slacks and whiskers drawn on with eyeliner, and she had taken three butterscotch discs from the bowl on the bench that nobody had put there, and by eight-thirty the plate sat where she had left it. Mrs Han lowered the phone. “Mr Mahajan,” she said. “You will find Mrs Whitmore.”

Left was on the ground floor with its doors open and its light on, and it was a Friday, and it did not stick. I rode up with my arrow crumpled against the rail. The display read 4, and then, for as long as it takes to blink, 4B, and then 4.

She was at the far side of the corridor, facing the wall. She stood nose to the wood with her left hand flat on it, at the height of a man’s chest, the keys in her right hand silent, and the cat ears bright against the beige. I should say that to Mrs Han, or to Espie’s camera, or to anyone in the lobby with a phone, there was a hose cabinet there and Noreen Whitmore standing in front of it in a headband. I could see the door because I had been through it. So could she.

“You can see it,” she said, without turning round.

“Since the twenty-third.”

“I saw it for three years, hon. From January of 2016 until August of 2019, plain as a cupboard. Then she went in, and it was a cabinet again. Six years of a red cabinet with a hose, and my husband inside it. You don’t know what that was.” She took her hand off the wood and looked at the palm. “Thursday week I came off the elevator and there it was again. Somebody had given it back its knob.”

“Mrs Han sent me with—” I said, and did not have the end of the sentence.

“Tell her I’m powdering my nose.” In her right fist the lanyard moved, and I saw that one of the fourteen keys had been drawn out and held apart, a small brass key with a green tag, the twin of Rafa’s. “Margie had it cut in 2016. I’d asked her where Gary was, and she looked at me a long time, and then went to the hardware on Merrow with her coat on. Nine years I’ve carried that. I’ve never once put it in the lock.”

I said her name, and she said “Okay, okay, okay,” in the way she does when she’s going to be polite until it kills her, and told me what it was.

“January the sixteenth,” Noreen said. “A Saturday. Ten past four, I was in the office because we had a leak in 6C, and I was on the phone with a roofer who wanted to know if I understood the term flashing. Gary came in with my lunch. He did it Saturdays, because he knew I’d forget, a Tupperware of chicken and rice, with the lid on. He stood at the counter. He said something. I had my hand over the other ear. I said, ‘Put it on the counter.’” She said it in the voice she must have used then, brisk, absent, kind. “I didn’t look up. That is the whole crime. I didn’t look up.”

“Mr Grieve thinks—”

“I know what Mr Grieve thinks.” She laughed, one hard note. “You think I put him in the wall. Everybody does. I could see him think it every time I took his mail up. He’s a man who takes down what he hears, and he’s heard the word wall a great many times in forty years.”

“I didn’t,” I said. “I mean I did. For about a week.”

“Well, it’s a good theory. It has a body.” She leaned her shoulder on the plaster beside the door. “When I put the phone down it was twenty to five and the office was empty and the Tupperware was on the counter with the lid still on. His truck was in the lot until Monday. Margie came in at five past, from the filing room, and said, ‘Noreen, dear, I think you’d better sit.’ She was good. She was kind, even. She told me about the clerks, and the room, and what happens to a man who stands in the wrong place in this building at ten past four with nobody looking at him.” She looked at the door. “I’ve known since that afternoon, hon, and I have not once asked. That’s the part I want to be accurate about. I don’t know how you’d get him out, or whether you can. I know what I’d rather not be told.”

I thought about a woman of fifty-eight who had been pinning a joke over a hole for nine years. I thought about the interview, the form on the desk, my voice in the little room saying my sister, I guess.

“I hired you knowing,” she said, as though I had said it aloud. “The building was dying, Dev. The pipes froze twice in the winter of ‘twenty-two. We were at eighty-one percent and falling, and nobody in the building was keeping the books. And I asked you who we’d call. I’d asked it of nine men. I wrote down ‘sister,’ and then I wrote ‘guess,’ and I underlined it, because I thought: that’s a man nobody will miss. God forgive me, I was relieved.”

“No worries,” I said.

It came out on its own, like a hiccup, and we both heard it. Noreen laughed once, a bark, and put her hand over her mouth, and her eyes above the hand were wet. “Oh, hon.”

“I’m sorry, I didn’t mean—”

“Don’t you dare apologize to me.” She wiped under her eyes with the side of a finger, careful of the whiskers. “And the one. ‘Put a one, it won’t hurt anything.’ I knew what it’d cost, I’ve watched it cost Margie for twenty years. I wanted that door open. I’d have said anything. I said it to your face.”

The elevator opened at the far end. Chioma came down the corridor with the sign on her chest, DO NOT ASK ABOUT MY LUNG, at the pace of a woman who has been on her feet at night for ten years and has learned to arrive without hurrying. She looked at Noreen in her cat ears and at me in my cardboard, and last at the door, the beige door, with a quarter inch of lamplight under it. She did not say hello.

“For the record,” said Chioma, “I have questions.”

And she sat down on the carpet with her back against the plaster, folded her long legs, put her phone face down beside her, and waited, like a person at a bedside who has all night.

Noreen looked at her. Then she looked at the key in her hand with its green tag. “He’s got a blue recliner in there, I’d bet money on it,” she said. “He always wanted one, and I said no, it’s a bad advertisement for the marriage.” Her voice cracked on the last word, and she did a thing with her jaw. “I wash his socks on the weekend. I leave them on the dryer for Thursday.”

Nobody said anything. Chioma reached out, without looking, and took hold of the hem of Noreen’s cardigan, as you would take the sleeve of someone about to step into a road, and held on.

I did not stay. It was not mine. I went down in Left with the arrow bent over my chest and, in the lobby, sat on the bench among the orange lights, where the party was thinning into coats and foil, and took out my phone.

Dev (office), 9:52 PM: Good night, quiet ones. Dev (office).

I turned the phone face down on my knee after I had sent it. Within thirty seconds I felt it buzz, and buzz, and I turned it over, and eleven thumbs had appeared under the message, one after another: Mrs Han’s, and Owen’s, and Espie’s with a bee, and Zofia’s, and Mr Grieve’s, who has never in his life used one and had apparently learned. And one more, from the member whose name sorts ahead of all the others, with a gray circle where a face should be.

chapters.title: The Recliner
chapters.html:
The room smelled of pipe-joint compound and stale coffee, and before I had counted past three I knew I was in a basement. I had expected hotel wallpaper. I got knotty pine, a drop ceiling with a water stain the shape of a kidney, brown carpet tiles, and a space heater ticking orange in the corner like a small animal with a grievance.

I should go back an hour, and a day.

The clocks had gone back on Sunday. The building, which has never been able to settle an account without a clock, found itself with two ten-past-twos in one night and kept both. I lay in the dark at Tolliver, in the stove light, and listened to it: the pipes singing, the stove clock stuck, the radiator under the kitchen window knocking its twice, and then an hour later by the wall, all of it again. As far as I could tell, it billed Friday’s rush a second time, and the second pass took what the first had left that was cheap. The toaster. The bathroom scale. A thing I could not name, and knew had gone because the shelf in my head had a gap in it.

On Monday morning my chair at the office had lowered itself an inch, or I had. I sat at the desk that fit Margie’s back and felt my feet reach the floor too easily, as though the room had been told to expect a smaller man. Forty new flags stood in the queue: the software had found forty ledger entries stamped with an hour that had happened twice, and raised a banner on each. I do not think Brent had thought about the autumn. Pugh had not said a word. I opened HT-4B out of habit, and it read as follows.

HT-4B | Tenant: WHITMORE, G. | Rent: $1,840.00 | Balance: 0.00 | Validation: FAIL (3 required fields empty)

“The señora was here last night,” Rafa said, when I went down for the key at one. He did not look up from the bench. “Ten o’clock. In her coat. She puts a shirt on the dryer, a flannel, folded, and goes. She says nothing. She says nothing so hard I hear it.” He turned the clipboard to me. Under Purpose I wrote Gary, and he looked at it for some time before he gave me the key.

Nine paces. The window at the end of them was a basement window, a slot high in the wall, with a well outside it where rain came down onto gravel. There was a workbench along one side with pipe wrenches on pegs in descending order of size, and a clock from a plumbing-supply house that said ten past four. On the shelf above the bench, in a row, stood ten mugs, each from a different supplier, and I counted them and said nothing about it. In the middle of the floor, facing a television on a rolling cart, was a blue recliner with duct tape on the left arm, and in the recliner, with a thermos on the floor beside him and a pre-game show talking about someone’s hamstring, sat a man in a flannel shirt.

“Chief,” he said, without turning his head.

He was fifty-two. He had a square gray moustache, cut as straight as a level, and a heavy, quiet, pleasant face that had been in the weather, and one thumb was wrapped in white tape to the second knuckle. The shirt was red and black. The boots were laced to the top. He turned the sound down on a man in a headset and looked at me over the footrest.

“Noreen send you?”

“No. Not exactly.”

“She mad?”

“She hasn’t said she’s mad.” I stayed where the nine paces had left me, at the window end, with my back to the rain. “She brought you a shirt.”

“I know.” He plucked at the front of the one he had on, a man checking whether it was still there. “Came through last night. Smells of that softener. She never used that. Always said it was for people with time.” He drew a thumb along his moustache. “How long?”

I had known he would ask, and I had worked out the answer on the stairs, and still it came out smaller than I’d meant. “Nine years and nine months.”

He nodded slowly, like a man hearing the cost of a repair. “That’s a long Saturday.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Not yours.” He pointed with his chin at a cooler by the wall. “Sit down, you’re making the place look nervous.”

I sat on the cooler. For a while neither of us said anything, which I think was the best thing he could have done, and the rain went down the well, and on the television a man laughed at a joke about a kicker. He told it in short pieces, with his eyes on the screen. He said that he had been a pipefitter thirty-one years and had never in that time gone into a space without knowing the way out of it. “First time,” he said. “Hell of a first.”

“I’m not sure what happened,” I said. “Noreen said—”

“She’d say she didn’t look up.” He grunted. “She didn’t. That’s not the thing. I wasn’t missing, Chief. I was done being looked past. I come in with the lunch, and I stand there, and the whole of me is going, turn around, Noreen, and I think, I’ll go up the stairs and see if she turns. Five minutes. See if she comes looking.” His taped thumb went to his mouth and came away. “Then I couldn’t turn around myself. It’s a funny kind of stuck. You know the way out. You just can’t want it enough at the right time.”

There were noises through the wall, as there are in any hour. Somebody sang, low, a few bars of something in Spanish, and stopped. Somewhere a pipe was struck, once, twice, a pause. “Inez,” said Gary. “She does the mornings, whatever they are. That’s Nils in the stack, one-two-pause. Mr Ambler’s got his ball game. And Ellis, you can hear him if you’re quiet. Writing. Like a mouse in the wall.” He said the names the way a man reads off tools in a box. “You get to know them. They’re not bad company.”

“Margie told you how to get out.”

“Margie says it like a lease clause.” He nearly smiled. “The door has to be real. All the papers. The plan and the permit and the count. Somebody’s got to make it a unit with a number. Then someone’s got to say my name at the door, the whole name, out loud, when I’m the one in front, and I got to walk.” He looked at the television as if it had asked him a question. “Noreen’s scared of me. Of the look. I’m scared of her face. Ten years. I don’t know what I’d say to a woman ten years older, that I left on a Saturday.”

“She washes your socks,” I said. “On the weekends. She leaves them on the dryer for Thursday.”

He did not speak. He took a hand off the arm of the chair and put it over his eyes, a big hand with a taped thumb, and kept it there, and I looked at the wrenches on their pegs until the television said something about a quarterback and he took it away.

“Eleven feet,” he said, in a different voice, level, a man changing the subject to a thing he could lift. “You walked it? The width of this place? Eleven. Read the drawing for the riser, R-4, on the plan. Somebody drew a riser eleven feet wide. I never saw a riser eleven feet wide in thirty-one years. That’s not a riser, Chief, that’s a unit. Any journeyman with a tape could’ve told them. Whoever ran the pipes in ‘eighty-six didn’t know a flange from a fish.”

“I’ll look at the plan again.”

“Do.” He picked up the thermos and set it down again unopened. “One thing. Say it exactly. The anode rod on the number one heater, in the basement. It’s due. I told her Thursday at the kitchen table, and she said hush, she had the roofer on her mind.” He stopped. His mouth worked under the moustache. “Tell her—” he said, and shut it, and shook his head. “No. Just the rod.”

“The anode rod. Number one.”

“That’s it, Chief.”

I counted out. Nine, window to door, not fast. The corridor was the corridor, and the maroon carpet, and my phone said 1:44, and I wrote the nine in the notebook, and my hand was not quite steady.

I took the stairs. Rafa was on an upturned bucket in the boiler room, with the toothpick, and the big heaters in a row behind him, three of them, gray, tall as men, with their numbers stenciled on in white. I told him all of it. I told him that the husband of the señora, which is what he had always called her, was named Gary, and Gary was inside.

Rafa did not move. “In nine years,” he said, “I never hear his name. She says ‘my husband.’ I say ‘señora.’ We are very polite.” His hands were hanging between his knees. “Ten. You said ten.”

“Ten.”

“Four times I bleed the stack on four for the knocking. Nils, you say? Four times I put the key in the valve, and I say to myself, is air. Is air.” He looked at the stub of toothpick. “Is people.”

“I didn’t know until Thursday either.”

“Mira.” He stood up the way a very large animal stands. “I turned one key. I am going to ask, and you will not like the question. If I turn it for the second, is it for him?”

“He didn’t ask for you. He asked for a rod.”

That was the best I could do, and it worked, because Rafa laughed, a short noise, and went to the toolbox. The big heater on the left was number one, with a hex head on top the size of a fist. He put the wrench on it and it took Rafa and me and a length of pipe slid over the handle, and it came out of the tank with a sound like a tooth, and he held it up under the caged bulb.

I had thought an anode rod would be a rod. This was a stub of corroded wire as long as a finger, gray and furred, the end of it like a root pulled from a flowerbed. He turned it over. He said the word in Spanish I will not set down.

The maintenance log hung from a nail by the door, a ruled ledger with a cloth spine and Rafa’s square capitals down every page. He ran his thumb back through the years to a line in January of 2016, and it was not his hand. It was in pencil, in heavy, upright, careful capitals, a hand used to writing on the back of pipe.

ANODE #1: INSPECT / REPLACE. DUE JAN. (G.W.)

“Is not my writing,” Rafa said.

“No.”

“I never saw this line.” He ran his finger under it. Nothing had been ticked. The next line was a thermostat in March. “It was there. Nine years. In the book I wrote in every day.” He was not looking at me, and he had his hand flat on the page, as you hold down a map in the wind. “A man writes you a note in the log, you have to read the log.”

He went back to the bucket and sat, and I put my hand on his shoulder for a second and took it away, because I did not know the rule.

At five I came up in Right, because Left was on four and did not answer, and Noreen was sitting on the corridor floor with her back against the plaster of 4A, a little way from the mat, with her legs out in front of her and her shoes off. She had her glasses in her lap on their beaded chain. She had not put on lipstick. In the lamp-light she looked like what she was, a woman of fifty-eight on a carpet, and I thought of what a person looks like who is trying not to be seen to have been sitting somewhere for an hour.

I stopped about ten feet from her. I did not know how to do it, so I did it the way I do everything, and said it precisely.

“I saw him. I was inside. He’s well. He’s in a blue recliner.”

She shut her eyes.

“He asked me to tell you one thing. He said to say it exactly. The anode rod on the number one heater in the basement. It’s due.”

For a long time she did not move. Then her face folded, from the mouth first, and she brought both hands up over it, the glasses sliding off her knees onto the carpet, and a sound came out through her fingers that I hope never to be responsible for again.

“He said that in January 2016,” she said. “At the table. He said it on a Thursday and I told him to hush.”

“I know. He said.”

“He said I’d the roofer on my mind.” She took her hands from her face and looked at them as though they were somebody’s she was minding. “Did he say anything else?”

I thought of a man with his hand over his eyes. I thought of the shape the sentence had taken in his moustache. “He started to,” I said. “He said, just the rod.”

She nodded, a slow, wet, practical nod, and the nod went on a moment too long. Then she turned over onto one knee, and with a hand on the baseboard got up, and stood, not quite facing the door. She put her palm flat on the plaster at the height of a man’s shoulder, seated, in a chair, and left it there. She did not say anything. I picked her glasses up off the carpet, folded them, and set them on the mat of 4A, where she would find them.

chapters.title: Status Pending
chapters.html:
My badge said OCCUPANT. It had said MAHAJAN, D., RENT ROLL CLERK, with a photograph from my first week in which I look like a man whose chair has been taken away, and at ten to six on Wednesday morning, on the loveseat in the leasing corner where I had lain down for ten minutes at midnight, the name line read OCCUPANT, and the position line CLERK-RR-001, and the photograph was my face. It was the only thing in the building that hadn’t been revised.

I sat up. The ring on my belt was lighter. I did not need to go round it. The replacement key from the Tolliver leasing office, cut on Monday for thirty-five dollars, was gone, and I knew the way you know a tooth.

I had stayed at the office on Tuesday to finish the forty duplicate-hour flags, and I had finished them at eleven, and I had meant to take the 14, and at 2:10 I had been lying on a vinyl loveseat with a coat over me, listening to the pipes. I had not been at home to see it taken. That was a mercy, if the building trades in mercies, and I have never been sure.

At noon I rode the 14 out to Kessler Avenue and walked into the leasing office at Tolliver Court. The woman at the desk was named Pam, with reading glasses pushed up into her hair and a calendar of kittens, and she smiled at me in the way one smiles at an application.

“3F?” she said, and tapped. “That’s been vacant since August. I’ve got no lease on that unit for a Mahajan. Would you like to fill one out?”

“I’ve lived there four years. My rent’s eleven hundred and twenty-five. I pay on the first, by the portal.”

“Mm.” She tapped again. “I’m so sorry. There’s just nothing.” She was nice about it. She was nice about it all the way, with her hand moving the mouse and her eyes sliding off me, and she offered me a lollipop from a bowl, as one does to the children of tenants.

I walked up the thirty-four stairs and along the fourteen steps of the breezeway. The blinds in 3F were open. Through the glass I saw a bare gray carpet, an empty counter, a stove with its door ajar, and no table, no chair, nothing on a wall. The bed was gone. The counter by the stove, where a steel tiffin had stood for four years with a photograph leaning on it, was bare. I did not let myself finish that sentence. I could not see the hall from the breezeway. I thought of the stain the shape of Ohio on the baseboard, and hoped it was still there, a thing the building had no use for.

On Thursday, at six, Noreen came in and found me. I had slept on the loveseat, with the coat. She opened the glass door with her keys chiming, and stopped, and her hand went to the lanyard.

“Can I help you?” she said, politely.

It was the voice she uses with prospects, the very kind one. She meant it. She looked at the coat, and the loveseat, and my face, and for about the length of a breath something moved across hers, a flicker, as of a screen between two channels, and her mouth opened on a word she did not find. “I’m sorry,” she said. “Are you waiting for Espie? She doesn’t come till nine.” And she went into her office and shut the door, and I heard her keys hit the desk.

Joyce arrived at eight with the shortbread and the calculator. She stopped at my desk with her tin in both hands. “Noted,” she said. I have heard her say it ten thousand times. I had never heard it with something under it, like a hand under a tablecloth, and when her eyes met mine they were frightened, and she looked away from me at once, and I understood that she was trying to find out what she was afraid of. Espie came in at nine in a coat the color of mustard, nails dark plum with a single gold accent on each ring finger, and stopped in the door.

“Hi! Oh my gosh, sorry, are you the new IT guy? Because the printer is having, like, a whole moment.”

“I’m the clerk.”

“Ok so you’re, like, the clerk,” she said, with lovely goodwill. “No because that’s so real.”

That afternoon the answer came back from the shared inbox in Human Resources. I had written to ask for a verification of employment, because I thought that if I could have it on paper I could show it to someone, and I think now that I was hoping a form would hold me up, as a form always has.

From: Corvane HR Shared Services | To: RRCLERK | Subject: RE: Employment verification request (Mahajan, Devendra)

No employee record found for Devendra Mahajan. Payroll shows an active position, CLERK-RR-001 (Rent Roll Clerk, Harwick Terrace), paid biweekly to the account on file. We are unable to discuss position holders by name. Regards, HR Shared Services

I printed it, and folded it twice, and put it in the notebook with the floss slip. At the vending machine in the hall my card was refused with a message in a stately font, ACCOUNT NOT FOUND, and a bag of pretzels hung in the coil above the tray and went on hanging. The man who brought the pizza at six, which I had ordered on the office line and paid for with a twenty from a coat pocket, asked whether I was waiting for someone, and I said yes, and he opened his mouth to say something else, and shut it, and handed me the box with a puzzled look at the bag, and walked out and forgot to take the tip.

People addressed the chair. This is the thing I would like to be able to explain and cannot. Espie came to my desk with a stack of leases and said, brightly, “Does anybody know who keeps moving the stapler?” She said it to the chair, which was empty by then, since I was standing next to it. Joyce put a cup of coffee on the corner, where she had put one every morning for fourteen months, and when I took it, she stood looking at her own empty hand.

I wrote the order out in the notebook that night, under the lamp, in my sevens. First the building had taken what I did not look at. Then what I looked at sometimes: a chair, a bicycle. Now it was taking what I held, and I had done it to myself with two hundred and fifty-one flags in nine days, and the batch had done the arithmetic. It does not give change. Where the sum was bigger than the thing, the rest was simply gone. And I thought, with a wretched clearness, that the sum was not finished.

My phone had said NO SERVICE since the morning, and by evening it said EMERGENCY CALLS ONLY, and under Settings, in the line marked My Number, it said Unknown. Anjali had called at six on Wednesday as she had every day, and told me Tia’s tooth had come out into a piece of toast. On Thursday she did not call.

At eight on Thursday night I sent Chioma my name from the office laptop, through the building chat, since my phone had stopped being a phone. Dev Mahajan. It was the best I could do. I did not know whether it would arrive.

Her answer reached me at ten to six on Friday morning, on the laptop, with a time stamp from the end of a double shift.

Chioma Eze, 5:48 AM: who is this

I read it six times. At noon the glass door opened and she came in, in the hospital hoodie, with her red frames sliding down her nose, and a face like a woman who has been told her car was never hers. She stood in front of the desk, and I stood up, and she looked at me politely and did not seem to know why she was looking.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “I got a message. It’s weird. I know I should know you.” And she pushed up the sleeve of the hoodie on her right arm, the one with the burn scar on the inside of the wrist, and read off her own skin, where someone had written in black marker, in capitals going shaky at the end, what she must have written in the night.

“Dev Mahajan,” she read. She frowned. “Wall guy.”

“That’s me.”

“I’ve been writing it on myself since Tuesday. It keeps coming off in the shower.” She looked at me as if I were a blood pressure. “I skipped the wall. Two nights. I did a double on the Tuesday and a double on the Wednesday and I got in and fell on the bed and I said, tomorrow, and then it was tomorrow.” Her voice was careful, and getting higher. “Mahajan. I’m so sorry. For the record I do not forget people. It’s the only thing I’m good at.”

I put my hand out, and she took it, and held it hard, with the other hand over her mouth. I thought: a text is a thing you read. I do not believe the building reads. As far as I could tell, it listens. For ten days she had texted me at eight and eight, and said it to the wall at night, and I had counted both as one thing, and on the two nights she skipped the wall there had been nothing for the building to hear.

Zofia came by at two, with a pair of Mr Grieve’s trousers over her arm for a hem, and the tape around her neck. She stopped in the door and looked at me, and her eyes went up and down, the way a person’s do who reads a thing by its dimensions. She did not say hello. She put out the tape.

“You lost eight,” she said.

“Centimeters?”

“Eight.” She did not measure. She had it by eye, to a hair. “Since September. Is not shrink. Is leaving.” She wound the tape round her fist. “I have your numbers in book. I keep my book, so I keep you. Is only reason.” She nodded once, severely. “Eat something.”

On Friday night I borrowed Chioma’s phone. She had decided to keep me in sight until her shift, and sat on the bottom stair in her scrubs with her clogs in her lap, watching me not do it. I knew the number. It is the one thing I have dialed more than any other in my life, and I did it without looking, on the stairwell landing, with my thumb.

She answered on the second ring.

“Hello?” said my sister. In the background a dishwasher ran and a child laughed at something. It was her voice, and it was warm, and she did not know me. “Sorry, who is this?”

“It’s Dev.”

“Dev who?”

I had my mouth open. I heard, behind her, a man’s low voice ask a question and a chair scrape, and then her breath. She was being kind. She was exactly as kind as she is with a parent in a clinic who has called the wrong number and is embarrassed. “Is this about the account?” she said. “Because I already told the other person, we’re not interested.”

I hung up.

I know the silence that came after. It is the one after the ring runs out, before the voice begins, and I sat in it on the eleventh of January last year at forty-one minutes past nine, with my phone face down and my hand in the air, spelling the name of a city. In that silence, in January, a message had been waiting. This time there was nothing in it. I held Chioma’s phone against my chest and I thought of my father’s voice, which I’d lost at Diwali without noticing, and of how many of the things I had lost I had not noticed, and how this was the first that I had.

On Saturday at nine minutes past nine, at the desk beside the loveseat, I logged in as the clerk, which was the only thing the building still let me be, and opened HT-4B. The field that had said WHITMORE, G. on Monday, and AMBLER on the Monday before, had changed again.

HT-4B | Tenant of Record: MAHAJAN, D. | Status: PENDING | Effective: 11/09 02:10 | Source: SYSTEM

I read it as I read every row. I looked at the date. A pending tenant is a tenant who has not yet been entered. I had about seventeen hours.

I went out and sat on the lobby bench among the left-over orange lights, which no one had taken down, and did nothing for most of the day, which is not an easy thing to do in a building that does not see you. A woman I’d said good morning to for fourteen months went by with a stroller and said, to nobody, “Is somebody there?” Mrs Han’s greeting had gone up at six: GOOD MORNING TO ALL, INCLUDING THE QUIET ONES. I read it on a borrowed phone. I did not know which I was.

At nine that night the glass doors opened, and Chioma came in. She had changed out of her scrubs into a hoodie and jeans, and she carried under one arm a stack of folding chairs from the basement, five of them, steel, with HARWICK TERRACE painted on the backs in white. She set them down against the bench with a clatter that rang in the lobby like a dropped tray. She straightened. She had the red frames pushed up in her hair and her sleeve rolled to the elbow, with the black marker on the inside of the wrist, and she looked at me directly, for a long time, as at a name she had decided not to lose.

“I’m going to say your name until it takes,” she said.

chapters.title: Good Morning, Dev
chapters.html:
A foil tray of sticky rice was steaming on the lobby bench when I came back from the office with the laptop, and for a moment I took it for something the building had left there itself. Then Mrs Han lifted the corner of the foil with one thumbnail and the smell came out: sesame oil, brown sugar, and a note like a cough drop that I would learn was a jujube. The rice was the color of strong tea and packed as tight as a brick, with chestnuts in it, and pine nuts, and dark dates cut in half. She had carried it down from 5C in the arm that did not hold the thermos. She set it beside me on the bench the way you set a casserole on a step where there has been a death.

“Eat,” she said.

“Thank you, Mrs Han. I’m not really—”

“A person cannot be said good morning to on an empty stomach.” She put a plastic spoon in my hand and folded my fingers around it. She had put the quilted vest on over a church blouse, and the jade pin was in her bun, and she gave me the whole of her attention, which in a woman four feet ten inches tall is a great deal to stand under.

I ate. It was sweet and chewy and scorched a little at the edges, and I remember thinking that a man who was about to be filed should not have been able to taste anything, and I could taste all of it.

I had read the notices at seven on the office laptop, which was by then the only machine that would still let me into the building chat.

Chioma Eze, 4A, 7:12 PM: ALL TENANTS TO THE LOBBY AT 9 PM TONIGHT. THE CLERK. DEV MAHAJAN. OFFICE GUY, WALL GUY. HE IS BEING LOST AND I AM NOT GOING TO WATCH IT. BRING A CHAIR. YOU WILL SAY HIS WHOLE NAME OUT LOUD, TO HIS FACE. NOT HERE. THIS IS NOT A THREAD.

Sook-ja Han, 5C, 7:31 PM: GOOD EVENING TO ALL. THIS IS A SECOND NOTICE. MS EZE IS NOT POLITE BUT SHE IS CORRECT. THE LOBBY, 9 PM. THOSE WITH KNEES MAY SIT. I WILL BRING FOOD. NO ONE IS TO WRITE THAT THEY DO NOT KNOW WHO HE IS. YOU DO NOT KNOW. COME ANYWAY.

By a quarter past nine there were nineteen steel chairs in a ring around the bench, HARWICK TERRACE in white paint on every back, and Rafa was still bringing them up from the cage in the basement two at a time with the toothpick going in the corner of his mouth. The bench stood in the middle of the ring like the single item on an agenda. I sat on it. Chioma stood in the gap between two chairs with the red frames pushed up into her twists and the marker in her fist, and gave the rules.

“One. Out loud. Not typed, not texted, not thought about really hard.” She held up a finger for each. “Two. The whole name. Not ‘hey,’ not ‘him,’ not ‘the guy.’ Dev Mahajan. Three. You look at him when you say it. Not at his shoes. Not at the rice. In the unit we say the name to the patient, never to the chart, and I don’t have a better theory than that.”

“Is it a theory?” I asked.

“It’s a Friday,” said Chioma. “I watched a text do nothing for four days. Sit up.”

The rules had not been discovered. They had been improvised, the way you set a ventilator, from what the patient was doing. As far as I could tell the building listened, and it did not listen to a screen. It listened to a mouth pointed at a face.

They came in coats over pajamas. Owen Fenske arrived at twenty past with his headphones around his neck. He took in the chairs, the foil tray, the laptop and Chioma, and said, “Is this a cult?”

“It’s a roll call,” said Chioma. “Look at the bench.”

He looked at the bench. I watched it happen. His eyes went to the rice, to the spoon, to the laptop and back, and they did not stop on me, in the way that eyes pass a coat on a hook. “I see a bench,” he said.

“Say it anyway.”

Owen sighed through his nose, the sigh of a man who has filed complaints about the elevator and been invited to a meeting. He said, to a spot about a foot to my left, “Dev Mahajan.” And his eyes arrived. They moved, and they stopped, and he took a small step back from the shock of it.

“Oh,” he said. “You’re the space guy.”

“Technically I’m the clerk.”

“You took the space off the end of my name.”

“I did.”

“I thought that was the Department.” He sat down in the nearest chair. He did not say another word for three hours, and he did not leave.

Mr Grieve came down at ten in Right, one hand on the brass duck, his hearing aids whistling at the acoustics of the lobby, in the full brown tweed with the gold hunter watch across his waistcoat. He did not take a chair. He crossed the terrazzo over the worn brass H and stopped in front of the bench, as he must have stopped in front of a great many people who did not want to be on the record.

“State your name for the record,” he said.

“Dev Mahajan.”

“Strike that,” said Mr Grieve, “and say it as if you meant it.”

Until then I had said my name in the voice I use to order a sandwich. I tried again and it came out apologetic, as if I were giving my name to a drawer. “Again,” he said. The third time I said it the way I would have said it to my mother, to explain who had telephoned, and I thought the pipes in the wall behind the mailboxes ticked once.

“Quite so,” said Mr Grieve. He coughed into his handkerchief, a drawer being opened, and sat down at the end of the bench, and took out the watch. “I shall time it.”

Zofia sat on my other side with my raincoat across her knees, the collar turned out under the orange lights, a needle in her mouth and red thread pulled from the pincushion on her wrist. She was sewing in capitals, one stitch at a time. DEV MAHAJAN, inside the collar, where it would lie against the back of my neck.

“What is it for?” I asked.

“Is not spell,” said Zofia, around the needle. “Is thread.” She bit the end off. “My mother sewed names in all coats. For school. Coat gets lost, child gets found.” She turned the collar down and smoothed it flat and put the coat around my shoulders, and I could feel the letters through the lining, a small ridge against the neck. “Is not for building. Is for you.”

Espie came at half past ten with the ring light in her tote and a tripod under one arm and her nails painted a plum so dark it was nearly black. “Ok so I’m going live,” she said.

Chioma started to say something.

“No, because hear me out. I have eight thousand people who watched a door that isn’t there. They love him. They’ve never met him and they love him.” She set the tripod up by the dead doorman’s desk, among the plastic spiders nobody had taken down, and propped the laptop on the foil lid, and showed us that she could bring a viewer up on the screen one at a time. “But typing doesn’t count, right? Chioma says it doesn’t. So I’m telling them. If you want to count, you have to come on and look at the lens. The lens is his face.”

By eleven there were two thousand and some people in the comments, going up the side of the screen faster than I could read. DEV. dev!!! who is dev. is this the door guy. DEV. I felt none of it. A sentence typed into a box is a sentence in a box.

The ones who came on were different. A night nurse in a break room, in a scrub cap printed with pickles, looked into the camera and said “Dev Mahajan,” and then “I have a patient,” and was gone. A boy in a gaming chair did it as a joke, and Espie said, “Again, like you mean it,” and he did, and went quiet. A man in a parked car with the dome light on said it very slowly and added, “Hope you’re okay, man.” I said thank you to each of them, to the lens, which felt absurd and was right. The ones who did it properly I felt in my hands, like blood coming back into the fingers after you have come in from outside.

Chioma kept the count on a legal pad on her knee, in tally marks, with a stroke through each five like a gate. At half past twelve she held it up.

“Sixty-one.”

“Sixty-one,” I said. “Which is a prime number.”

“Mahajan,” said Chioma.

“Sorry.”

At twenty to one the glass doors opened, and the keys came across the terrazzo before she did. Noreen had on a quilted coat over a sweatshirt, the burgundy hair flat on one side as if she had been lying on it, and under her arm the lid of a banker’s box. She stopped inside the door and looked at the chairs and the laptop with its small lit rows of strangers. She did not look like a person arriving at a gathering. She looked like a person arriving at a hearing.

“Okay,” she said. “Okay. Okay.”

Nobody answered. Rafa took the toothpick out of his mouth.

“I don’t know you, hon,” she said to me, over the heads. She did not say it unkindly.
