She said it with the careful politeness of someone reading out a statement. “I want you to know that I know I don’t. I was at my kitchen table looking at the roll, the way I do, and there was a name on a line where it shouldn’t have been, and I knew what that line was. And I didn’t know who you were. I haven’t had that feeling since January of 2016.” Her jaw worked on the gum. “I asked a man a question once, in an interview. I don’t remember the man. I remember the question.”

“Who would we call,” I said.

“Yes.” Her eyes came to me and stopped, and stayed, and I am not going to describe what went by in them. “I wrote it down.”

Under the lid was a manila folder gone soft at the corners. She had dug it out of Margie’s filing room, she said, in the dark, after four boxes. “It was the fourth. It’s always the fourth.” She put the form in my hand.

CORVANE PROPERTY GROUP | EMERGENCY CONTACT | Employee: MAHAJAN, DEVENDRA | Contact: Kowalczyk, Anjali Mahajan | Phone: 919-555-0147 | Relationship: sister (guess)

The name and the number were in my own hand, small capitals, the sevens crossed. The word under Relationship was in Noreen’s round purple gel pen, and the second word had been put in brackets and underlined twice.

She took out her phone and looked at Chioma. “You do it,” said Chioma. “It has to be you. You’re the one who asked.”

It rang out. She tried again and it rang out, and in the ring of chairs nobody moved. On the third try the screen jumped, and a kitchen came up on it, sideways and then level.

It was my sister’s, in Raleigh, with the light over the stove on and the corner of one of our mother’s recipe cards held to the refrigerator by a magnet shaped like a tomato. Anjali stood in it in Ben’s old college sweatshirt with the claw clip hanging by three teeth out of her hair and a glass of water in her hand. She had the face of a woman who has been woken by a telephone and has gone straight to the one thing that matters, which was upstairs, asleep.

“Hello? Is this the school? Is it Tia— no. She’s upstairs. Who is this?”

“Ms Kowalczyk? My name is Noreen Whitmore. I’m so sorry about the hour.” Noreen’s voice had gone into the register she uses for a resident with a burst pipe, warm and level, the rasp underneath. “I manage a building in another state. I have your name on a form as the emergency contact for a man named Devendra Mahajan. The form says sister.”

“I’m sorry. I think you have the wrong number.” Anjali looked at the glass of the phone with the polite frown she gives a parent who has mistaken her for the front desk. “I don’t have a brother.”

“I believe you,” said Noreen. “Say it anyway.”

“Say what?”

“His name. I’m going to turn the phone around. I’d like you to look at him and say it.”

She held the phone out at arm’s length in front of my face, with the screen toward me, so that I saw my sister, and my sister, through the little lens, saw me. She was a thumbnail with a gap in her teeth and a pale scar through her left eyebrow. I did not say anything. I had been told the rules.

“Dev Mahajan,” said Anjali.

She said it with her eyes on my face, and then her mouth stayed open on the last syllable. I have seen my sister cry twice in my life, at eight with a scooter and at our mother’s funeral, and both times she did it with her chin up, angrily, as though it were a form of argument. This was different. The tears came out of her without her face changing, in rows, and she looked down at them on the counter as at something that had been spilled.

“Why am I— I’m so sorry, I don’t know why I’m—”

“Anju,” I said.

“Say that again.”

“Anju.”

“Oh,” said my sister. “Oh, you idiot.” And then, in the voice she has used since I was five, for the moments when she is frightened and wants no one to know it, “Dev-u. Dev-u, where are you? What’s— okay. Okay. Ben! Ben, I need the laptop. There’s a five-forty. I’m taking the five-forty.”

The screen showed her kitchen ceiling for a moment and went dark. Noreen stood with the phone still held out, as though it might ring again. Then she lowered it and looked at me for the third time that night, and this time she said it herself, once, with her eyes on mine and the gum stopped in her cheek. “Devendra Mahajan.”

She went into the office and shut the glass door and did not say another word.

At ten to two, Left opened.

The doors slid back on an empty car. Above them the floor display, which has never been accurate, read 4B. And I discovered that I was standing. I had not decided to stand. My feet were going, in the borrowed socks, across the terrazzo toward the open car at the unhurried pace of a person who has been told his table is ready. I counted: one, two. I counted because I count, and because it is the one thing in all of this that has always been mine.

The chairs scraped all at once. Chioma got my left arm and Owen Fenske, who had not spoken in three hours, said “Nope” and took my right. Rafa came in behind me and put both arms around my chest, like a man holding a door in a wind. And Mrs Han walked past all of us, a woman who would have come up to the middle of my chest, and stood between me and the doors with the thermos hugged against her vest and said to the elevator, in the voice she uses for the group chat, “This one is spoken for.”

Zofia was down on one knee. She passed the tape around my waist, twice, and tied it, and ran the other end across the floor to Chioma and knotted it round her wrist, with a tug to test it, as she would test a hem. “Louder,” she said.

They said it, in a ring, over each other, with no chant and no rhythm. Mahajan became Mah-HAH-jan and MA-ha-jan, and in Rafa’s mouth Mahahan, and I have never heard it said so warmly. From the laptop on the bench, small and clear, the strangers said it too. My feet took the third step, and the fourth, and each one went into Rafa’s arms like walking into a wall of coats.

At ten past two, by the lobby clock, which stopped at four minutes past, the pipes began to sing.

It starts in the risers behind the mailboxes and goes up, and the radiators knock twice, and the elevator doors slid shut on the empty car with no more sound than a page. Through the frosted lettering on the office door I could see Noreen bent to a monitor, the burgundy of her hair lit from below. She had gone in at five to two to watch the line. I will say for her that she did not look away.

The feet stopped. I did not stop them. They were simply mine again, all at once, and I leaned back into Rafa, and he held me, and said “Mira” into my coat. The minute went by. Everyone was still saying it. When the clock began to move again, a few of them did not notice, and went on for another breath, to nobody, in the dark orange light.

The glass door opened. Noreen stood in it with her keys silent in her fist. She read it off the screen to herself in her head, then aloud, in the voice she used for EMBRACE THE CHANGE.

HT-4B | Tenant of Record: MAHAJAN, D. | Status: CANCELLED (WITNESSED) | Effective: 11/09 02:10 | Source: SYSTEM

She looked up. It was the first full sentence she had said in an hour, and she said it to me across the whole ring of chairs, across the tray and the stroller and the old man with the watch, as she might have said it any Monday, at the front counter, past the butterscotch.

“Good morning, Dev.”

By three they had gone up in twos and threes, and Rafa stacked the chairs. Chioma walked me to Right. On four the door was there, fourteen paces from her mat, and neither of us looked at it. I did not have an address. I had a raincoat with my name in the collar, a notebook, a steno pad, a floss slip and a couch, and for the first time in four days I could tell you which of them I was holding.

At ten past five my phone, which had said Unknown beside My Number since Thursday, lit on the arm of the couch and told me in a green bubble that Anju was at the airport and that I was not to move. The line marked My Number still says Unknown. I assume that if I asked the carrier they would find an error and correct it, and so I have not asked.

Chioma woke me at six with a mug. She sat on the arm of the couch in her scrubs, with the red frames crooked, and took my right hand and turned it over. “Hold still,” she said. She uncapped the marker with her teeth. “Name, age, bed. That’s how we don’t lose anybody between floors.”

I held it up in the gray light from her window when she had finished. The ink was still wet. It said DEV, 29, 4A couch.

chapters.title: Anjali Takes Off Her Coat
chapters.html:
A small woman in a navy puffy coat was standing at the lobby’s glass doors with a wheeled suitcase, looking in.

I had been on the bench since ten. The text at 7:02 said the plane was still at the gate and they kept saying ten minutes. The one at 9:48 said Landed. The one after that said Cab. By my phone it was twenty past eleven, and I saw her before she saw me, which in twenty-two months of Sundays on a small screen had never once happened. She was shorter than the screen makes her. She had the claw clip in and her strong forearms pushed out of the sleeves around the suitcase handle, and she was reading the names on the brass mailboxes through the glass the way she reads a chart.

I went to the doors and pushed one open. “Anju.”

She looked straight at me. She gave me her whole attention, with polite concern in it and no recognition at all, the way you look at a stranger who has called you by a name that might be yours. “I’m sorry,” she said. “I’m supposed to be meeting someone. I had a name.” She patted the pocket of the coat for her phone, and a gap showed between her front teeth when she frowned. “I had it written down.”

I stood in the open door with the wet air coming in on my shoulder. I knew exactly what I was looking at, in the sense that I had watched Joyce and Espie do it, and I could not do anything with the knowledge. There was nothing in the rules about saying it to your own sister. She had already heard it from me.

“Dev,” said Chioma, behind me, from the elevator. She had come down in the hoodie with the frames pushed into her twists, and she said it without hurry, as she would say it to a patient on the edge of a bed. “Mahajan.”

My sister’s face changed. It did not brighten. It came back, from wherever it had gone, the way a screen does after a power cut, and she looked at me, and then she hit me in the arm with the heel of a hand that has spent ten years lifting children, and then she took two fistfuls of my raincoat and held on.

“I almost didn’t come,” she said into the collar. “I booked it, and I sat on that plane with a boarding pass with my own name on it, and I thought, who is this for? I had the dal in my bag and I thought, why is there so much of it.”

“You said it on the call. You said my name.”

“I know I said it. I remember saying it. I remember crying in the kitchen.” She pulled back with her hands still full of coat. “I remember that I was crying, Dev-u. I don’t remember who for.”

I will put down what I thought, because it was the first thing I thought and I have not found a better one since. As far as I could tell, a name said aloud holds for a while, and a while is not the same as for good. At one in the morning there had been sixty people around me. By the second hour of a flight, with nobody’s mouth near her, there had been less of me in my sister than the night before.

Chioma’s kitchen was the width of a hallway, with a table that sat three if two of them liked each other and a red kettle on the back burner. Anjali put the suitcase by the radiator and took out of it a rectangular container with a blue lid, wrapped in a bath towel, a freezer bag and a second towel. She set it on the table the way you set down a sleeping child.

“Dal,” she said. “I made it at two in the morning, after. Mummy’s, with the lemon at the end.” She peeled the lid and the smell came up: cumin in hot ghee, hing, the sourness of the lemon. I held the door frame. I had not smelled it since the winter before last. “I made enough for two,” said Anjali. “I stood there with the spoon and I couldn’t remember why I’d made it for two.”

“For the record,” said Chioma, getting down bowls, “that’s the best reason I’ve heard for making anything. I’m Chioma. Sit. Take your coat off, you’ll boil.”

“I’m fine.”

“It is seventy-eight degrees in here. The radiators are, let’s say, enthusiastic.”

“I’m fine,” said my sister, and kept the coat zipped to her chin, and ate.

I told her a version. I had had all of Saturday on the bench to choose which, and I chose the one with the fewest numbers in it. I started with “Technically,” and she held up one hand and said, “Start with the building.” So I said there was a unit that was not on the plan and was occupied. I said I kept the books, and that what I entered in the books was charged to me, and that it was not money. Small things at first. “What things?” “A mug.” “Dev.” “Some keys. A gym tag.” I did not say the voicemail. I did not say the Rascals or the bicycle or the first name of her husband, which I had had to look up in a text. I did not say the price. I said that last week the building had stopped being able to see me, and that on Saturday night it had been talked out of it.

She listened as she listens to a parent explain a child who does not like to be touched: head a little to one side, hands loose, interrupting only to ask for the next fact. I would estimate that she believed a third of it. The rest of the believing she did with her hands.

“Where’s the wall?”

“Which—”

“The wall, Dev. You said it answers.”

Chioma lifted one shoulder at me. “Bedroom,” she said.

The bed stood against the east wall, and the plaster above the headboard was covered in pencil, in rows, in small square capitals, from the baseboard to as high as a woman can reach lying down. Six years of it. Anjali stood at the foot of the bed in her coat with her arms folded and read, as I have seen her read a school report.

Rain tonight, Margie. Bus late. Radiator on. Two knocks if you’re up. C.

Rain tonight, Margie. Mama’s scan was clear. Told nobody but you.

Dry tonight, Margie. Cold. Wear the cardigan.

She put her knuckles to the plaster above the pillow, and knocked twice.

From the other side, at the same height, unhurried, two knocks came back.

She did not jump. She went still, in the way that she goes still when a child she is treating does the thing it was not supposed to be able to do. “Okay,” said my sister. “Okay.” She sat down on the edge of Chioma’s bed in the coat, with her hands between her knees. After a while she said to the wall, in the voice she uses to introduce herself to a classroom, “I’m Anjali.”

The voice came through the plaster, dry and flat and Midwestern, a little muffled, like a radio in the next room of a house. “Pleased to meet you, dear. You’ll be the sister. He crosses his sevens, you know. I thought it must have come from someone.”

“Our mother,” said Anjali.

“Yes,” said the wall. “I thought it must.”

She was quiet through the rest of the dal. Chioma washed up with her back to us, which is how Chioma gives privacy. I waited until the water ran.

“Anju. I have to tell you something and I need you to let me finish.”

“You always say that. You never finish.”

“In January last year. The night before. She called me at nine forty-one. I was at a trivia night, I’d been asked to make a ninth, and I saw it come up, MUMMY, on the screen. I was in the middle of a question.” I looked at the table. “I let it ring.”

Anjali did not move. The spoon stayed where it was, over the bowl. The kettle ticked as it cooled. I said I was sorry. I said I had been going to say it for twenty-two months and each time I had made a coffee.

“She left me one too,” said Anjali. “It was about the dal.”

That was all. She put the spoon down. She did not say what the message had said, and I did not ask, and I understood that I was being told something about a door that opened one way. “Have you listened to yours?” she said.

“No,” I said. It was true in the way that a form is true.

“Okay.” Her voice had slowed and her shoulders had come down and her eyes had lowered to the level of mine, which is her professional calm, and which I have seen turn a screaming four-year-old into a boy stacking blocks. Her hands were not calm. She had pulled a paper napkin from the holder and folded it in half and in half again until it was a coin, and she went on folding it long after it would fold.

At three we went down to the office, because Anjali said she wanted to see where I had been working when I stopped being seen. On Friday I would have taken that for a figure of speech.

The office was dark, with the blinds down, and Noreen had not gone home. A blanket lay squared on the leasing loveseat. She stood up behind her desk as we came in, under LIVE LAUGH LEASE, and the keys chimed. She had washed her face in the staff bathroom and combed the Merlot and put on lipstick, and I understood that she had done it as other people dress for a funeral.

“Mrs Whitmore,” said my sister.

“Noreen, please.”

“Mrs Whitmore. On the twenty-fourth of October, a Friday, at about eleven in the morning, you told me my brother was at his desk.”

“I did.”

“And then you said you’d circle back.”

“I did.”

“I treat four-year-olds who can’t tell me what’s wrong,” said Anjali, “and some of them lie to me better than that. They at least look at the ceiling.”

“I looked at the banner,” said Noreen. The banner, EMBRACE THE CHANGE, hung in the front window behind us in reverse. “I’m sorry. I lied to you because I was frightened, and I told myself I was being professional. In my line they feel the same.”

Anjali looked at the form, which Noreen had put out on the desk, squared to the blotter. “You wrote ‘guess.’”

“I did. In pen. I’m sorry for that too.”

“It was the right guess.”

“It was,” said Noreen. Her hand had found her lanyard.

“Don’t do it again.”

“Okay. Okay. Okay.”

Chioma left for her shift at half past six, in the green clogs. “For the record, nobody sleeps near that wall without saying goodnight to it,” she said, and shut the door on us.

Anjali blew up the air mattress herself, with a foot pump, on the floor of Chioma’s front room, and would not be helped. She lay down on it in the dark with her shoes off and the coat over her like a blanket, zipped, and I lay on the couch above her with my hand with its Sharpie on my chest. The streetlight came in the window. Two floors down a bus braked on the wet road and pulled away.

“How long have you been like this?” said my sister.

I considered pretending not to know what she meant. “Since January last year, I think.”

“Same.”

That was all for a while. Then she told me she had told the clinic a week. Ben had said take two. “He said I haven’t taken a day since the funeral, which is true, which is the worst thing about him.” And, after a time: “Dad asked if you were eating. That’s the whole of what he’s said about any of this.” I tried to hear my father say it and got the announcer on a train platform. I said nothing.

“Take two,” I said.

“I’ll see.”

The radiator under the window knocked twice. “Is that her?” said Anjali.

“It’s the radiator.”

“Is that her?”

“It’s both.”

She put one hand out from under the coat and knocked twice on the floor with a knuckle, and in the pipes there was a long sigh, and then nothing.

In the morning I heard her in the corridor with the door open, on the phone. She said, “Two, then,” and “No. I’m fine. Ben, I’m fine. Kiss her.” Chioma came in at twenty to eight off shift, gray with it, and stopped in the doorway of her own kitchen. By the door was a row of three hooks. On them hung a scrub top, a hospital lanyard and a canvas bag.

Anjali came in from the corridor, put the phone in her pocket and unzipped the coat. I had not seen her without it in that city. She took it off, shook it out once, and hung it on the hook between the scrub top and the lanyard, and put her hand flat on the shoulder to settle it, the way you pat someone who has agreed to stay.

Chioma looked at the coat, and at her, and put the kettle on, which is as much as she says about anything she is glad of.

chapters.title: Walk-Through
chapters.html:
A red dot slid along the beige wall of the fourth-floor corridor at a quarter to four on Wednesday the twelfth, stopping at each door frame the way a finger stops on a line of print.

Behind it, holding the instrument at the height of his sternum, was Woo-jin Cho of Larchmont Residential Partners, who had been in the building since nine. He was six foot three and carried the stoop of a man who has been hitting his head on doorframes since junior high. Round glasses, a neat side part, a Casio on a steel band, and a badge on a retractable reel that he pulled out and let go, pulled out and let go, like an anxious tape measure. A pocket notebook in one hand and a clipboard under the other arm. “Woo,” he had said to Noreen at the front door. “The badge says Woo-jin. Nobody has used that since college.”

He had done the three lower floors in the order of the checklist. On two, Owen Fenske had handed him a list of eleven complaints, and Woo had listened to all eleven, written them down and said “Out of scope” to each, which Owen told me afterward was the happiest he had ever been.

Randall Pugh was with us in the form of an iPad in a leather folio, which Noreen carried against her chest like a hymnal and held up at each door. Behind him were a lemon tree and a very blue sea. He had the tan of the sixth of October. “Going forward,” he said at the door of 4D, to nobody’s bathroom.

Espie had made an event of the corridor. There was a rolling garment rack, a folding table, a hand-lettered sign saying FOLD LOUNGE (POP-UP), and eight tenants in a row with baskets of laundry. Mrs Han held one corner of a fitted sheet that was beating her. Zofia made hospital corners and measured each with the tape for show. Owen had dark T-shirts. Rafa stood in the stairwell door with a radiator key, bleeding a radiator that did not need it. They stood very still, in the manner of people who have been told to look natural.

“The dryers are in the basement,” said Woo.

“Ok so that’s the old model,” said Espie. “We’re activating the corridor as an amenity.”

“I love an activation,” said the iPad.

I stood at the 4A mat in the raincoat with my name in the collar. Anjali had been left upstairs in 5C with a bowl of chestnuts and instructions.

“Per the checklist, common-area dimensions are verified against the plan.” Woo planted his shoes on the mat and aimed the laser across the maroon diamonds at the frame of 4C. It beeped. “Twenty-two feet, zero inches. Per plan.”

“It’s thirty-one,” I said.

“Thirty-one what?”

“Paces. Mine.”

He looked at me over the round glasses with the polite horror of a man who has been handed a receipt in a foreign currency. Then he walked it, with a long even stride, like a heron going through shallows, and said “Eight” at the far door. He walked back. “Eight.”

“It was twelve on the way back,” I said. “On the sixth.”

“A count is not a measurement.”

“Technically it’s a measurement of me.”

He wrote that down. I could not tell if it was a joke he was recording or a finding.

At the middle of the wall he stopped, because the checklist stopped him. “Fire hose cabinet. Recessed, glass front, riser R-4, per plan.” He bent to the nozzle and found with visible joy that the paper inspection tag had expired in March. He wrote it under Life Safety. He went a little pink.

“Mr Cho,” I said. “Would you put your hand on the wall? Just there. Left of the cabinet, about here.” I showed him, chest height, where I had always heard it.

“There’s no hand-on-wall step on the checklist.”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“Because it’s the only evidence I can give you that you can carry.”

He considered that, over the glasses, the way he must have considered a good many requests that were not on the form. Then he let the reel snap back, and put his palm flat on the plaster.

Two knocks came out of the wall under his hand. Unhurried, like someone confirming a delivery.

He took the hand away as if it were hot. “That’s the riser.”

“That’s two knocks.”

“Pipes knock.”

“In pairs,” I said. “With a pause. And then they wait. Please. Knock back.”

On the iPad, Pugh was explaining to a ceiling tile that what we were really solving for was optics. In the row of tenants no one folded anything. Woo looked at the plaster, and at me, and made a fist, and knocked on the wall twice with the second knuckle.

“Good afternoon, young man,” said the wall.

It was dry and flat and clear, and a little muffled, and entirely courteous. “Would you mind terribly not deleting me?”

I have thought about that sentence more than any other in this note. In six years Margie had asked for nothing. She had said, to me, that she would have liked to see a spring but was not asking. And here she had put a request to a stranger with a clipboard, in the tone of a woman asking whether the window could be shut.

Pugh was still talking. He had not heard it. I will say that for the record, since it was the point: he did not look up, and the folio did not flinch, and Noreen, with her eyes shut, held it very straight.

Woo opened his mouth, and shut it, and opened it again. “Good afternoon,” he said.

The laser was still in his other hand, switched on, the dot lying on the wall beside the cabinet. As I watched it, the dot ran across the plaster by itself, or so it seemed, and lit on brass: a 4 and a B, beaded like drops on a window, and under them a beige door with a knob, standing in the corridor where it had stood since the twenty-third of October for everyone who had ever paid it any attention. He took one pace back. I saw him count. Down the row, Zofia put the tape back around her neck and said, to the sheet in her hands, “Is door.” Nobody else spoke.

“Woo?” said the iPad. “You’ve frozen on my end.”

He wrote with his back to the iPad, quickly, in a small hand. He showed me the page afterward, and I have it here, because he gave me the leaf.

HT-4B. Corridor 22.00 ft (laser) / 31 paces (Mahajan, D.). Cabinet: hose, tag expired 03. Audible: female voice, wall, courteous. Door: present (visible on laser dot; brass 4B; knob). Door of record: DISPUTED. Status: UNDER REVIEW. W.C.

“I’m not hearing an audible,” said Pugh, who had been told. “That’s not a metric. Woo, let’s not boil the ocean here. Is the unit validated or not?”

“No. Per section 4.3, a unit that can’t be documented can’t be signed off.” He had his badge out on its reel again. “I can log it as a discrepancy, under review.”

“Great. Whatever gets us to the twenty-fourth. Going forward, I need bandwidth on the actual deliverables. Great walk, everybody.” The iPad went dark and Noreen let out a breath through her nose and closed the folio on her own reflection.

Woo came over to the 4A mat and spoke without looking at me, in the voice of a man reading from a binder. “I’m going to need that in writing. All of it. What you know about that wall. Dated, signed.”

“I’ve been keeping a record. In a steno pad.”

“That will do.” He wrote something. “Under review is a hold, not an approval. It gets you until the twenty-first, when the integration runs. I can’t make it not run. I’m an analyst.” He turned the reel in his fingers. “I have filed three deviations in nine years. A boiler, a lease, and a sub-basement that one party stated did not exist. In each case I was thanked and nothing happened. This is my fourth.”

“I count too,” I said.

“I noticed.”

The stairwell door opened.

Mr Grieve had come up from 6A on the stairs, which he was forbidden to do, with the tray in both hands and the cane hooked on his forearm: the cup, the saucer, the one Rich Tea. It was five to four. “Mr Grieve, you shouldn’t be—” said Noreen.

“Strictly speaking, Mrs Whitmore, I live here.” He crossed the diamonds, past the Fold Lounge, past a tenant who had stopped breathing, and set the plate down on the ledge of the west landing with the handle turned left. “Four o’clock, Mr Ambler,” he said, and the cough took him.

It was the one I knew, a drawer being opened, but the drawer did not stop. It came out of the runners. He had the handkerchief up, and when he took it down there was a thin bright red on the white linen, in a shape like the shadow of a leaf. He looked at it with interest. Then he sat down on the carpet with his back against the wall under the window, with the cane across his knees, as a man sits at a station.

“Strictly speaking,” said Mr Grieve, “I am not dying. I am sitting.”

Chioma was there before I had moved. She had come out of 4A in the hoodie at the first cough and she was on her knees with a pulse oximeter off her pocket onto his finger. “Mr Grieve. It’s Chioma. Look at me. Eighty-four. Mahajan, call it in.” Mrs Han got down on the carpet beside him, which I had not known she could do, and said, “Good afternoon, Mr Grieve,” and he said, “Quite so.” Woo was holding the cane. He had picked it up without noticing, in both big hands, with the brass duck against his chest. “Is there a defibrillator?” he said.

“There’s a lobby,” said Noreen, which I took for a no.

The paramedics came up in Right with a stair chair, two women, brisk, who called him sir and Mr Grieve and let him correct the pronunciation of the second. Chioma went down with them with her hand on the arm of the chair. Rafa put the cane in my hand. I took the plate off the ledge, because I could not leave it, and then put it back.

I walked to Merrow General. It is six blocks and twelve minutes, and by the fourth block the umbrella had lost a spoke. I got there at five.

Chioma was in the Emergency hallway in her own scrubs, the green ones with the hospital’s name on the pocket, her badge reading RESP THERAPY on its clip. “I’m not on until seven,” she said. “I came in early and I’m using my badge to be rude to a registrar. Curtain seven.” She walked me to it. “The oncologist says weeks. It was months. It’s in the fluid now, and we’re going to be careful about how it goes.”

“Chioma. He’s going to ask me for something I’m not sure is safe.”

“For the record, I’m not a doctor of whatever that is.” She pushed the frames up. “But I’ve sat with a lot of people at the end, and they all want one thing, and it’s almost never the thing in the chart.”

He was propped on two pillows behind the curtain with a cannula in his nose. The brown tweed waistcoat was unbuttoned and folded on the chair, with the tie on top, and the gold hunter watch lay open on the sheet, ticking. The hearing aids whistled on the tray where a nurse had put them. Without them he was smaller, and I saw how much of him had been the formality.

He put out his hand and took my wrist, with fingers like pencils.

“Mr Mahajan. Put my name down.”

“Where?”

“The roll. The register. Whatever it is you people keep.” His breathing made a sound like a page being turned. “Let me go in. I have been talking to the gentleman for thirty-six years, and I should like, before the end, to see what sugar he takes.”

“Mr Grieve, I don’t know what it would cost you. I don’t know what the room—”

“I am eighty-four years old with fluid in my chest,” he said. “Cost has lost some of its purchase.” One eyebrow went up. “I am not asking to be rescued. I am asking to be introduced.”

I looked at the watch on the sheet. It said 5:10. It was the only clock I had ever trusted in that building, and it was correct.

“I’ll ask him,” I said. “I’ll ask the gentleman.”

“Do,” said Mr Grieve. “Strictly speaking, it is the gentleman’s to say.” He let go of my wrist, and closed his eyes, and the pale hand lay on the sheet beside the watch.

chapters.title: What Margie Wanted
chapters.html:
Toast comes first, at the door, and then the rain: that is the order, every time. By the second pace there was water running down a window that faced a brick wall, and by the fifth the light had gone the color of tea, and I heard my sister behind me, counting under her breath in the voice she uses on stairs.

“Six. Seven. Eight. Nine.”

“Nine,” I said.

“I know. I counted.” She stopped on the worn path in the oak boards with her hands pushed into the back pockets of her jeans, and looked at the room the way she looks at a client’s kitchen from the door. Floor. Walls. Exits. Anything on the floor that could take an old person’s foot.

It was Saturday the fifteenth. On Thursday I had put a note through the flap marked LETTERS, asking whether I might bring a guest, and on Friday morning the answer had come out folded in three, on yellow paper, in the round hand. Bring her. I’d like to see the face that goes with the voice. M. Rafa had taken down the key with the green tag at ten and had written Guest in the Purpose column of his clipboard. Last time I had written Depends. He looked at the word for a while, and nodded, and did not come in.

Anjali and I had counted the corridor first, thirty-one paces from the 4A mat, she in her stair voice and I under my breath, and at the door she had stopped and looked at the brass 4 and the slightly crooked B. “Okay,” she said. “It’s a door.” She is the only person I know who can make that sentence sound like a diagnosis.

“Right then,” said Margie.

She stood up from the wing chair with the dent in it. She was a head taller than I was and she stooped from forty years of desks. The oatmeal cardigan had its third button missing and the glasses were on their cord and the big hands hung at her sides, not knowing what to do with a visitor. Behind her the clock said ten past four. Under the window the radiator knocked, and on the shelf over the sink stood the ten white teacups. The curtains in the bay were the oatmeal ones, lined, thirty-eight by sixty-two. “You’ll be the sister,” she said.

“Anjali.”

“I know, dear. I heard you introduce yourself to a wall.”

My sister did something I had never seen anyone do in that room. She took the kitchen chair with the tied cushion, the low one, and turned it a quarter, so that she sat at an angle to Margie rather than in front of her, with her knees tilted and her hands open in her lap and her head a little below Margie’s. It is how she sits for a child on the floor. “Tell me about your day,” she said.

“My day?”

“What happens. When you wake up. What matters. What gets in the way.”

I have watched Margie be dry and I have watched her be exact. I had not seen her be delighted. “Nobody has asked me that,” said Margie, “since the twenty-ninth of August, 2019. I should say that it doesn’t begin. It’s ten past four, dear. There’s rain. I make tea. I listen to the others. Nils taps in the pipe, and Inez sings on what I take to be Wednesdays. Mr Ambler’s wireless has the ball game on and I know the score by heart. I write things down.” She sat, slowly, as one who has been waiting. “Mostly it’s what the clerk is doing. Lately that’s been a good deal.”

“Who else do you hear?” said Anjali.

“Vera hums three notes, and I have never found out the song. Wendell whistles the quarter hour, though we have no quarter hours. Constance does Lady Macbeth on Tuesdays and Cole Porter on Fridays, and Hector snores like a bus idling at a stop. Mr Whitmore says almost nothing, which I find restful.” She looked at the row of cups. “Only as sounds, dear. Like a family in a house with thin walls.”

“That’s most families,” said Anjali, and tilted her head at the knocking. “Is that the radiator? It’s on the wrong interval. It needs bleeding.”

“Rafa’s never been in.”

“Then I’d like it seen to,” said Margie, and I understood that it was the second thing she had asked for in a week.

“You’ve a little one,” she said. She had seen the photograph on Anjali’s phone lock screen, a small girl in a pink kurta holding a clay lamp as if it might be taken from her.

“Tia. She’s four. She thinks my brother is a spreadsheet.”

“He is a very orderly one,” said Margie. “I’ve read fourteen of his receipts.”

They talked for twenty minutes, and I will not put down all of it. I will put down the part where my sister said she was tired, which she had not said to me. She said it flatly, looking at the teacups: I’m so tired, Margie. Not of the work. Of being the one who knows where everything is.

“Of course you are,” said Margie. “I wasn’t taken, dear, I should say that to you before anything. Nobody took me. I stepped in. I didn’t want a retirement party or a funeral. I wanted a room where nobody would say how are you, Margie, because then I would have to answer.” She turned her cup on its saucer. “Don’t confuse being tired with being alone. I did. They look the same from the inside. This is a very good room for being tired. It has been a poor one for the other.”

My sister did not say anything. After a moment she nodded, once, and got up, and went to the window to look at the radiator.

Margie touched my sleeve. At the card table she poured me a cup from the brown pot and took down from the shelf over the sink a long ledger with a cloth spine, the kind that has not been made since the clerk’s office had a rubber stamp. It fell open where it had been opened before.

HT-4B | Nov. 1998 | Rent received: cash | Paid From: me | E. Kwan

In the margin, in pencil, in a small slanted hand: It asks who.

“This is Ellis’s,” she said, low, with her eyes on my sister’s back. “I found it in the desk in January of ’99. I want you to understand what it says. I’ll say it plain, as nobody said it to me.”

I am setting it down here for you, whoever you are, at the desk, because I wish somebody had set it down for me in those words, and because the folder tabbed NEXT is empty and I would rather you did not find it so. This is what she said.

“There are three fields, dear. You’ve done the count. A floor plan says the room is there. A permit says that somebody allowed it. Each one is an entry and each one is charged, as you know. And then the last, the thing at the end that asks whom.”

“Source of Funds,” I said. “That’s what it’s called now. The default is PREPARER.”

“Then you’ll have run out of preparer by the time you get there. I had, after twenty-one years.” She had not touched the tea. “Ellis said me, in ’98. He had the plan and the count, he’d made them himself. He never found the permit. He was twelve years in by then and there wasn’t anything left in his drawer, and the book asked, and he wrote the only name he had. The building took him whole and certified nothing. It doesn’t certify in installments, dear. Have all three before you answer the question.”

“The sheet A-4 draws the riser eleven feet wide. Gary says that’s a unit. And I have the number off the window.”

“Mr Whitmore is a sensible man. Yes. You have the plan and the permit, and you’ve paid, I think, rather a lot for both already.” She tapped the ledger. “It goes in a certain order. The drawer first, which is what you stopped looking at. Then the shelf, which is what you look at on Tuesdays. And when those are spent, it takes whoever you’d miss.”

From behind the shelf, from inside the wall, came a small dry sound, a pencil going along a line.

“That’s Ellis,” said Margie, without turning. “He’s in the margins. I can hear him writing.”

“What does it take?” I said. “If I answer. What does the building do with a person?”

“It files them. It doesn’t make change, and it doesn’t ask. If you spend a person on a sum that wanted a mug, the rest is simply gone.” She said it as she said everything, as a thing about books. “I’m not trying to frighten you. I’m telling you what’s in the column.”

The sum was bigger than what was left in my drawer. I did the arithmetic that I have always done, with my lips closed. Six flags had cost a ring of keys and a kitchen drawer. Forty flags had cost a home. Two fields and the question would cost more than any forty flags, and I had already spent the drawer, and the shelf, and some of what stood behind the shelf, and I did not like the figure.

“Mr Grieve is in the hospital,” I said. “He’d like to come in. He wants to meet Mr Ambler. He wants to know what sugar he takes.”

“Then that’s for Mr Ambler to say, dear, not for me. He’s the host.” Something went across her face that was not quite a smile. “Ask him at four. Don’t be solemn about it, he takes it for a bad quarter.”

“And you, Margie?” I said. “If it were certified. If there were a door that worked. Would you come out?”

For a while the only sound was the rain.

“You want to rescue everybody, dear. I noticed it in the receipts. You take the long way round a bus stop so as not to walk past a man.” She said it gently. “Some of us want the radiator. Ask Mr Ambler. Ask Nils, if you can get him to stop tapping. A door is only worth having if it opens both ways, and only if the person it opens for walks through of his own accord. You’ll have to ask them one at a time, and you’ll have to believe what they say.”

“Margie,” said my sister, from the window.

She had come back across the oak. She stood by the card table with her hands at her sides, not folded, and she was looking at Margie’s face and not at mine. “Take it out of me. Whatever it is. If it has to come from someone, take it out of me.”

I did not say anything. I had a mouthful of tea, and I swallowed it.

“That isn’t how it’s written, dear,” said Margie.

She looked at me. I looked at her. She said nothing, and I said nothing, and I will say for Margie Dunleavy that she did not lie to my sister and did not tell her the truth, and that it was the kindest thing anybody did that day.

Then she got up and went along the shelf of what the clerks had lost, past the keys and the gift card and the white mug, and took something down from the end. It was the size of a matchbox. The label on it was in my capitals.

“I’ve had this since the twelfth of October,” said Margie. “I didn’t think it was mine to play.”

MUMMY 1/11 9:41.

My sister, who was beside me, did not look at it. She looked at the clock instead, and the clock said ten past four.

The display above Left said 4B while we were still in the corridor, and then 4, when the doors opened. Anjali walked in ahead of me and put her back to the mirrored wall.

“Okay,” she said to the car. “Okay.”

In Chioma’s bathroom I sat on the edge of the tub with the door locked and the taps off. I opened my hand. It was a plastic cassette not much bigger than a book of matches, scuffed at one corner, with a window onto a brown reel that had not moved in twenty-two months. I read the label. Block capitals, my own, level and a little too careful: the building had written it for me, in my hand, though not with any hand that I remember.

Twenty-three seconds, according to my phone. I knew the figure the way you know your own weight.

I put it in the pocket of the raincoat, against the lining, where the name was.

“Later,” I said, to the tub.

chapters.title: Sugar for the Gentleman
chapters.html:
The hospital’s wheelchair had a number stenciled on its back, HC-0447, and a strip of tape reading PROPERTY OF MERROW GENERAL, and Mr Grieve had already asked twice whether he was permitted to take it out of the county. It rolled over the oval of carpet worn to canvas in front of the window in 6A on Monday evening and stopped where his own chair had stopped for thirty-six years. He looked down at 31st Street, at the bus shelter and the wet black road, and said “Quite so,” as if the street had given a satisfactory answer.

They had sent him home with an oxygen concentrator that hummed like a refrigerator, a hospital bed that Rafa and Owen Fenske had carried up in two pieces and put together in the front room under the window, and a pamphlet. Priscilla Obi had come down from 5E in her scrubs to look at the dials. I had seen her twice in fourteen months, in the elevator, with her hood up. She read the pamphlet standing, and put it in the bin, and showed Chioma and Anjali how to turn a man in a bed without hurting the shoulder. “I’m on nights,” she said to the room, which was the longest speech I had heard from her. “Knock on the floor.”

“I would like to go on Tuesday,” said Mr Grieve. “At four.”

“Mr Grieve—”

“Strictly speaking, Mr Mahajan, I have asked, and you have said you would ask, and I should like the answer.” He had the cannula in, and the tweed waistcoat on over the pajama top, and the brass duck across his knees. “Not in the abstract. At four.”

I had gone in alone at five to four that afternoon, nine in and nine out, and found Mr Ambler in his shirtsleeves by the radio with the ball game on and a pencil behind one ear. I said there was a gentleman in the building who sent him tea, and that the gentleman was unwell, and would like very much to shake his hand. Mr Ambler put the pencil down. He said, “The fellow with the tea,” and then, “Well, I’ll be.” He said he would ring down for a tray. He said Tuesday would suit him, since his afternoon calls were all in, and that I should tell the fellow not to trouble about a hat.

On Tuesday we carried him, because the threshold of the door is a hand’s height and a wheelchair is not a thing that the room will let in. Chioma and I made a seat of our crossed hands and took him down from the corridor chair like a man being carried out of a river, and he weighed what a coat weighs on a hanger. Rafa folded the chair. He stood with it under his arm in the corridor with the key in the lock, as he had stood on the twenty-third of October, and gave me the face of a man at a funeral, and a nod.

“Count in,” I said.

“Nine,” said Mr Grieve, who had been counting since the corridor. Chioma carried the oxygen in a canvas bag over her shoulder, like a sack of mail. It was thirty-one paces to the door, and nine from the door to the window, and on the ninth I heard a ball game, small and cheerful, and a man’s voice say, “Well, there he is.”

It was the same room I had been in on the twenty-seventh of October, the striped paper and the chenille bed and the sample case, and the window with the green HARWICK awning and the tan Pontiac below it. There was a hotel tray on the table by the radio with two cups, a pot under a cozy, a bowl of cubes with tongs, and a plate of soda crackers. I did not see who had brought it. I have stopped asking the room how.

Mr Ambler had put on his jacket. He had pulled the bow tie off the hook and tied it, a little crooked. He came around the bed with his hand out, round-faced and brisk, the wet side parting combed across, and then he saw the cannula and slowed, and said, “Sir, are you ill?”

“Strictly speaking,” said Mr Grieve, “I am concluding.” Chioma had set him in the hotel armchair. He took the hand that was held out, in both of his. “Ptolemy Grieve. The P is silent.”

“Tol-uh-mee. Thaddeus Ambler, Rosewell Dental Supply, Dayton, Ohio—”

“Of Dayton, Ohio. A salesman. I know. I have had the pleasure of knowing it for a long time.”

“Good man,” said Mr Ambler. “Good man. You’re the one with the tea. I’ve been wanting to say thank you for I don’t know how long.” He glanced at me. “Mr Mahajan. The floss gentleman.”

“Technically I’m the buyer.”

“He is a very good buyer, Mr Mahajan,” said Mr Ambler. “He paid thirty-five cents and didn’t ask for change.”

Mr Grieve took the pot. His hands shook, and Chioma took one step and he looked at her and she stepped back. He lifted the cozy and poured, one cup and then the other, and put down the pot and took up the tongs. “I have been sending you this cup for thirty-six years, Mr Ambler, and have never once seen it drunk. Permit me.” He lowered a cube into the saucer’s edge and held the tongs up. “Two lumps. You take two lumps, I think.”

“Two, thank you,” said Mr Ambler.

I want it on the record that nobody had told him. I do not know if he was right, or if the room was being kind, or if there is any difference in a room like that, and I have decided it is not a question with an answer. He put in the second cube. His hand did not shake at all.

They talked for ten minutes. I have written down some of it on the pad, and the rest I will not need to. The home nine were two up in the sixth. “I follow the local nine, Mr Ambler,” said Mr Grieve, “which is a form of mourning.” Mr Ambler laughed so hard he had to put down his cup. He offered to sell Mr Grieve a gross of floss, and Mr Grieve said that he had his own teeth, and had had them since 1948, and Mr Ambler said that a man with his own teeth at his age was a credit to the profession. And then, because the plate of soda crackers had been going round, Mr Ambler said, “I’ll tell you the hotel has been doing a decent biscuit lately. A sort of plain sweet one. It used to be nothing but soda crackers.”

“A Rich Tea,” said Mr Grieve.

“That’s it.”

“I have sent you a Rich Tea at four o’clock every afternoon since 1989.”

Mr Ambler looked at the plate, and at him. “Those were yours? I took it for the hotel improving.” He put his hand over his mouth, and laughed, and then did not. “Well. Well, that’s the best thing that’s happened to me in some time.”

It is the best thing I have ever watched two people do. I have watched people sign leases and I have watched Brent from Tenantry say super at a camera. I have never seen anything better than two lumps.

“There is a matter,” said Mr Grieve, “that I should like to place on the record.”

The ball game had gone to a commercial. Mr Ambler turned down the radio, with a look at the black telephone on the night table that I recognized from my first visit and had not understood. “In 1994,” said Mr Grieve, “I wrote to Dayton. To the register of deaths for the county. I had a name and a date of arrival. I should have asked first, and I did not.” The cough took him, and let him go. “Lorna Ambler died in the spring of 1979. I am so sorry. I have known for thirty-one years and I did not know how to say it.”

Mr Ambler looked at the telephone. He picked up the cup and looked into it. “I thought as much,” he said quietly. “I couldn’t tell you when I began to. The cables stopped being answered. A woman who answers a telephone in Dayton doesn’t let it ring twelve times.”

Nobody said anything. In the pipes behind the wall someone tapped once, a long way off, and stopped.

“I’m waiting anyway,” said Mr Ambler. “I hope you’ll understand. If I step out of this room, the call’s gone. It rings and there’s no one.”

“Then I shall take your call,” said Mr Grieve. “On Sundays, at a quarter past four. As long as I am able.”

Mr Ambler pulled the hotel pad over, and wrote, and tore off the sheet and held it out. HARWICK 6A, in a salesman’s slanting hand. Mr Grieve read it with his lips and folded it into his waistcoat. “Quite so,” said Mr Ambler.

I did not ask how a telephone from 1961 would find a number from this year. I had stopped asking the room how.

At the door, with Chioma’s arms under Mr Grieve and mine under his knees, I turned around. I had thought about what I would say for three days, and I said it plainly, as one says the name of a guest at the head of a table. “Thaddeus Ambler.” He looked at me over the cup. I should say that the door was not finished. I did not say it as an order and I did not say it as an offer. “If there were a door that went out onto 31st Street, in daylight, a proper one. Would you come?”

He thought about it properly, which was why I asked him. “I’m obliged to you, Mr Mahajan. I truly am.” He set the cup in its saucer. “But I think not. I’d rather be in the room it rings in.”

That was the first answer anyone in that room had given me, and I wrote it down on the pad with a crossed seven in the date.

Mrs Han, Zofia and Chioma took shifts at the bed in 6A that evening, with Priscilla Obi on the chair by the door from eleven, and Anjali beside her with her hands loose in her lap. Rafa made coffee in the kitchen with the toothpick in his mouth. At half past one Mr Grieve asked for the steno pad.

He dictated slowly, with his eyes on the ceiling, as he must have heard it in a thousand court rooms, and I wrote it in longhand. When I had finished he made me read it back, and corrected a comma.

Let the record show that I, Ptolemy Grieve, of 6A Harwick Terrace, being of sound mind and indifferent lungs, was attended. I leave to Devendra Mahajan the steno pads, ninety-one of them unused, the dictation recorder, and the tenancy of this apartment, at the pleasure of the management, who is requested not to be difficult. The cane to Mrs Han, who will need something to point with. The watch to Miss Eze, who has the better use for time. The clocks are to be left as they are.

“Is that correct?” said Mr Grieve.

“Yes.”

“I did not ask you,” he said. “I asked the record.” He moved his hand on the blanket, and found the saucer on the bed table, with its cold cup, and let his fingers rest on the rim.

At ten to four he asked what time it was, and Zofia said, “Is nearly,” and measured his wrist with the tape, without a word, and wrote it in her book. At four Mrs Han said, “Good morning, Mr Grieve,” in the voice she uses for the chat, and he said “Quite so.” I looked down at the pad to write the time. When I looked up, at ten past four by the gold watch that I had in my hand, the saucer had been turned. The handle pointed left. His fingers were on the rim and he had stopped breathing.

Priscilla Obi looked at her own watch and wrote it down, and said the time aloud, for the record, and then none of us said anything. Chioma took his hand. The concentrator went on humming in the next room, a long time, until Rafa went in and switched it off.

At four that afternoon Mrs Han went up to the fourth floor with the plate. She carried it in both hands, the cup and the saucer with the rose and one Rich Tea, as she carries the thermos, in front of her chest. She had put on the church blouse again. I stood on the stair landing below the ledge with Chioma and Zofia. She set it down, and turned the handle of the saucer to the left, as she had been shown.

“Four o’clock, Mr Ambler,” she said. “Mr Grieve sends his regards.”

She went down. I did not go with her. At ten past, I climbed the half-flight and looked.

The cup was warm and empty. The Rich Tea was gone. The saucer had been turned, and the handle pointed left: yes.

chapters.title: Too Much Dal
chapters.html:
The church hall had folding tables, a serving hatch with a roller shutter, an urn of coffee the size of a fire hydrant, and thirty-eight residents of Harwick Terrace in their coats. I knew the figure because Mrs Han had made me count them at the door, so she could mark them present. There were more than thirty-eight, in fact. There was Woo-jin Cho of Larchmont, at the back by the coat rack, in a black tie, standing.

Mr Grieve had died on Wednesday morning and was being buried on Thursday for two reasons. The first was that in 1994 he had prepared a binder. It lived on the shelf in 6A between the steno bundles for February and March, with tabs from A to K, and it was titled PTOLEMY GRIEVE: ARRANGEMENTS (REV. 1994; AMENDED 2009; AMENDED AGAIN IN OCTOBER). The second was that Mr Danziger of Danziger & Sons had had a cancellation, which he reported to Noreen without any visible shame. The binder specified the hymn, the hall, the sandwiches, and the form of service, and Chioma had the typed sheet.

ORDER OF SERVICE: Hymn (one verse; I have made my views known). A reading of the morning greeting by Mrs Han. Remarks, not to exceed four minutes each, timed by Miss Eze with the watch. Tea. Strictly no flowers.

We sang one verse. Mrs Han climbed onto a step stool that she had brought in her bag, in the quilted vest and the jade pin, and read in her capitals, in a voice that could have taken the roof off, “GOOD MORNING TO ALL, INCLUDING THE QUIET ONES.” Then she looked at the closed box at the front of the hall and said, in her ordinary voice, “Good morning, Mr Grieve.”

Rafa spoke first, in the suit he had borrowed from a brother. “Mira,” he said. “Mr Grieve was a man who knew what sugar a person took before he asked. I fixed his tap in 2011. He gave me tea and he said, strictly speaking, the leak was in the washer and not the tap, and he was right, and I have been thinking about that for fourteen years—”

“Time,” said Chioma, holding the gold hunter watch open in her palm.

“I haven’t said it yet.”

“Four minutes.”

“I was at two.”

“You were at four, Rafa. He’d have stopped you at three.”

Rafa sat. The hall laughed, the kind of laughter that has crying behind it like a second room.

The sandwiches came from Tab F: egg salad, in triangles, with the crusts off, crusts being, according to the binder, a form of aggression. Zofia ate three and measured the length of the buffet table with her eyes. Owen Fenske, in a tie I had never seen, sang the one verse a half-beat behind everybody and a third flat, with total conviction. Anjali sat beside me on a folding chair with her coat folded over her knee, and when Mrs Han said Good morning, Mr Grieve she put her hand on mine on the seat between us and left it there.

Afterward, at the urn, Noreen tapped a plastic stirrer on her cup. She had the lanyard around her neck and both hands on the cup. “I want you to hear this from me and not from a memo,” she said. “If the Larchmont sale closes on Monday, I won’t be staying on. I have thirty-one months to my pension. I’ve decided I would like to spend them somewhere else.” Nobody said anything. Mrs Han inclined her head, the way a general does when told of the loss of a position. Noreen added, to the urn, “I’m sorry. I should have said a lot of things a lot sooner.”

I went to the back. “You didn’t have to come.”

“The binder has a dress code.” Woo had a hand at his badge reel. “Black or, failing black, brown. Anyone who has been in the building in an official capacity wears a black tie.” He looked at the box. “I counted that as me. I read the footnotes. Footnote nine concerns the Larchmont person, whoever he may be, and states that he is to be given tea.”

“Did you have some?”

“I am waiting to be asked.” So I asked, and he had two cups, with sugar, and wrote nothing down.

At noon I went up to the roof of Harwick by the steel door that sticks. It was between the church hall and the cab, and I had forty minutes. The tar paper was wet, and a pigeon sat on a vent, and the water tank stood on its stilts. From the parapet you could see the beltway and the roof of Halloran’s and the bus shelter on 31st Street, small and bright, and on the other side of the parapet the fourth floor, bay 2, the infill of lighter brick, from above.

I sat on an upturned bucket. The pigeon watched me out of one orange eye and did not leave. From the pocket of the raincoat I took Mr Grieve’s dictation recorder. It was the size of a bar of soap, and he had left it to me with the steno pads, and it still had the cord wound round it. I unwound the cord. From the other pocket I took the microcassette with my block capitals on the label. I do not know how I knew it would fit. It fit. It went in with a small, definite click, like a key.

I pressed Play with my thumb, the split one.

There was a hiss, the sound of a small room somewhere with the door open. Then my mother.

Dev, beta, it’s Mummy. I made too much dal, so, if you’re passing, no, never mind, it’s the wrong day, Anjali says you’re busy Thursdays. Call me when you can. No rush. Okay. Bye bye bye.

That is all of it. I have copied it here exactly, and I have not corrected her. It was twenty-three seconds. She was slow, with the long pauses of a woman on a great deal of morphine, and she was pleased, in the way she was pleased when she had made a pot of something for a boy who might be passing. There was no dal. I knew that, I think I knew it on the roof as a fact, my mother had not stood at a stove since Thanksgiving, and the kitchen had belonged to the aunties for weeks. She had made it in her mind. It was a Thursday in my childhood and I was a person who might drop in.

I had been afraid for twenty-two months of a sentence. It was not in the tape. There was nothing in it that I could have answered and failed to answer. There was a request that I call, when I could, with no rush.

I listened to it nine times. I counted, naturally. The fifth time I heard Anjali says you’re busy Thursdays, and understood that my sister had told our mother where I would be, and had told her kindly, and had never mentioned it to me. On the ninth time I did not listen to the words at all. I listened to the last few seconds after bye bye bye and before the click, in which, as far as I could tell, she was still holding the phone.

The curb at Departures was wet and loud with taxis. Anjali’s flight was the 6:15 and we were two hours early, because she cannot be late, and because Tia’s pageant was on Friday morning. “She’s a sweet potato,” said my sister, getting the suitcase out of the cab. “She has one line. ‘I am a sweet potato.’ She’s been practicing for two weeks and it’s gone to a whisper and Ben says, Mommy has to be there to hear it.”

She took the coat off the cab seat, the navy one, and did not put it on. She held it. She put the suitcase upright.

“Tell Chioma she’s to take her glasses off when she sleeps. She wakes up with a mark on her nose, I saw it.”

“I’ll tell her.”

“And tell Margie I’ll be back for the radiator. Don’t say it like a promise. Say it like a work order.”

“Technically that’s what a work order is.”

She looked at me, and then she did what she has done at train stations since I was seven, and took my face in both hands, and pulled it down, because she has to reach.

“Sunday at six.”

“Six.”

“I mean it. If you don’t pick up I’ll get on a plane and sit in your lobby, and I’ll bring Tia, and she’ll tell everyone you’re a spreadsheet.”

“Technically—”

“Don’t.” From the tote on her shoulder she took the blue-lidded container, in its bath towel. “I made it Tuesday night in Chioma’s pan. It’s too much. I know it’s too much. Don’t microwave it on high. A splash of water, medium.” She put it in my arms. “I’m not flying with it.”

I stood with the dal against my chest. I opened my mouth. I had the sentence; it had three clauses and her name in the second one. She watched my face with her head a little on one side, as she watches a child about to say the thing it has been rehearsing.

“You’re doing the thing,” she said.

“What thing?”

“Where you start a sentence and end up in a drawer.”

“I’m fine.”

“Okay,” said my sister. “Okay. Say it back.”

“Sunday at six, Anju.”

She kissed me on the cheek, hard, and went in. The doors opened for her and closed and opened for the next person and closed. I counted them, because I count. Eleven. A man in a high-vis vest came from the next lane with a whistle in his hand and asked whether I was all right, and I said that technically I was parked in a loading zone, and he said that wasn’t what he’d asked.

Noreen had given me the key to 6A in an envelope after the hall. 6A. Temporary. Lease to follow. N. I sat at Mr Grieve’s desk at ten to nine under six clocks that said eight forty-four, eight forty-seven, and four others. The recorder was in front of me with the cord wound round it again, and the stenotype slept under its dust cloth. I had not turned on a lamp. At eight I had said my name aloud to the six clocks, as Chioma requires, and typed it as well, and she had sent back from the break room at Merrow General Good. Sleep., which was not an instruction I intended to follow.

At 8:51 by my own phone, which was right, the screen lit on the blotter. ANJU. I looked at it.

I want it on the record that I let it ring. I want it noted that I knew, exactly as I had known in January, what I was doing. In January I let it ring because I was in the middle of a question. On the twentieth of November I let it ring because I was in the middle of an answer, and if I had heard her voice I would have given it to her. It rang eleven times and stopped. Then, after a minute, the phone buzzed once and a small red number appeared.

My sister has never left a voicemail in her life. She calls back. She says leaving them is for people who have time.

Landed. Tia’s asleep on Ben. You are an idiot and I love you. Call me Sunday at six or I will fly back and sit in your lobby. Okay. Okay. Bye.

I listened to all of it. It was the first voicemail I had played on the night it was left since the eleventh of January last year. At the end a woman’s voice said that I might save the message by pressing nine, and I pressed nine.

I had known since Saturday what the last field would ask. I understood that sitting there. I had not been putting off the entry. I had been putting off the answer.

I took the tape out of the recorder and put it in the pocket of the raincoat, with the collar that had my name in it. I went down six flights by the stairs and unlocked the office. The night-drop safe ticked. The blinds were down and the vision board was dark. I put the tape in the sticking drawer with the lemon-drop tin and the horn button, and the drawer stuck, and gave. I do not know what the building would have done with it. I know where I wanted it.

Then I sat down in the chair that fits my spine because it fit hers, and turned on the monitor, and logged in as the clerk. HT-4B came up red at the bottom of the roll, where it had been since the sixth of October, and I put my hands on the keys.

The cursor in the FLOORPLAN_ID field blinked once a second, white on pale gray, at about the rate of a pulse that has been asked to wait. I had been watching it since ten past ten. At half past, the others came in.

I had texted each of them at nine: I am going to do the last field tonight, in the office, at 10:30. You don’t have to say anything. Rafa answered Voy. Noreen answered Okay. with the period, which in her is a speech. Chioma answered No, then Mahajan, then Trading my shift.

Noreen wheeled Joyce’s chair to my left elbow and sat with the lanyard in both hands, the fourteen keys quiet in her lap. Rafa unfolded the canvas chair he had brought on the night of the twenty-third and sat by the filing room door with the thermos between his boots and a toothpick he was not using. Chioma stayed on her feet in green scrubs under a parka. She had given the last six hours of her shift to a respiratory tech named Dwayne for a Saturday in January, a rate she described, for the record, as extortion.

The blinds were down, and the night-drop safe ticked in its corner the way it does when the building cools. I had the plan sheet from the Annex flat under the keyboard and the half sheet from my wallet beside it. I typed HT-A4-L4-R4, which is sheet A-4, level four, riser R-4, and pressed Tab.

FLOORPLAN_ID resolved: HT-A4-L4-R4 (Harwick Terrace, plan sheet A-4, level 4, riser R-4, 1986). Footprint 11.0 ft x 22.0 ft. 1 of 3 required fields remains.

“Eleven by twenty-two,” said Chioma, over my shoulder. “That’s a room.”

“It’s nine paces,” I said. “If you’re me.” I saved.

It did not hurt, and I want to be exact about that. There was a dull ache low in the chest, like standing in a room where someone has left a window open, and the smell of toast came out of the corner by the filing room, thick enough to taste, and thinned. Then I tested it, as I had after every entry since the sixth of October, because I am a clerk and that is the discipline. I thought of my father.

He was a cardigan with worn elbows. He was a steel tumbler, and a flat palm raised at the end of a table: no thank you, go on. I could put the palm in its place and the cardigan under it, and I could not put anything above the collar. Where a face goes there was a gray rectangle with clean edges, like the patch on a wall where a picture has hung for years and been taken down.

“What did it take?” said Noreen.

“My father’s face.” I heard how that sounded. “Technically I hadn’t looked at it in a year.”

“Oh, hon.”

“He’s fine. He’s in Edison. It’s only my copy that’s—” Chioma had put a hand on the back of my chair. She did not say anything, which for her is a large gesture.

The permit number took longer. I typed BP-1986-04417 from the half sheet, although I knew it, and Tenantry went out to the county with its small blue wheel and came back with a green tick.

PERMIT_NO verified: BP-1986-04417. Infill existing window opening, north elevation, level 4, bay 2. Status: FINAL. 3 of 3 required fields complete.

“It is a window,” said Rafa.

“A system only checks the number.” Mrs Tuck had told me that in October. The work was a quarter inch of extra mortar and some lighter brick, and as far as I could tell that was plenty.

I saved, and this one went through the drawer. For a month I had carried six names the way you carry a coin you have found and not spent. They were in the notebook, in my hand, from the nineteenth of October: Priya. Big Ted. Lorraine. Amir. Femi. Hae-won, who did the music rounds. I started saying them as the ache came on, to hold on, and I had Priya and Big Ted, and by Lorraine I was reading names off a page, and by Hae-won they belonged to a book I had not read. Then there was a table for nine in a bar, and I could not have told you I had ever sat at it. I know from the notebook that I did, on Tuesdays, for six years. I remember only that the notebook says so.

That was the last of what I had not been looking at. I knew it before the screen did.

Selection will be debited at settlement, 02:10. This action cannot be undone.

Grieve’s line had a stroke through it, gray on gray, like a name on an invoice already paid.

“Mira, I’m on it?” said Rafa. “I oil a key.”

“You oil it every morning at seven. Technically that’s the most attention anybody has paid a piece of hardware in the history of the building.”

“Depends who’s asking,” said Rafa, not steadily, and put the toothpick in his mouth to have something to do with it.

I did what I do with a column. I sorted it.

“Self first, because it’s the only one that’s mine to spend. It would balance. It would be the cleanest entry I’ve ever made. And then there’s a chair at that desk with nobody in it.” Nobody looked at the chair. “From 2019 to 2024 there wasn’t a clerk, and the elevators failed and the pipes froze twice. On the nineteenth, at 23:58, somebody has to post the rent for everyone in that room. If it’s me, I’m in there with them, and nobody does.”

I looked at each of them. “And the four of you. You’re the reason I’m sitting here and not on a shelf. Spend Chioma and I lose the roll call. Spend Rafa and I lose the key. Mrs Han has the chat and Zofia the thread. I can’t afford any of you.”

“Which leaves one,” said Noreen. She had not taken her eyes off the screen.

“She has a husband,” I said. “A daughter. A clinic full of children who tell her they’re fine. Our mother’s recipe cards on the refrigerator. She has a whole life that stands up without me. I made sure of that. I’ve stood a little to one side of it for fourteen months so as not to be in the way, and there’s a place in it the shape of a man who rings on Sundays, and it will close. It’s the only line on the list where the loss falls on someone who can go on.”

“Don’t say it like that.”

“It’s what it is.”

“Then take it from me.” She had come forward in the chair. “I mean it, hon. I owe this building more than anyone alive, and I’m the one who hired you knowing. Let it be mine.”

“It doesn’t take what’s offered. It takes what I’d miss.”

“Then miss me.”

“I do,” I said. “That’s why you’re on it. And in the morning you have to stand at a door and say a name, and if I spend you, you won’t know why you came.”

She sat back. She said “Okay. Okay,” and not the third.

“For the record,” said Chioma, “I’m not going to tell you not to.” She had her arms folded across the parka, the red frames pushed up into her twists. “I don’t tell people what to give. But you are not picking her because she’ll be fine.” Her voice had gone quiet, which was worse than loud. “You’re picking her because she’s the only one who can’t come down here and stop you.”

I looked at the line that said Mahajan Kowalczyk, and at the cursor.

“Yes,” I said. “That’s also true. I don’t know how to make the second one lighter by pretending about the first.”

“I know they’re both true,” said Chioma. “That’s why I’m this angry.”

She went out. The glass door swung on its closer for a long time and settled. She came back in twenty-five minutes with two cups from the basement machine, which had refused my card since the sixth of November and had taken hers, and put one by my keyboard. “I wanted to be angry somewhere with a vending machine. It’s tea. It’s terrible. Drink it.” She sat down on the floor with her back against the filing room door, beside Rafa’s boots. “I’m not here to approve. I’m here because afterward somebody has to be the first to say it.”

“Say what?”

“Your name, Mahajan. Obviously.”

I took the phone into the filing room and played my sister’s message once more. I had listened to the words. This time I heard the baggage carousel under them: a rubber belt, a buzzer, a woman walking with a suitcase in one hand and a small backpack in the other. She said Okay. Okay. twice, as she does, to make sure a thing is set down. She had been carrying everything else the whole time.

At 11:58 I sat down. I had not chosen the minute. I understood by the second keystroke that it was no accident: it was the minute at which my login had posted the rent on the nineteenth of every month for fourteen months. I clicked the last line but one. The dropdown closed and a box opened, which was the Delete dialog of the seventh of October in a different coat.

CONFIRM SOURCE OF FUNDS. Type the full name of the selected source to confirm.

In October, at that box, I had typed 4 and B and stopped. Now I typed Anju. It fit the field. I looked at it for as long as a cursor takes to blink six times, and I deleted it a letter at a time, because the box wanted her name as it appears on a lease. I typed Anjali Mahajan Kowalczyk. Twenty-two letters. I counted them as I went.

Noreen’s hand came across and lay flat on my phone on the blotter, face down, the way you cover a pot. I had not been going to pick it up. I saved.

POSTED. Pending settlement 02:10.

There were two hours and twelve minutes. I want it noted that I could have called her. She would have answered on the second ring and said Dev, what’s wrong, and I would have said nothing, and she would have known from the nothing and gotten on a plane. That was the sum. At twenty to two Noreen said “Okay. Okay. Okay” to the safe, and we went up by the stairs.

We stood on the maroon diamonds in a row, Chioma at my left and Rafa at my right, and Noreen half a step behind with the spare key off her lanyard and in her fist. The beige door stood fourteen paces from the 4A mat with its brass 4 and its B a little out of true. Rafa’s wristwatch, which he has kept to the building’s time out of politeness since 2008, stopped on 2:04. My phone, which keeps true, stopped on 2:10.

The pipes began behind the plaster, and the radiator at the end of the corridor knocked twice, and the corridor began to come in.

I did not try to walk it. It was changing faster than I could pace, so I did what a clerk does and took readings, looking from the mat to the bicycle at 4C and counting by eye, as you judge a field. Thirty-one. The diamonds drew together under our shoes the way Zofia’s tape goes back into its case, steadily, with a faint ratcheting. Twenty-four. The door came toward us, or we toward it. Seventeen. The bicycle bell ticked against the wall. Nine. Then a sound like a long drawer being pushed all the way home, and the door stood in the wall four paces from the mat and four from the bicycle, with one for itself, and the B was straight.

At the west end by the stair, a red hose cabinet stood behind its glass as though it had always been there. “It was always there,” said Rafa, to himself, trying it out.

His watch said 2:11 and moved. Every clock in the building began again at the right time, and I discovered that I minded. I had not known I would miss the six minutes.

Chioma said it before I had put the phone away. “Dev Mahajan,” she said, looking at me, her hand on my sleeve. “Twenty-nine. Fourth floor. Say it back.”

“Dev Mahajan.”

My phone had reloaded itself.
